entries.title: record that WP38's --cpu bar is met once the noise is measured
entries.body:
S2's opt-in `--cpu` level was declined because vec3 came out 0.3% to 1.2% slower at `-march=x86-64-v3`, and the bar allows no loss. wp38 §7 named the measurement that would settle it: a binary timed against itself.

`bench/simd-s0.mjs --self` now takes that measurement. It adds a byte-for-byte copy of the baseline binary as a third column in the -march rows' rotation. The rotation takes any number of builds and rounds the count up to a multiple of it, so each build goes first equally often; with two builds it runs as before.

vec3's dip does not reproduce. In two samples of fifteen rotating rounds on the same machine:
- vec3 gains 1.1% to 1.7% on every figure, while the baseline differs from its own copy by 0.3% at most.
- nbody's only negative figure, −0.8% on the minimum, sits inside the 1.1% by which the baseline missed its own copy in that sample.
- spectral gains about 20%.

So the bar is met. The flag is still not built: its cost is mostly `tests/ct-asm.js` reading every level it accepts, and whether one benchmark's gain is worth that is left to the owner.

entries.title: record that WP38's S4, the lexer on indexOfAny, is declined for now
entries.body:
WP38's S4 would have moved the compiler's lexer onto `indexOf` and `indexOfAny`, which 0.18.0 ships. Its bar is a measurably faster `scripts/bootstrap.sh --verify`, and no lexer change can meet it:
- the lexer is about 1% of the front end;
- the front end's three runs are about 2% of the bootstrap.

A spike put `skipTrivia`'s two comment loops on `indexOf`. It produced the same token stream and identical IR. It made the lexer 4% faster at the minimum, which would save about 1 ms of a 135.6 s bootstrap.

String-literal bodies have `indexOfAny`'s shape too, but they were not measured. The decline rests on the lexer's share, not on that.

`docs/wp38-simd.md` §7 records the decline beside S2's paragraph:
- the figures, the machine and the commit;
- the spike's exact code and how to re-apply it;
- what reopens S4: a front-end profile that shows a scan-bound loop in `src/`, or a bar restated in front-end time.

The status line, §2.2, §4 and §5, `docs/MASTER_PLAN.md` and `docs/README.md` follow it.

`bench/lexer.ts` is new. It lexes one file through `src/lexer.ts` 25 times, with a different text on each pass, and folds every token into a printed checksum and token count. It refuses to time a pass that hits a lexical error. Since `bench/` is in the self-host oracle's corpus, `tests/self/goldens/checked.txt` is regenerated with it. No compiler code changes.
metrics: lexer 9.82 ms min, 11.62 ms median per pass over src/ (2.8 MB, 338,856 tokens, 9 runs of 25); indexOf comment skips 9.46 / 10.50 ms, 4% at the min; front end 919 / 1,046 ms; bootstrap --verify 135,556 ms in one run, lexer about 30 ms of it (0.02%)

entries.title: skip JSON string bodies with a memchr search
entries.body:
A string body in std/json is read a byte at a time for its first 16
bytes and, past them, searched for its closing quote with
s.indexOf("\"", from), one memchr in the runtime. The run of
backslashes before the quote found says whether it is escaped. This
covers keys, string values and strings inside nested values; answers
are byte-identical to before.

A line of short strings only is slower: 4-11% min, 10-18% median,
+18% instructions. It pays the per-string limit check and the
registers the indexOf call costs, and has no long body to skip. The
owner accepted this trade for the gain on every other shape; removing
it is left to a noinline/cold attribute or the WP38 SIMD work.

entries.title: warn when a loop drops an allocation on every pass
entries.body:
A local declared outside a loop and given a new allocation on every pass
drops the value the pass before gave it, and nothing frees that value while
the loop runs. The pass cannot take an arena scope, because its fresh value
outlives it in the local, and a `using a = arena()` block refuses the same
assignment (NL2418), so memory grows with the number of passes:

```ts
let last = "";
for (let i = 0; i < 10000000; i++) {
  last = `item ${i}`;
}
```

This compiled with no warning at all. NL9003 reports an allocation assigned
over an allocation, but only when the local was *declared* holding one, and
`let last = ""` holds a literal. That guard is right for a local given its
one value in a branch, and wrong for a loop, where every value dropped from
the second pass on is the assignment's own.

The new performance warning, NL9016, reports `x = <allocation>` when the
assignment is a statement of its own at the top of a loop body, `x` is a
local declared outside that loop, and nothing in the loop may keep the old
value. It names two rewrites: a `const` inside the loop when only the pass
reads the value, or numbers kept across passes and the value built once
after the loop. It is silent for an assignment in a branch, which may run
once (a search loop's `found = ...` before its `break`), for a body that
runs at most once (one whose top level ends the loop, or a
`do ... while (false)`), and on a line NL9002 or NL9003 already reports.

The capture check that decides both rules now counts a constructor
argument (`head = new Node(i, head)`), either arm of a conditional
(`picks.push(i > 0 ? tag : "none")`), a method called on the value
(`cur.attach(reg)`, which may store `this`; a string's or an array's methods
never do), and anything in the assignment's own right-hand side. NL9003 is
correctly quieter on those shapes, and its counts over the corpus are
unchanged. The rule errs towards silence: a few shapes that do drop a value
every pass (a capture after an inner loop, a `return` inside the loop) are
not yet reported.
metrics: 10,000,000 passes of the loop above peak at 392,156 KB RSS; the rewrite at 11,128 KB
0 warnings over std/, examples/ and src/; 1 over the 2,704 corpus programs, a real drop

entries.title: hold the x25519 timing to its domain and re-measure CT-13
entries.body:
`tests/ct-timing.js` now times each x25519 fixture function on the
inputs `std/crypto/x25519.ts` actually gives it.

- Signed limbs below 2^27 go to `fieldMul`, `fieldSquare` and
  `fieldMulA24`. Signed limbs below 2^26 go to the reduced-element
  functions.
- `swap` and `bit` are masked to one bit.
- Each bound and mask in use carries its own control, a leak written in
  C and emitted by the same `fillArray`/`fillScalar` lines, which must
  differ. A narrowing that erases the secret, or a control that prints
  no reading, fails the run with exit 2.
- CT-12's `expect=branch` control is still required on its own.
- A domain entry that names an untimed function, misses a timed one, or
  narrows a secret the function does not take is refused.

CT-13's |t| = 35–42 reading of `ladderStep` was re-measured on a 4-vCPU
Xeon VM: 34 runs, in domain and out, in the full driver and linked alone,
on today's fixture and on 0d362c59. Every run read 1.46–3.22, and the
weekly CI run read 1.17 (x86-64) and 2.09 (aarch64). The original host
was never re-run and the cause is unmeasured, so CT-13 stays Open as not
reproduced. The record now tabulates every reading, the machine and
harness behind it, and what it does and does not establish.

entries.title: derive the TLS resumption master secret, completing RFC 8448 §3
entries.body:
`TlsServer` now derives `resumption_master_secret`:
`Derive-Secret(master, "res master", ClientHello..client Finished)`, per
RFC 8446 §7.1. It is computed in `sign`, beside the client application
secret and the expected client Finished, and exposed as
`resumptionSecret` only once the client's Finished verifies.
`net_tls_rfc8448` and its f64 twin pin RFC 8448 §3's value
(`7df235f2…`) byte for byte, from the server and from the schedule
alone. A SHA-384 case is pinned too.

The secret lives in a ninth array of the server's secret pool. `fail`
wipes it with `secureZero`, and a test reads the pool array after a
forged Finished to pin that wipe. `restart` wipes it with the rest.
TLS-1 records what the carriers' wipes do not reach: the secret stays in
the slot's array after a connection closes, until the slot's next
`restart`, on TCP and QUIC alike. A `TlsServer` grows by 80 bytes, to
31,192. NewSessionTicket, PSK and 0-RTT remain out of scope.

entries.title: do not hoist a loop's array header across a new whose constructor resizes it
entries.body:
A loop over an array whose body ran `new C(xs)` kept the array's header
hoisted, even when `C`'s constructor pushed to `xs`. So the loop read a
stale length and data pointer. #435's program printed 6 where Node
prints 706.

`callMayResize` now treats a class `new` as a call to its constructor,
using the constructor's fixpoint `resizesArray` fact. The checker
already records that constructor as the node's callee. CG-10's
`rightSideMayResize` is folded into the same predicate, now `mayResize`.

This has two effects:
- Loops over a resizing constructor lose the hoist.
- Compound element stores whose right side holds a non-resizing `new`
  drop the second range check, which no constructor proven not to
  resize can need.

No golden other than the new case moved, and no corpus program other
than the new case changed against main's compiler.

entries.title: run Wycheproof for HMAC and HKDF, and wipe their state
entries.body:
HMAC-SHA-256/384/512 and HKDF-SHA-256/384 now pass Project Wycheproof. Its 522 HMAC cases and 169 HKDF cases are carried at upstream commit 3fa63dd, the same form as the K2/K3/K5 vectors. Each case is checked three ways: one-shot, streaming or scratch, and the new `Secret`-keyed entry points. All three must agree, and the oversized and truncated cases must be refused. HMAC-SHA-512 is new: `HmacSha512`, `hmacSha512` and `hmacSha512Verify`.

HMAC and HKDF now wipe the secret state they used to leave behind:
- HMAC wipes its key block, a long key's hash, the inner digest and both keyed hashers.
- The scratch hashers wipe before every `begin`.
- HKDF-Expand wipes every T(i).
- `hkdfSha256Secret`/`384Secret` wipe the PRK between extract and expand.

`hmacSha*Secret`, `hkdfExtract*Secret`, `hkdfExpand*Secret` and `hkdfSha*Secret` take a `Secret<u8[]>` key and read it only inside `exposeWith`. The plain-array entry points keep their signatures, so no `std/net` caller changes. Moving those callers onto `Secret` is #430's.

A test in `tests/run.js` pins the wipes under `opt -O2`. It counts the volatile wipes reached from 20 roots, and each count must match exactly, so deleting any one wipe turns it red. Docs/security/crypto-k1.md records this as K1-7.

Refs #476

entries.title: compare indexOfAny's non-ASCII byte offset between native and --profile wasi

`indexOfAny` counts bytes both natively and under `--profile wasi`. Node counts UTF-16 units, so the existing Node-compared fixture could not check the non-ASCII edge of the SIMD path, the case #524 raised.

A sibling program, `std_text_index_of_any_non_ascii_offset`, now pins the byte offsets themselves: two-, three- and four-byte characters around the 16- and 32-byte vector boundaries, plus `from` landing on a continuation byte. A wrong offset fails the native run on its own. `tests/run.js` also builds the program under `--profile wasi` and requires the two builds to print the same thing. The program stays out of the Node comparison, and the existing Node-compared line is unchanged.

Fixes #524

entries.title: a method of a non-exported class called from another module links
entries.body:
A value of a non-exported class can reach another module through an exported signature, such as `Conn.space(): Space`. The rule for reachable layouts already lets the importer hold that value and call its methods. Those methods were still emitted `internal`, though. The call passed the checker and then failed at link with `undefined symbol`, whether the two modules were in one package or two.

Now a method that another module calls, or an instantiation of a generic one, gets `hidden` linkage. This is the linkage WP29 already gives a private function that an imported instantiation calls. The final link resolves the method, and the output exports it to nothing. A method that only its own module calls stays `internal`. The call site picks its `Result` ABI from `visibleOutside()`, so a hidden method returning a small `Result` is called with the same ABI it is defined with. The class's name still belongs to its module, so importing it or naming it in an annotation is refused as before.

docs/LANGUAGE.md states the rule under "Linkage": a method another module calls is in the link.

Fixes #442

entries.title: plan WP27 S3, strings across the C boundary
entries.body:
A `declare function` takes scalars and `CPtr` only, so every C API that
takes a name, a path or a message needs a hand-written C shim today. This
adds the plan for S3 to `docs/wp27-ffi.md` (§8); nothing is built yet.

A `string` parameter becomes `const char *`, passed without a copy because
`nish_str` is already NUL-terminated. The string is borrowed: C may read
it until the call returns and must not keep the address. That is a
decision, not a proof, in the same way S1 decided `nounwind`, and §8b
explains why copying every argument would not make it any safer. A string
that holds a NUL byte panics (the new `ffi-nul` kind) rather than being
cut short, and a literal is proved free of the check. A returned
`char *` is copied into the arena, and a `NULL` for a non-nullable
`string` panics (`ffi-null`). A C allocation the caller must free comes
back as a `CPtr` and is read with a new `nish:unsafe` function,
`readCString`. A literal `null` may be passed for a `CPtr | null`
parameter, so `realpath(p, null)` and `setlocale(LC_ALL, null)` become
callable.

The work is three pull requests (S3.1 to S3.3), each listed with its
tests. `string[]`, byte buffers, callbacks and variadic functions stay
refused.

entries.title: refuse retained arena memory with --deny-retention
entries.body:
A long-running program cannot afford arena memory that stays allocated after
nothing can reach it: in a command-line tool it is returned when `main` does,
and in a server it grows until the process is killed. Four performance
warnings are exactly that finding: quadratic string building (NL9002), an
allocation dropped by an assignment (NL9003), a loop over a call that leaves
its memory behind (NL9011) and an allocation dropped on every pass (NL9016).
Until now each was advice a server could ship with.

`--deny-retention` makes each of them an error, NL2462, in the program's own
modules. The error keeps the warning's text after the code of the rule that
found it, so it still names the rewrite:

```
error: `--deny-retention` refuses this NL9016 finding, because the arena
memory it describes stays allocated after nothing in the program can reach it
any more: `last` is given a new allocation on every pass of this loop ...
```

The restated warning is not printed as well, and `--no-warn-performance` does
not silence the error. A dependency's warnings stay warnings, as its panic
sites stay outside the no-panic scope: the program's author cannot change that
code. Like `--deny-panics` it changes no byte of the IR; `nish run` and `--fix`
accept it, and with `--emit-ast`, which stops before the checker, it is a
usage error.

The four rules err towards silence, so a program the flag accepts can still
retain memory in a shape no rule recognises; docs/LANGUAGE.md says so where it
states the rule.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: report where every allocation's memory goes with --emit-arena
entries.body:
The memory model places every allocation by proof, and a performance warning
speaks only where it can name both the memory and a rewrite. Everything else
it decides silently, which left no way to ask the compiler where a given
string's memory goes, or to find retention no rule recognises.

`--emit-arena <file.json>` writes it down: every function, every allocation
site in it, and the placement the emitter gives it, read back from the facts
the build already computes, in the order the emitter applies them:

| Placement | Where the memory goes |
| --- | --- |
| `stack` | an entry-block `alloca` |
| `pass` | released at the end of each pass of a scoped loop |
| `block` | released when a `using a = arena()` block ends |
| `function` | released when the function returns |
| `returned` | handed to the caller with the return value |
| `caller` | released at each call by the caller's reclaim of the returned string |
| `kept` | stored into memory older than the function |
| `unscoped` | released by nothing in this function; in `main`, the rest of the run |

A site that runs pass after pass in a loop that releases nothing per pass,
and whose memory is unreachable before its release, is marked
`"accumulates":true`: the question a long-running program asks first. The
format follows `--emit-panics`: one object, one function per line, a generic
function once per instantiation. Like it, the flag changes no byte of the IR
and is a product, so `nish run`, `--fix` and `--emit-ast` refuse it.

The escape analysis now keeps each arena site's flow beside the site, which
is the one fact the report needed that the analysis used to discard: whether a
value goes to the caller or nothing here releases it.
metrics: over std/ 20 sites accumulate and 16 are unscoped; over the compiler's own source 735 accumulate and 3,789 are unscoped

entries.title: the diagnostic-fix-2 follow-ups — NL9007 wording, uncheckedGet in the range analysis, one-round migration
entries.body:
These are three follow-ups to the diagnostic-fix-2 work, tracked in #461.

**An unsigned index needs only the upper bound.** NL9007 already said so, and the range analysis now credits it. `toU32(i) < toU32(xs.length)` removes the bounds check for a `u8`, `u16` or `u32` index, in both number modes; f64 mode goes through `llvm.fptoui.sat`. The `--fix` guard rewrite now offers that form for unsigned indices, where it used to refuse any index that was not `i32`. It is still refused for `u64`, and in a module that declares its own `toU32`. NL9007 and NL2457 name the unsigned guard when the index is unsigned.

**`uncheckedGet`/`uncheckedSet` are array reads and writes, not opaque calls.** The range analysis now walks through them. An unchecked access proves nothing about a later checked one, and that is pinned by `arr_bounds_unchecked_kept`. A function with a migrated `a[at[0]] + b[at[1]]` now settles in one `--fix` round.

**Migration settles in one round.** `sink.reportDeprecationFix` is added. `acceptedEdits` treats an identical edit as already applied rather than as an overlap. The `--unchecked-indexing` build records the facts it would have proven without the flag.

Item 1 of #461 (unsafe-wrap) is still open.

Refs #461

entries.title: release a loop pass whose own string goes to a parts + join callee
entries.body:
Take a loop that builds a string in the pass and passes it to a callee. If that callee pushes the parameter onto its own local `parts` array and then joins it, the pass now releases its arena. Before this change the parameter counted as captured, so every pass kept the string alive.

The rule is narrow on purpose. The parameter is `nocapture` only when the callee's `parts` meets all of these conditions:
- it is a fresh local `string[]`, bound to an array literal or `new Array`;
- every reference to it is `.push(...)`, `.join(...)` or `.length`.

`join` always copies into a fresh string, so its result never aliases the pushed parameter. Any other use keeps the parameter captured: indexing, iteration, aliasing, passing `parts` on, returning it, or a closure. The five #500 negative cases still keep the release off, and so does a new kept-parameter case.

No callee in `std/` or `src/` matches yet. `jsonField` and `replaceAll` need string parameters to enter the capture fixpoint, which is what #503 still asks for.

Measured: Arena.used() after 1,000 passes, 2,912 B before and 16 B after (mem_join_parts_same_pass)
Refs #503

entries.title: fixes for !xs.length and non-boolean && / || operands, and code-checked nofix cases
entries.body:
`--fix` now rewrites two truthiness diagnostics, in the cases where the rewrite keeps the program's meaning.

- **NL2263:** `!xs.length` becomes `xs.length === 0`, and `!n` becomes `n === 0`, for an integer, a string, or an array or struct behind `| null`. Parentheses are added where the operand or the enclosing operator needs them. A float operand gets no fix.
- **NL2099:** a non-boolean `&&` or `||` operand becomes an explicit comparison, so `s.length && …` turns into `s.length !== 0 && …`. This happens only where the expression is read for truthiness: an `if`, `while`, `do` or `for` condition, a `? :` test, or a `!` operand. Where the value itself is used, as in the `n || def` defaulting idiom, there is no fix, because changing `0` to `false` would change the program.

Every case where no fix is offered is pinned by a `*.nofix.ts` case. Each of those cases now has a `.code` sidecar, and the runner checks that the diagnostic named there is the one reported. A nofix case can therefore no longer pass because some other diagnostic happened to stop the program first.

Items 1 and 2 of #440 are still open.

Refs #440

entries.title: NL9007 and NL2457 offer only a guard that compiles and is credited
entries.body:
NL9007, which reports a bounds check a loop keeps, and NL2457, which reports an index under `--deny-panics`, now take their advice from one helper, `indexGuardAdvice`. It names a guard only when that guard type-checks against the length and the bounds pass credits it. When no such guard exists, the message says so and gives the reason, instead of suggesting a spelling that either fails to compile or leaves the check in place.

- A `u64` or `i64` index used to be offered `if (i >= 0 && i < xs.length)`, which does not compile against the `i32` length. The message now says no guard removes the check, and names the index types that have one.
- A `u8`, `u16` or `u32` index in a module that declares its own `toU32` used to be offered `toU32(i) < toU32(xs.length)`. That guard calls the module's function, not the credited builtin, so the message now says the module's `toU32` hides the builtin.
- Under `--number-mode f64`, an `i32` index is offered `if (i >= 0 && i < toI32(xs.length))`, the spelling the fix already inserts. This holds for NL9007 and NL2457 alike: `CheckedProgram` now carries the number mode so that `panics.ts` can see it.
- A float (`number`) index under `--deny-panics` is offered no guard, because no compare of a float index is credited.

`docs/LANGUAGE.md` and `docs/AI.md` now say which index types have no guard.

entries.title: a native-only helper that draws the key and serial for x509MintSelfSigned
entries.body:
* feat(crypto): a native-only helper that draws the key and serial for x509MintSelfSigned

`nish/crypto/x509-random` draws what `x509MintSelfSigned` takes from its
caller, from the kernel's CSPRNG:

- `x509DrawP256Key()` answers a `Secret<u8[]>` P-256 private key. It draws 32
  octets from `crypto.getRandomValues` and draws again until `p256PublicKey`
  accepts them as a scalar in [1, n), wiping each refused draw. Rejection
  rather than reduction mod n, so no key is likelier than another.
- `x509DrawSerial()` answers twenty octets whose first one's top bits are
  `01`: a positive, non-zero serial that is always twenty octets long, with
  158 random bits.
- `x509MintSelfSignedDrawn(priv, commonName, notBeforeMs, days)` is the mint
  with a drawn serial. The key stays the caller's to wipe, since the server
  that presents the certificate signs its handshakes with it.

The module is native only: it calls `crypto.getRandomValues`, so a program
that imports it is refused for wasm32. That is why it is its own module and
`nish/crypto/x509` imports nothing from it. A wasm32 program can still parse,
verify and mint with a key and serial it is handed. This closes X509-6.

entries.title: check the owner of the run cache root and the package root, and take the first executable nish on PATH
entries.body:
`nish run` now checks who owns its cache root before it starts anything from it, a cache hit included. It refuses the root with exit 3 and `NL0002` when the root:

- is not a directory (a symbolic link is refused, not followed);
- is owned by another user;
- can be written by its group or by every user.

The message reads `run: refusing the cache root <root>, which …; remove it, and the next run makes it again`. Until now only a miss ran the `chmod 700`, so a root another user had made at your cache path, filled with a key and a binary, had its binary started by your next hit (CLI-7).

The package root that `--link` takes `scripts/build.sh` from, and that `nish/<module>` imports take `std/` from, is now refused when it is owned by neither you nor root, or when every user can write it. When no trusted candidate holds the package, every compile stops with `NL0002` and names the root it refused and why. A compiler kept directly under `/tmp/x/` used to trust `/tmp/scripts/build.sh`, which anyone can create. A root that only its group can write is still trusted: whoever can write it can already replace the compiler in `bin/`. A compiler started by a bare `nish` now takes the package of the first *executable* `nish` on `PATH`, the one the shell ran, rather than the first readable one (CLI-9).

These are behaviour changes. A world-writable checkout, or one owned by another non-root user (a root-run container over a runner's checkout, for example), compiled before and is refused now.

The checks ask `/bin/sh` and `/bin/ls` rather than calling the `lstatOwnerModeSync`, `geteuid` and `isExecutableSync` builtins. The checker refuses those three on wasm32, and `src/` is also linked as the web compiler (`nish.wasm`).

- One probe per root: `ls -ldn` gives the type, mode and numeric owner without following a link, and the shell's `test -O` checks the effective uid.
- Both tools are named by absolute path, so nothing on `PATH` is trusted. Every path is passed as an operand, never as script text.
- A probe that cannot run, fails, or prints output that does not parse refuses the root (fail closed).
- `--version` and `--help` spawn nothing.
- No probe runs in the web compiler, which has no `PATH` and no package-root candidate.

The builtins, their wasm32 refusals and their LANGUAGE.md rule are unchanged.

The check only probes the root directory itself, not `scripts/`, `std/` or `build.sh` inside it. A write grant made through an ACL is not seen. `docs/security/cli.md` records both limits, the fail-closed rule and the cost.

Measured: against main ed929f1 in three interleaved rounds, each the median of 41 runs, with a byte-identical copy of main as the noise band. A compile of examples/add.ts (one probe) costs +3.11 to +3.33 ms, about 3.2 to 6.6 ms, against noise of -0.17 to -0.04 ms. A `nish run` cache hit (two probes) costs +6.00 to +6.42 ms, about 5.5 to 11.8 ms, against noise of -0.20 to +0.13 ms.
Refs: docs/security/cli.md#status-after-the-owner-checks-486
Tests: tests/nish/cli.ts (CLI-7, CLI-9)
Fixes #486

entries.title: restate WP38's S3 bar after checking a portable-SIMD benchmark against LLVM 18
entries.body:
Erio-Harrison/simd_benchmark found that Rust's portable `std::simd` and
hand-written NEON run at the same speed once both versions do the same
work. A new §3.2.1 in `docs/wp38-simd.md` records what that means for
`nish:simd`, with each claim checked against LLVM 18 or measured on S0's
machine.

- **S3's comparator does the same work as the vector kernel.** Integer
  lanes wrap, so the scalar kernel wraps too. A float comparator has one
  accumulator per lane, and is timed with indexing checked and unchecked.
- **Four scalar `f32` accumulators.** Unchecked, they vectorise and run
  4.2x faster than one accumulator. A length guard alone keeps all eight
  bounds checks, because the range analysis learns nothing from
  `i + 3 < n`, and NL9007 warns for only two of them. `uncheckedGet`
  inside the guard reaches the unchecked speed.
- **`any` and `all` join `bitmask`.** On AArch64, `bitmask` lowers to 8
  instructions and `any` to one `umaxv`.
- **No `mulAdd`.** `llvm.fma.v4f32` becomes four calls to `fmaf` on the
  x86-64 baseline and on wasm simd128.
- **The 128-bit-only rule (Q4) costs `ld3` on AArch64:** 23 instructions
  against 4. Q4 stands, and the cost is recorded.
metrics: four f32 accumulators 4.2x over one when unchecked (125 vs 527 ms min, 133 vs 559 median); a length guard alone 411 ms, uncheckedGet inside it 130 ms; SSE2 dot product 1.9x from a second accumulator (62.2 vs 119.3 ms min), 2.3x from four. Noise not measured against a byte-identical copy; each column's seven runs spread at most 22% above its minimum, inside every ratio claimed.

entries.title: decide WP29 P3, the lock and the channel
entries.body:
WP29's third stage is now decided. It has two parts: `Mutex<T>`, a lock that owns its data, and `Channel<T>`, a channel of scalars, both from `nish/threads`. §4.3 and §4.4 give the rules and the reason for each.

A lock's data is reachable only through a guard bound by `using g = m.lock()`. That data must be fresh all the way down when the lock is made. A read through the guard must end in a scalar, or lead to a further access or a store. Every store through the guard writes a scalar. The release runs at every exit of the block. At a `return` it runs after the returned value is computed, so the read happens under the lock.

Inside a guard's block there is no second lock, no spawn, no P1 call and no receive, directly or through any function it calls. So a P3 program cannot deadlock, and no lock-order analysis is needed.

A channel is unbounded and has one receiver. It closes when every task that may send on it has returned. Senders are spawned before the receiver, so it means the same natively and under Node, where tasks run at their spawn. That same order rules out deadlock.

§4.2 now lists the guarantees P3 relaxes. Guarded updates that do not commute exactly are the author's responsibility. So is a receiver whose answer depends on how two senders interleave.

entries.title: cache the compiled runtime between links
entries.body:
`--link` and `nish run` no longer compile the C runtime on every link.
For the debug, speed and size profiles, the runtime's six translation
units are compiled once per recipe into a private cache,
`$XDG_CACHE_HOME/nish/runtime` (or `~/.cache/nish/runtime`), and each
later link compiles only the program's own modules, in parallel. The
binaries are byte-identical to the uncached recipe's. Speed and size
keep the runtime as LTO bitcode, so it is still optimised together with
the program.

An entry is keyed on the compiler's version, the profile, `-g`,
`--threads`, `CC` and what `$CC --version` prints, and on the SHA-256 of
`scripts/build.sh`, every runtime file and `nish.h`. A link reuses an
entry only when its stored key equals this one byte for byte. The cache
follows the run cache's rules: an absolute XDG or HOME root only, made
`0700` and checked for its owner on every link, filled through a
scratch directory and one rename, with the key written last, so two
links on a cold cache both succeed. `--link` with no usable root
compiles the runtime itself, as before. The wasi, wasm and napi
profiles, PGO builds and direct `scripts/build.sh` calls are unchanged.
`scripts/build.sh` gains the `--runtime-objects <dir>` and
`--runtime-from <dir>` modes that do the work, and stops the compiles
it started if it is itself stopped.

Binaries byte-identical (hello 56,928 / 4,712 bytes, awfy 71,584 / 25,040 bytes, debug / speed)

entries.title: prove an offset index `xs[i + c]` from a guard on the sum
entries.body:
A loop that reads several elements a pass, such as
`for (let i = 0; i + 3 < xs.length; i += 4)`, kept a bounds check on
every read: the range analysis learned nothing from a test on `i + 3`,
and only a plain local could be an index. Now a test on `i + c` is a
bound on `i`, and `xs[i + k]` is proven where it holds, so the loop
keeps none of its four checks and LLVM vectorises it with indexing
checked.

- `i + c < w.length`, and `i + c < n` with `n` a hoisted length, say
  the length reaches `c` past `i`; `i + c <= w.length` reaches `c - 1`;
  `i + c < N` for a literal `N` is `i < N - c`.
- `w[i + k]` needs `i >= 0` and a reach of at least `k`, or a literal
  bound on `i` that `k` more still fits under a known length. A checked
  `w[i + c]` that ran leaves its reach behind.
- The reach also bounds `i` below `INT_MAX`, so `i + 1` through `i + 3`
  and the step `i + 4` are `add nsw`.
- The rule rests on the sum being exact: a signed add either panics on
  overflow or is proven not to. Under `--wrapping`, and for an unsigned
  index, the sum may wrap, so an offset proves nothing and the check
  stays.

This is the safe route to the speed `--unchecked-indexing` buys on this
shape: every access the proof cannot reach keeps its check. It does not
reach indexes that add two variables, such as AWFY Queens's `c + r`.
metrics: a guarded four-accumulator f32 dot product (4,096 elements, 200,000 calls, 15 interleaved rounds) runs 3.1x faster on the minimum and 3.2x on the median: 379 / 408 ms on main against 122 / 128 ms. A byte-identical copy of main's binary ran 388 / 420 ms, a noise band of 2.4% / 2.9%. The 21 programs of bench/instructions.json run identical instruction counts.

entries.title: warn on an offset index that keeps its bounds check
entries.body:
The performance warning NL9007, which names the guard that would remove
a surviving bounds check, spoke only when the index was a plain local, so
`ys[i + 1]` in a hot loop kept its check without a word. Since #561 a
guard on the sum proves such an access. The warning now speaks for an
offset index too, names the sum as written, and offers that guard:

`if (i >= 0 && i + 1 < ys.length)` proves both ends, and so does a loop
condition `i + 1 < ys.length` on a counter that starts at 0.

Under `--number-mode f64` the length is spelled `toI32(ys.length)`. The
warning carries no `--fix`: an inserted guard would stop at `i === -1`,
whose index `i + 1` is in range, so it could change what a working
program does. Every other computed index stays silent, because no guard
proves it.

Turning the warning on found fourteen such checks in code the project
ships, each paid on every pass of its loop, and each is now proven away:

- **TLS ClientHello reader** (`std/net/tls/codec.ts`): its key-share and
  extension walks now read all four bytes before the `push`, which as a
  call had forgotten the guard. The reader no longer reaches the bounds
  panic at all.
- **HKDF label** (`std/crypto/hkdf.ts`): a guard in the copy loop's body,
  leaving its condition the counted `k < fullLength`.
- **The relay example** guards against `argv.length` itself, not a copy
  hoisted above the loop.
- **The compiler**: three insertion sorts carry their hole as a plain
  local stepped by `j = j - 1`, and two walks over pairs test the second
  of each pair. Same order, same output.

entries.title: Channel<T> of scalars, closed when its senders return, in nish/threads
entries.body:
A scope's tasks can now pass numbers, `boolean`s and enums to one receiver through `Channel<T>` from `nish/threads`, the second half of WP29 P3. The channel is unbounded and nobody closes it: it closes once the scope has started to join and every task that may send on it has returned, so a receiving `for (const x of ch)` loop ends by itself.

```ts
const ch = new Channel<i32>();
{
  using s = scope();
  s.spawn(produce, new Pipe(ch, 100), sent, 0); // p.ch.send(i) for 1..n
  s.spawn(consume, new Pipe(ch, 0), sums, 0);   // for (const x of p.ch) sum += x
}
```

The checker proves each program free of a hang or a lost value, with rules C1–C7 and codes NL2475–NL2484:

- **C1:** the element is a scalar.
- **C2:** the channel is a `const` beside its scope, never stored, returned, captured or used in an arrow.
- **C3:** the channel has no capacity.
- **C4:** the channel belongs to one scope. The parent sends only before the scope's block, and a channel-holding constructor uses `this` only to set a field.
- **C5:** there is one receiver, outside any loop. The parent receives only after the join.
- **C6:** every sender is spawned before the receiver, and no task both sends and receives.
- **C7:** there is no receive while a lock is held.

The runtime keeps the buffer outside every arena, because a sender's arena is freed at the join. It counts open senders in a word beside the buffer, and frees the buffer once the channel has been drained. On a build without threads (WASI, Node), every sender has returned before the receiver runs, so there is no lock and no wait.
metrics: runtime `.text*` at -Oz grows from 304 to 609 bytes (954 to 1,424 threaded); ceilings 768 and 1,536

entries.title: mark WP29 P3 built, with a measured example
entries.body:
WP29 P3 is built, and the repository's maps now say so. The status lines in wp29, wp20, MASTER_PLAN, the docs index and std/README.md mark it built. They point at the `Mutex<T>` (#562) and `Channel<T>` (#566) sections of LANGUAGE.md, and the runtime budget rows record what the channel added.

`examples/histogram.ts` is the lock at work. Four tasks each bin 25 million xorshift values into a local tally, then add it to one shared `Mutex<Hist>` under a single lock. That runs over eight rounds, each seeding its shards afresh and folding its bins into a printed checksum. The checksum is the same natively, in sequence, and under Node. Taking the lock once per task rather than once per value is the shape to copy: locking per value makes the whole loop body the critical section, and the program ends up slower than one thread.

The runtime figures in #566's entry were the pull request's earlier measurement. What `tests/run.js` records on `main` is 597 bytes of `.text*` at -Oz, or 1,403 threaded, against ceilings of 768 and 1,536.

entries.title: prove a computed index from the range of values it can take
entries.body:
An index that is neither a plain local nor an offset from one, such as
`freeMaxs[c + r]`, `freeMins[c - r + 7]` or `cells[r * 4 + c]`, kept its
bounds check even when every value it can take fits the array. Now, where
the other rules fail, the access is judged by the index's range: the
interval the overflow proofs already compute, from every local's bounds
and declared range through `+`, `-`, `*`, masks, conversions and a call's
known return range. When the bottom of that range is not negative and
the top is below a length the array is known to have, the access needs no
check.

The range is a proof only where it is the value's own:

- **The arithmetic is exact:** a signed `i32` or `i64` outside
  `--wrapping`, where a sum panics on overflow rather than wrapping. An
  unsigned index, an `f64` one and every index under `--wrapping` keep
  their check.
- **The length is the one the index leaves behind:** a call, or a `new`
  whose constructor shrinks the array while the index is computed, proves
  nothing.
- **Nothing inside the index writes.** The checker refuses such an index
  today; the proof does not rest on that.

Twenty checks in `std/crypto` are now proven: AES 8, P-256 4, SHA-1 4 and
SHA-256's message schedule 4. `aesPack` and `aesUnpack` reach no panic and
become `willreturn`. This is the first of the two pieces AWFY Queens needs.
The second, the length of an array a helper returns, is still to come, so
on its own this moves no benchmark.
metrics: against a compiler built from main, 20 fewer bounds checks across std/, examples/ and bench/, all in the four crypto modules, and identical instruction counts for the 22 programs of bench/instructions.json. entries.title: a JSON writer that writes into a byte buffer, in nish/json
entries.body:
`JsonWriter` in `nish/json` writes any JSON value into a `u8[]` the caller
owns and reuses: `beginObject`/`endObject`/`beginArray`/`endArray`/`key`,
`string`/`i32`/`u32`/`i64`/`f64`/`boolean`/`nullValue`, and `raw` for a
fragment encoded already. It inserts every comma and colon itself and writes
byte for byte what `JSON.stringify` writes: the seven short escapes, `\u00xx`
below 0x20, `/` and 0x7f as themselves, integers as their digits (the i32 and
i64 minimums included, written right to left with no negation), an `f64` as
`String(v)` spells it with `-0` as `0`, and NaN and the infinities as `null`.

Nothing is allocated per call except an `f64`'s digits, which the function's
own arena scope gives back before it returns, and the writer itself holds no
array: the kind of each open container is a bit of two `i32` words, up to
`JSON_WRITER_MAX_DEPTH` (64). Misuse never panics. The first call that cannot
be honoured sets `failed` to a negative `JSON_WRITE_*` code, the way
`HpackDecoder` reports errors, and every later call does nothing. The codes
cover a value where a key is due, a key where a value is due, an unbalanced
or mismatched `end*`, nesting too deep, a full buffer (nothing written past
`buf.length`), a second top-level value, and a bad `raw` window or `start`.
`jsonStringifyString(s)` is the same string rule answered as a string.

The method for `null` is `nullValue`, because the parser refuses `null` as a
member name. A string is its bytes (WP33 class C): UTF-8 passes through as the
UTF-8 `JSON.stringify` encodes to, and a lone 0xFF passes through raw.

Fixes #571

entries.title: a persistent FIFO worker pool, an affinity-aware core count and NISH_NUM_THREADS
entries.body:
A divided `parallelMapInto` or `parallelReduce` region, and a scope's join, no longer create and join a thread per chunk or task. The first one that divides starts a pool of workers, one per CPU but the caller's, and they park between calls. The compiler is unchanged: this is `runtime/runtime-parallel.c`.

- **The queue is strictly first in, first out**, and the caller helps. It runs the first chunk or task itself, then takes queued jobs off the same front until the queue is empty, and only then waits. So a job no worker is free for runs on the caller, in spawn order. That is what keeps channels deadlock-free at every pool size, none included: a receiver is spawned after every task that sends to it (wp29 C6), so every sender has a thread by the time anything takes the receiver. Work stealing is declined, because a LIFO deque breaks that.
- **A worker rewinds its arena after every job**, keeping at most one ordinary 64 KB chunk. It spins about 20 µs before it sleeps, and so does a caller waiting for its last job, so back-to-back regions rarely pay a futex wake. A region or a scope inside a job still runs on that one thread.
- **`nish_cpu_count()` is the smallest of** the CPUs online, the affinity mask (`taskset`, a container's cpuset), the cgroup v2 `cpu.max` quota rounded up (read at the process's cgroup and every one above it), and `NISH_NUM_THREADS` when it is a positive number. The variable lowers the count and never raises it. The answer is read once and cached, as before.
- **A Node addon keeps the per-call threads**, because Node can unload an addon and a parked worker would outlive its code. `nish.h` defines a constructor that calls the new `nish_pool_disable()` when `<node_api.h>` was included first, which the generated shim does. A forked child starts with no workers.

`bench/par-regions.ts` is new: a 2^17-element map called 1,000 times, the input changed on every call, and a checksum printed. It measures what one divided region costs. The threaded build of `runtime-parallel.c` grows from 1,403 to 2,660 bytes of `.text`, and its ceiling goes from 1,536 to 2,816.
metrics: an empty four-way region, 100 µs median (93 µs minimum) per region before, 11 µs (8 µs) with the pool, 11 interleaved rounds, four-core Xeon 2.10 GHz VM. bench/par-regions.ts min / median of 11 interleaved rounds: 256 / 298 ms before, 188 / 249 ms with the pool (-26% / -16%). Noise band: the old binary against a byte-identical copy of itself, 256 / 298 ms against 276 / 318 ms (8% / 7%). par-compute, par-alloc, par-nbody, par-short, examples/histogram.ts and examples/tasks.ts print the same answers and move within the band.

entries.title: measure AES-GCM and write WP38's S5 row with its bar
entries.body:
WP38 S5 puts AES-GCM on AES-NI and PCLMULQDQ (and ARMv8 AES and PMULL)
as a runtime kernel. This is its baseline, recorded before anything is
built, with the bar the kernel must clear.

`bench/aes-gcm.ts` times AES-128-GCM seal and open on a 16 KiB TLS record
and a 1,200-byte QUIC packet, ChaCha20-Poly1305 on the same sizes, and
`aesHeaderMask`. Every input changes on every iteration, and the answers
are folded into a printed checksum. `bench/aes-gcm.mjs` builds it and runs
it in rotating rounds. It can put a byte-identical copy (`--self`),
another build (`--binary`) or an environment variant (`--env`) in the same
rounds. It reports minimum and median MB/s and cycles per byte. `--check`
runs one short round against a pinned checksum.

A callgrind profile of the interop server shows AES is on the real path.
On one `curl --http2` GET of 1 MiB, `std/crypto/aes.ts` is 80.7% of the
server's instructions under the AES-256-GCM suite curl negotiates, and
77.3% under AES-128-GCM. So S5's stop rule does not apply.

The bar: AES-128-GCM seal on 16 KiB at least 5x faster on x86-64 with
AES-NI, a minimum at or under 15.208 ms for 4 MiB (275.8 MB/s or more).
The bitsliced fallback must also be no slower than this baseline, outside
the noise band, on any of the nine workloads. The new program joins the
self-hosting corpus, so `tests/self/goldens/checked.txt` is regenerated.
metrics: AES-128-GCM seal 16 KiB 55.2 MB/s at the minimum (76.04 ms per 4 MiB, 50.8 cycles/B at 2.8 GHz), open 57.6 MB/s; 1,200 B seal 54.8, open 54.9; ChaCha20-Poly1305 16 KiB seal 220.0 MB/s; aesHeaderMask 702 ns a mask; noise band 3.0% at the minimum and 11.1% at the median (the baseline against its own copy, two samples of 16 rounds); ce9d394's compiler and std, Xeon @ 2.80GHz

entries.title: write the language basics pages
entries.body:
The user guide's five everyday-language pages, written for a person writing programs rather than for the compiler's contributors. Each one teaches by example and links the `docs/LANGUAGE.md` sections that hold the normative rules.

- **Types**: `i32`, `i64`, `f64` and `number`, with the other widths. Mixing widths is an error, so conversion is explicit (`toI64`, `toF64`). Covers how a literal takes its type from where it is written, booleans with no truthiness, strings, `T | null` with narrowing and its limits, and ranged integers.
- **Functions**: arrow declarations with every parameter and the return type written out. There are no optional, default or rest parameters, and parameters are read-only. Covers `main` and `process.argv`, and passing a named function or a non-capturing arrow to a parameter of function type.
- **Control flow**: boolean-only conditions, `if` and `?:`, the loops, and `switch` with no implicit fallthrough. Unreachable code is an error. `i32` and `i64` arithmetic and division are checked, and wrapping is chosen on purpose with an unsigned type or `nish:unsafe`.
- **Arrays and strings**: the complete array and string method lists, bounds checks, and byte-counted UTF-8 lengths and offsets. Template literals are how a number becomes text. Explains which arrays store records back to back and which hold pointers.
- **Classes and interfaces**: fields and definite assignment, and `readonly`. Covers interfaces and object literals, and `implements` with its field-prefix rule. Explains why there is no inheritance, with the replacement for each thing `extends` is used for.

Every marked example is compiled by `npm test`, and each program prints what its comments say.

entries.title: give std/crypto/aes.ts four private seams, each called from one place
entries.body:
AES-GCM's work in `std/crypto/aes.ts` now runs through four private
functions, each called from exactly one place:

- `aesScheduleInto`, the key schedule, called from `aesKeyInto`, which
  `aesKey` now makes its key through;
- `aesBlockInto`, one block, called from `aesEncryptOne`;
- `aesCtrInto`, GCTR, called from `aesGcmCtr`;
- `ghashBlocksInto`, GHASH, called from `ghashUpdate`.

Each writes into arrays its caller passes and allocates nothing the caller
needs back. Each caller checks every precondition first: key shape, block,
J0 and state sizes, and lengths within each array. So WP38 S5's next
stage can replace each call with a runtime kernel that does no bounds
checks of its own. The bitsliced bodies keep their defensive checks.
Exported signatures, `AesKey`'s shape and the std/net callers are
unchanged, and the output is byte-identical.

GCTR's XOR loop now carries its bounds in the loop condition. With the
caller's length checks inlined above a per-byte `if`, LLVM emitted three
compares a byte. With the bounds in the condition, LLVM folds them into
one trip count and vectorises the XOR, so the fallback is no slower than
before.
metrics: bench/aes-gcm.mjs, 15 interleaved rounds with a byte-identical copy and main's build on a 2.1 GHz Xeon. Against main at the minimum: AES-128-GCM seal 16 KiB +1.1% (main slower), open 16 KiB +3.5%, seal 1,200 B +2.9%, open 1,200 B +2.4%; aesHeaderMask -1.8% at the minimum and +0.6% at the median (callgrind: +0.07% instructions over the run). Noise band of that run: up to 1.4% at the minimum and 4.0% at the median. aesGcmCtr's instructions 6.95M -> 3.01M at scale 64

entries.title: a streaming JSON tokenizer over u8[], in nish/json-tokenizer
entries.body:
`JsonTokenizer` validates and tokenizes RFC 8259 JSON held in a window of a
`u8[]`, one token per `next()`: openers and closers, keys, strings, numbers
and the three literals, then `JSON_TOK_END`, or a negative `JSON_TOK_ERR_*`
code that sticks in `failed`, with the byte offset in `errorAt`. No input
panics, and no byte outside the window is read.

Strings are checked as UTF-8: RFC 3629's table refuses overlong forms,
surrogates and code points past U+10FFFF. A lone surrogate escape is refused
too. That is the stricter reading, and it is what lets `stringInto` promise
valid UTF-8. `stringInto` decodes into the caller's array, and `keyEquals`
compares with a name without copying. `numberF64` is correctly rounded:
Clinger's fast path for up to 15 significant digits, `strtod` otherwise.
`isInteger` and `numberI64` read an integer that fits an `i64`, and
`skipValue` steps over a value. A window that ends mid-value is always
`JSON_TOK_ERR_TRUNCATED`, never a grammar error.

`JsonLimits` caps depth (128), string bytes (1 MiB), number bytes (256)
and total bytes (16 MiB). Each limit has its own code and is checked before
the work it bounds. `reset` reuses a tokenizer, so a reused request body
keeps `Arena.used()` flat. Duplicate keys are reported as tokens, and
whatever reads the tokens decides what to do with them. The module also
loads and runs under Node, through the prelude.

JSONTestSuite's `test_parsing/` (MIT) is vendored. Every `y_` file is
accepted with the token stream `JSON.parse` gives it, numbers bit for bit.
Every `n_` file is refused, and each `i_` verdict is recorded. A seeded
20,000-mutant fuzz runs in `npm test`. docs/security/json.md is the record.

Measured: 1,462 ns min / 1,518 ns median per 242-byte body (every token read, every string copied out, every number parsed); a byte-identical copy in the same 15 interleaved rounds read 1,468 / 1,593, a noise band of 0.4% (min) and 4.7% (median)
Refs: docs/security/json.md
Tests: tests/link/std_json_tokenizer, tests/json-suite
Fixes: #572

entries.title: decode JSON into a class and encode it back, with code the compiler writes
entries.body:
`jsonDecode(d, out)` and `jsonEncode(w, value)` in the new `nish/json-typed` read one JSON object into a class and write one back, with code the compiler writes at each call from the class's fields. The code is straight-line calls into `JsonDecoder` (a `JsonTokenizer` and a sticky error) and `JsonWriter`, one per field, and it recurses through nested classes, arrays of them and `| null` fields. A field may be an `i32`, `u32`, `i64`, `f64`, `boolean`, `string`, a declared class, an array of one of those, or a `string`, class or array `| null`. Anything else is refused at the call, naming the class and the field (NL2485–NL2488).

Decoding is strict. Every field is required and each key may appear once. A key that names no field is refused unless `ignoreUnknown` is set. A number must fit its field. Every outcome is a sticky `JSON_DECODE_*` or `JSON_TOK_ERR_*` code with its byte in `errorAt`, never a panic. Decoding into a reused object reuses its objects, its arrays and its strings where the input's are equal, so `Arena.used()` stays flat. Encoding writes `JSON.stringify`'s text in declaration order. Under Node the types are erased, so both calls panic: that is class C, recorded in LANGUAGE.md.

Measured: decoding `{"message":"Hello, World! NNNNNN"}` (its digits the iteration's, every decoded string folded into a printed checksum) into one reused object, 9 interleaved rounds of 2,000,000: 275.2 ns min / 279.0 ns median per decode; a byte-identical copy timed in the same rounds, 268.3 / 275.2, a noise band of 2.6% (min) / 1.4% (median). There is no earlier implementation to compare with.
Refs: docs/LANGUAGE.md#typed-json-nishjson-typed, docs/IR_COOKBOOK.md#typed-json, docs/security/json.md
Tests: tests/link/std_json_typed (main.ts, readers.ts, node.ts), tests/cases/json_reject_*, tests/wordings/nl2485_json_field_type … nl2488_json_constructor
Fixes: #573

entries.title: runtime-aes.c, AES-GCM on AES-NI/PCLMULQDQ and ARMv8 AES/PMULL
entries.body:
A new runtime unit, `runtime/runtime-aes.c`, implements AES-128 and AES-256 block encryption, GCTR and GHASH. On x86-64 it uses AES-NI, PCLMULQDQ and SSSE3; on AArch64 it uses the ARMv8 AES and PMULL instructions. The `lower` stage of WP38 S5 will make the compiler call these kernels in place of `std/crypto/aes.ts`'s bitsliced seams. The bitsliced code stays as the portable fallback and as the wasm32 path.

- **Choosing the path.** `nish_aes_hw` asks CPUID or `AT_HWCAP` once, on its first call, and stores the answer with relaxed atomics. Nothing runs at program start, and hello's bytes are unchanged. `NISH_AES=soft` pins the bitsliced path. On wasm32 and every other target the unit compiles to `return 0`.
- **Wiping.** The kernels read round keys and H's powers from `rk` at each use. The only two stack buffers they own, the keystream of a partial last block and the zero-padded last GHASH block, are wiped by volatile stores. A check pins those wipes under `clang -O2` on both targets. What a wipe cannot reach, vector registers and their spills, is recorded as AEAD-4.
- **Agreement.** `tests/simd/aes-gcm.c` holds every path a machine has to a textbook reference. That covers FIPS 197, the GCM test cases, RFC 9001's header-protection samples and every length from 0 to 4,096 under both key sizes. The counter wrap is pinned on every lane of a four-block batch. CI requires the `aesni-pclmul` line on x86-64 and `armv8-aes-pmull` on AArch64.
- **Constant time.** `tests/ct-asm-runtime.js` reads the kernels' `clang -O2` assembly for both targets using `ct-asm.js`'s taint model, with joins at labels and precise flags. It refuses any branch, address, call or divide that a secret reaches. It also requires the unit to export exactly the four kernels and the resolver. A deliberately leaky variant is refused. Reading vector code found instructions the checker misread: `pshufb`, SSE `shufps` and `palignr`, `movhlps` and `movlhps`, and `aese` and `aesd` (CT-17), and the SSE4.2 string compares (CT-18). Each is fixed and pinned by `AUDIT_CORNERS` rows.

`scripts/build.sh` does not pair the unit yet. The pairing lands with `src/run-cache.ts` in the `lower` stage, because pairing it alone would break every cached link.
metrics: runtime-aes.c is 2,532 bytes of .text at clang -Oz (clang 18.1.3, linux-x64), under a 2,560-byte budget; hello is byte-identical with and without the unit linked

entries.title: accept `??` on a nullable value
entries.body:
`a ?? d` now works when `a` is a `T | null`, not only on a `Map.get`
result. It answers `a` where that is not `null` and `d` where it is, and
runs `d` only then, as TypeScript does: `null` is nullish, so no
`undefined` is involved, and `tsc`, Node and the native build agree. The
result is `T` when `d` is a `T`, so it needs no narrowing, and because the
left operand is read once, a property path works where narrowing never
did: `cur = cur.next ?? cur`. The default takes its context from `T`, so
`xs ?? []` and an object literal need no annotation; a default that may be
`null` keeps the `T | null`.

One form is refused, `xs[i] ?? d` (NL2489). It is TypeScript's idiom for a
default past the end of an array, where Node reads `undefined` and answers
`d` but the bounds check panics, so the two would disagree.

It lowers to the compare a hand-written `!== null` test makes: a `select`
when the default is a literal or a name, otherwise a branch to the default
and a `phi`. The arena-scope analysis now reads both operands of such a
`??`, so a `using a = arena()` block that keeps a fresh value through one
names the assignment. `?.` stays forbidden; a `?.` chain that ends in `??`
is the second stage of `.claude/plans/nullish-on-null.plan.md`.
metrics: identical x86-64 code (opt -O2, then llc -O2) to the hand-written `!== null` test for all three functions of docs/cookbook/mem-nullish.ts

entries.title: give a call the length of the fresh array its helper returns
entries.body:
An array a helper built and returned kept a bounds check on every access in
the caller, because the length the helper gave it stayed inside the helper.
`const xs = filled(8)` now starts `xs` with eight elements when `filled`
declares `const arr = new Array<T>(n)`, touches it only by indexing it,
reading `arr.length` and pushing to it, and returns it, just as
`new Array<T>(8)` written in place would. A store `this.rows = filled(8)`
gives the field the same length.

The helper's body is read as written, not walked, so the rule holds whatever
order the bodies are checked in, and it takes only what the tree shows:

- **The callee is a plain function:** not a method, a generic or a lifted
  arrow, and its body holds no arrow, nested function, class or `try`.
- **The array never leaves the body.** Handing it to a function, storing it,
  `pop` or any use other than an index, a `.length` read or `push` gives no
  length, because each is a way another holder could shrink it.
- **Every return is the fresh array:** the one `const` local, returned only
  after its declaration in its own block, or a fresh array written in place.
  The call gives the shortest of them.
- **A size is fixed by the call:** a literal, a constant of the helper's own
  module where the call is in that module, or a parameter the body never
  declares again or writes, read from the argument's declared floor.
- **A field store keeps its receiver:** `recv.f = filled(8)` gives a length
  only when `recv` is `this` or a `const` local, which the call cannot point
  elsewhere.

This is the second of the two pieces AWFY Queens needs. With the computed
index proof (#581), a `--link` build of Queens carries no bounds check in
`getRowColumn`, `setRowColumn` or `placeQueen`, and runs 1.40x faster.
Elsewhere it proves one check in X25519 and one in ChaCha20; the ChaCha20
tag helper hands its array to `poly1305Finish`, so its sixteen reads keep
their checks.
metrics: AWFY Queens, `--link --profile speed`, 20 runs of 1000 inner iterations, 11 interleaved rounds: main 282 ms median / 261 ms min, a byte-identical copy of main 276 / 261 ms (a noise band of 2.2% / 0%), this change 202 / 193 ms, 1.40x faster at the median. Under cachegrind Queens runs 70,748,234 instructions against 191,116,467 (-63%), and the other programs of bench/instructions.json run exactly what main runs; the Queens baseline is lowered to lock the gain in. Surviving bounds checks across the linked programs of examples/ and bench/: 1,140 -> 1,131 (Queens 7, X25519 1, ChaCha20 1).

entries.title: test262- and V8-derived JSON conformance, and the JSONTestSuite round trip through the writer

`nish/json-tokenizer` and `JsonWriter` are now tested together against the JSON.parse and JSON.stringify cases of test262 (`test/built-ins/JSON/parse` and `stringify`, at `2e0a567`) and V8 (`test/mjsunit/json*.js`, at `a74948b`).

`tests/json-conformance/extract.js` runs each upstream file under Node with its own harness. It records every call the file makes about JSON text, with the answer the file's assertions require. Calls about JavaScript's object model are dropped and counted: reviver, replacer, toJSON, space-as-object, Proxy, getters, BigInt, and RangeErrors from nesting past V8's stack.

The data is kept with its BSD notices: 772 test262 cases from 64 files, and 684 V8 cases from 9 files.

- `extract.js --verify` recomputes every expected value with Node's JSON and checks the same three sets.

`tests/link/std_json_conformance` runs every case. A parse case is its text tokenized and written back; a stringify case is its value written. Each case gives upstream's answer, or is listed in `tests/json-conformance/divergences.txt` under a reason that says exactly what it answers instead. A case JSON.parse refuses must be refused for a grammar error, not a limit or a lone surrogate.

| Reason | Cases | What Nish answers instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| lone surrogate | 10, plus the 2,048 generated surrogates | `SURROGATE`: a Nish string is UTF-8 and cannot hold one |
| indent | 25 | upstream's text without its indentation, until writer-modes adds indentation |
| depth | 1 | `DEPTH`: refused at the 129th opener (V8 parses 10,001 levels) |
| duplicate key | 1 | exactly `{"__proto__":1,"__proto__":2}`: both members, because the tokenizer passes both on (JSON-3) |

Every y_ file of JSONTestSuite, tokenized and written back, is byte for byte `JSON.stringify(JSON.parse(x))`. This holds natively and under the Node prelude, non-ASCII files included. The exceptions are the two files that repeat a key: each must differ, and must parse back to the same value.

- `docs/security/json.md` names `JSON_TOK_ERR_TOTAL_LIMIT` and cites its three tests.
- `docs/cookbook/json-tokenizer.ts` and `json-writer.ts` now render in `docs/IR_COOKBOOK.md`.

entries.title: accept a `?.` chain that ends in `??`
entries.body:
`a?.b?.c ?? d` now compiles. Each `?.` link reads only where the receiver
before it is not `null`, and the whole expression is `d` where one is, as
in TypeScript. A `?.` is allowed only in a chain whose value is the left
operand of `??`: on its own a chain answers `undefined`, which Nish has no
value for, so `const x = a?.b`, an argument, a template hole or an
assignment target is refused (NL1062). Phase 0 decides that from the
syntax alone, which covers every place a chain can be written.

The last link may be a field of any type, a number included, a string's
or an array's `length`, or a method call. Only a `?.` link skips a `null`,
so a nullable link after a plain `.` needs a `?.` of its own, and the
message says so. `?.` on a value that cannot be `null` is refused
(NL2490), and so is a chain that ends in `Map.get` (NL2491); `?.[i]` and
`f?.()` stay refused.

Each `?.` lowers to an `icmp eq` against `null` at its receiver and a
branch to the default of the `??`, which every link shares, so nothing
after a `null` link runs, its arguments included. The bounds-check prover
no longer assumes a chain ran to its end: an index a chain read is not
taken as checked after the `??`, because the read may never have run, so
a later read of it keeps its check.

This reverses, for this one form, the refusal
docs/wp23-language-surface.md section 9 recorded.

entries.title: close the constructor hole in scope regions and admit a task's private writes
entries.body:
Between a scope's first `spawn` and its join, the parent may not write
memory a task can read, and that rule now holds however the write is
reached. A `new` is judged as the call it is (#564). A write counts
wherever an argument's memory reaches: a field of a field, an element, a
`const` alias, a helper, a method, or a field of `this` a constructor
filled from an argument. A function's own objects stay its own only until
memory an argument reaches may have got into them, through a store, a
`push`, an object or array literal, a Map or Set method, or a callee that
keeps it. Any non-number value rooted at an own object or at `this`
escapes that root wherever it is used as a value. The constructor of a
class that holds a channel may read and update its own fields when
nothing reached from them can send (#567). And a task or a parallel body
may write an array it allocated and hands to nothing that keeps it; the
length check of `new Array(n)` no longer counts as output.

The rule is sound but conservative: some code that writes only a
function's own Map, Set or array is refused inside a region (#602).

entries.title: keep a helper's array length through a call that keeps it
entries.body:
A helper that builds a fresh array may now hand it to a function of the
same module and still give the caller its length. Before, any call that
took the array as an argument ended the proof, so `chacha20Poly1305Tag`,
which builds its tag and has `poly1305Finish` fill it, gave its caller no
length, and the sixteen tag reads in `chacha20Poly1305TagMatch` kept their
checks.

A parameter keeps the length when the function's body only indexes it,
reads its `.length`, pushes to it, or hands it on to another parameter that
does the same, recursion included, and never returns or stores it. The
callee is read as written, like the helper, and only a plain function of
the caller's own module, called by a name the calling body does not
declare, is followed:

- **A returned or stored parameter keeps nothing:** returning it gives the
  helper a second name for the array, and storing it gives an object one.
- **A recursion is read once:** a parameter already being followed is taken
  to keep the length. That is sound because the walk reaches every body of
  the cycle, and a shrink needs a `pop` or a store somewhere in it. The walk
  refuses past eight functions.
- **Only an exact answer is remembered** on the function, one that rested on
  neither assumption: an answer drawn while a cycle was still open can be
  wrong once the cycle closes. The cache keeps a chain of helpers that each
  hand the array on twice from being read 2^8 times.

entries.title: JSON against serde_json, simdjson, yyjson, RapidJSON and Go on the same machine
entries.body:
`bench/json-compare` measures Nish's JSON stack against five other libraries on the same machine. Nish's stack is `nish/json-tokenizer`, `nish/json-typed` and `nish/json`. The others are simdjson 4.4.2 (On-Demand), yyjson 0.12.0, RapidJSON's Reader (SAX), serde_json 1.0.154 and Go's `encoding/json`.

`npm run build && node bench/json-compare/run.mjs --record` runs three workloads over nativejson-benchmark's `twitter.json`, `citm_catalog.json` and `canada.json`:

- **Tokenize.** Every token, on all three corpora.
- **Typed decode.** `citm_catalog`'s `performances` is decoded into a fresh value every iteration in every language. A separate, labelled Nish row decodes into one value it reuses.
- **Serialize.** The same values are written back minified. Only the writing is timed.

What is compared, and how:

- **Checksums.** Every implementation folds what it read or wrote into the same 64-bit `h * 31 + v` checksum.
  - Tokenize folds each token's kind and each string's length and last byte, then an untimed pass folds every string byte by byte.
  - Typed decode folds every decoded field, with strings folded byte by byte.
  - Serialize folds every byte of every output.
  - A run whose checksums disagree exits 1 and records nothing.
- **Builds.** Nish `--profile speed`, C and C++ `-O3 -DNDEBUG`, serde in release with LTO, and Go's default build.
- **Noise band.** Rounds are interleaved in an order that rotates and reverses by blocks. Each case runs a multiple of twice its implementations, so every implementation runs in every position equally often, a byte-identical copy of the Nish binary among them. The gap between the two Nish binaries is the noise band, and a ratio inside it is marked as no difference.
- **Inputs.** The corpora and the C and C++ sources are pinned by URL and sha256 into a git-ignored cache. Nothing is vendored, and RapidJSON's JSON-licensed `bin/jsonchecker` files are never fetched.
- **Recorded section.** `--record` writes a marked section into `docs/BENCHMARKS.md`. It holds the machine, the measured commit, each toolchain, the build flags, and what differs between the rows: simdjson's serialize is hand-written builder code, and its typed figure reads only `performances`. `bench/run.mjs` now keeps that section when it rewrites the rest of the file.
- **Network-free check.** A `tests/run.js` check holds the Nish program to the checksums every comparator printed on a committed sample. The sample's serialized strings carry quotes, backslashes, a control character and non-ASCII, and Node's own `JSON.stringify` checks the serialize bytes. Unit checks pin the round order at the default round count, and the checksum comparison.

The tokenizer reads `canada.json`'s numbers at 64 MB/s, where yyjson reads them at 625 MB/s. That gap is the largest in the table.

Part of #597

entries.title: a builtin that makes a string from a byte range in one allocation
entries.body:
`String.fromBytes(bytes, start, end)` makes one string from the bytes of `bytes[start..end)`. It takes a `u8[]`, `readonly` or not, and makes one allocation and one copy. The range is checked once, after all three arguments are evaluated. The check is `s.slice`'s, `0 <= start <= end <= bytes.length`, and so is the panic: `slice out of range: [start, end) of length len`, exit 1. `--unchecked-indexing` drops it.

It is lowered inline to that check and one `nish_str_new`, so it adds no runtime function. Both header fields are read in the header alias domain, through `loadLength` and a new `loadData` in `src/emit-arrays.ts`. As with `String.fromCharCode`, the bytes are not validated as UTF-8. Under Node the prelude installs it on `String`, with one UTF-16 unit per byte as `fromCharCode` makes them. That divergence is a C row in `docs/wp33-round-trip.md` §3.2.

`nish/json-typed`'s `JsonDecoder.string()` now builds every string with one `String.fromBytes`. A string with no escape is copied straight from the input, and one with an escape from its unescaped bytes. It used to make a `String.fromCharCode` per byte and then a `join`. `stringArray` reads through `string()`, so it moves with it.

entries.title: pretty-printed output and a strict non-finite mode for JsonWriter
entries.body:
`JsonWriter` can now pretty-print. `w.setIndent(n)` writes exactly what `JSON.stringify(v, null, n)` writes — one member or element a line, a space after each colon, an empty `{}` or `[]` kept on one line — with `n` clamped to 10, and 0 or a negative `n` giving the minified text, which stays the default. `w.setIndentTab()` indents with a tab. A misuse before the value keeps its own code. Both settings belong to the writer and survive `reset`, and `jsonEncode` writes in whichever mode its writer is in. The minified output is unchanged, byte for byte.

`JsonWriter.i64` now also runs under the Node prelude, where it used to throw.

entries.title: admit a scope region's writes to a function's own Map, Set and array contents
entries.body:
Inside a `using s = scope()` region, the checker now accepts ordinary code that writes only the called function's own memory, or that only reads an argument's table. That covers a memo `Map` filled by a recursive helper, a histogram walked by `keys()`, an index built from a parameter array, and `has` or `get` on a parameter's `Map`. #590 began refusing these with NL2394, and #602 listed them. Every refusal #590 makes is kept.

All of the changes are in the facts the region rule reads (`src/attributes.ts`):
- A `Map` or `Set` method writes only the table's own storage. A table call's receiver is written only when the method writes through `this`, so `has` and `get` are reads.
- What a table keeps is recorded as stores into it: `set` keeps its key and value, `add` its element, and `getOrInsert` its key and default. A lookup keeps nothing.
- A value read back from a table or array (`get`, `getOrInsert`, or a `for...of` over an array, a `Set`, `keys()` or `values()`) is a path into its container. A write through it counts against whatever was stored there.
- The escape rule asks for the path of any value expression, so a call that answers a table or what one holds escapes it in a `push`, a field or element store, or a literal.
- A number, boolean, enum, string or ranged integer, seen directly or through `| null` / `| undefined`, names no memory.
- Both arms of a `?:` or `??` count as stored.

Limits kept on purpose:
- A write through `x ?? y` counts against everything.
- The variable of any other walk is unknown.
- An own object `set` into a parameter's table escapes there.

A task reading a shared `Map` is still refused; that is #611.

Fixes #602

entries.title: scan JSON string bodies, whitespace and numbers in bulk
entries.body:
`nish/json-tokenizer` reads JSON faster. Before, every byte went through a bounds-checked helper call. Now a run of plain bytes inside a string, the whitespace between tokens and the digits of a number are each stepped over by one loop that reads the input directly. The window's end and the array's length bound that loop, and its index is proven in range once, so no per-byte check is left. A number that Clinger's fast path cannot take, such as one with more than 15 significant digits or a large exponent, is now copied for `parseFloat` with one `String.fromBytes`. Before, it built one string per byte and joined them. Every verdict and error offset is unchanged, and so is every token stream.

`JsonTokenizer` gains `isU64()` and `numberU64()`, which read a number written in digits alone, with no minus sign, fraction or exponent, that fits in a `u64` (up to `18446744073709551615`). They complement `isInteger()` and `numberI64()`, and the typed layer's coming `u64` field kind reads through them.

On the json-compare corpora, tokenizing is 1.35x faster on twitter.json, 1.17x on citm_catalog.json and 1.62x on canada.json, and the typed decode of citm_catalog.json is 1.14x faster. canada.json rises from 41 to 67 MB/s on this machine. Its numbers have 16 to 17 significant digits, so every one goes to `parseFloat`, and glibc's `strtod` is the largest single part of what remains: about 56% of canada's time in a profile of the new build. The rest alone would run at about 150 MB/s, still well short of yyjson's 625, so the scan and the number check are the next part of that gap after the float parser.

entries.title: JsonValue, a dynamic JSON tree with lossless numbers, in nish/json-value
entries.body:
`nish/json-value` is new: `JsonDocument` parses any JSON document into a tree a program can read, change and write back, when the shape is not known ahead of time — a configuration file, a body passed on after one field changes, a tool that prints whatever it is given. A value is a `JsonValue`, a handle into the document, and every reader is a method of it: `kind`, `boolean`, `string`, `stringEquals`, `numberText`, `length`, `at`, `keyAt` and `get`. A handle that names nothing answers an empty value instead of panicking, and a handle kept from an earlier document names nothing in the next one, even one of the same shape.

**Numbers are kept exactly as they were written.** This is where Nish differs from JavaScript: `JSON.parse` turns `12345678901234567890` into `12345678901234567000` and `0.1000000000000000055511151231257827` into `0.1`, and `JSON.stringify` writes those back. A `JsonDocument` keeps each number's text and reads it as what the program asks for — `isI64`/`i64`, `isU64`/`u64` for an integer that fits, `f64` for the nearest double (correctly rounded), `numberText` for the digits — and writes the text back, so integers wider than any integer type and decimals with more digits than a double holds round-trip byte for byte.

Objects keep their members in order. A repeated key is refused by default (`JSON_VALUE_ERR_DUPLICATE`, at the first key that repeats one), because two programs that read different members of one text can disagree about what it says; `duplicates = JSON_VALUE_DUPLICATE_LAST` gives `JSON.parse`'s answer instead. Every parse error and limit is the tokenizer's own (`nish/json-tokenizer`'s codes, `JsonLimits`), with the depth held to the writer's 64 so that whatever parses can be written back; nothing in the input can make it panic, and the parse keeps its own stack rather than recursing. `maxValues` (262,144 by default) caps how many values one document holds, which bounds the memory a long-lived document keeps.

Values are built with `newNull`, `newBoolean`, `newString`, `newI64`, `newU64`, `newF64`, `newNumber` (any JSON number, as text), `newArray` and `newObject`, then `push` and `set`. A value lives in at most one container, so a tree built that way can never contain itself. `stringify` answers minified text, and `write(v, w)` writes through a `JsonWriter`, so the writer's indented and strict modes apply. Each `parse` reuses the document's memory: a server that keeps one document and parses each request into it stops allocating once it has seen its largest request.

`JsonWriter` gains `stringBytes(bytes, off, len)` and `keyBytes(bytes, off, len)`, which write a window of a byte array exactly as `string` and `key` write a string of those bytes, without making the string, and refuse a window outside the array with `JSON_WRITE_BAD_WINDOW`. They are how `JsonDocument` writes with nothing allocated; `string` and `key` are unchanged.
