entries.title: u64, enum and Map fields, and key dispatch by length, in typed JSON
entries.body:
`jsonDecode` and `jsonEncode` read and write three more kinds of field.

- **`u64`** is exact to 2^64 - 1. It is read through the tokenizer's `numberU64`, so a negative number (`-0` included), one past 2^64 - 1, a fraction and an exponent are `JSON_DECODE_RANGE`. It is written as its digits, which `JSON.stringify` cannot do for a number past 2^53.
- **A numeric `enum`** is its number. An integer that is not one of its members' values is `JSON_DECODE_TYPE`, and the field keeps the member it held; a read that fails stores nothing. An enum whose members are strings is not part of the language (Phase 0 refuses it), so it cannot be a field either; that gap is recorded in the guide.
- **`Map<string, V>`**, for any `V` typed JSON can read (another map included, `| null` or not), is a JSON object. Decoding empties the map and fills it in the input's key order. A repeated key, raw or escaped, is `JSON_DECODE_DUPLICATE`, and a value whose read fails is not set. The maps of one decode take at most the decoder's `maxMapKeys` keys between them (4,096 unless set); the next is the new `JSON_DECODE_MAP_LIMIT`, which bounds what a body of hash-colliding keys can cost the whole decode. Encoding writes the entries in the map's order.
- Arrays of `u64` and of enums, and `| null` maps, work like the other arrays and `| null` fields. A `Map` with keys that are not strings, a `Set`, an array of maps, and a map of values typed JSON cannot write are refused at the call with NL2485, naming the field.

The code written for a class of three or more fields now sends a key to its field by the key's length in bytes, then, where three or more names share that length, by its byte at the one position where those names differ most, before comparing the whole key. A key written with escapes is compared with every name of its length. One or two names are compared in turn, as before. A class with many fields decodes markedly faster, and a class with a few is no slower.

entries.title: renamed and optional-with-default fields, and lossless number fields, in typed JSON
entries.body:
A class can now declare its typed JSON options in one `static readonly json` object literal, the only `static` member a class may have. `rename` gives a field the key it has on the wire, so `static readonly json = { rename: { userId: "user_id" } }` reads and writes `userId` as `"user_id"`, dispatched by length and bytes like any other key, escapes and non-ASCII included. `optional` lists fields whose key may be missing: a missing one sets the field to its initializer, on a fresh object and on one decoded into again, and allocates nothing. Every other missing key is still `JSON_DECODE_MISSING`. The literal is read where the class is declared, whether or not anything decodes it, and is not a field: it has no slot, and a field or method called `json` may stand before or after it, as in TypeScript.

Each misuse is a compile error with its own code: `static json` that is not `static readonly`, is annotated, carries `?` or `!`, or is on a generic class (NL2492); a value not written as a literal, such as a module constant (NL2493); an unknown option (NL2494); a name that is not one of the class's fields (NL2495); a rename to a non-string (NL2496); two fields with one key, a rename to another field's own name included, or a field renamed or made optional twice (NL2497); an optional field without an initializer (NL2498); and a rename to a key that is not valid UTF-8, a lone surrogate included, which no input could give (NL2499). A spread or a computed key in the literal is refused by Phase 0 as anywhere, and only `static readonly json` may leave out its type. A class without options compiles to exactly the code it did before.

`JsonNumber`, from `nish/json-typed`, keeps a number as the text it was written in, so a field of it round-trips an integer wider than a `u64`, a fraction longer than an `f64` holds, `1E+400` and `-0` byte for byte, alone, `| null`, in an array or as a `Map`'s value. Decoding into one reuses its bytes. It reads its text with the same semantics as `nish/json-value`'s numbers: `isI64`/`i64` through the tokenizer's integer read, `isU64`/`u64` for digits alone up to 2^64 - 1 (`-0` refused), `f64` as the correctly rounded nearest double, and `setText` accepting exactly one JSON number as `newNumber` does. The two differ only in storage: a `JsonValue` is a handle into its document's arena and cannot stand alone as a class field, so unifying them needs a typed field that holds a document plus a handle, which is left for a later change.

entries.title: give a hidden function a symbol C cannot spell
entries.body:
A private function passed to a template that another module instantiates (a `spawn` task, a `parallelMapInto` or `parallelReduce` body, an `expose` callback) is `hidden`, so its symbol is global in the executable. One of the program's own named `read`, `write` or `free` was linked in place of the C library function the runtime calls. A scope that joined two tasks named `read` crashed when it started the worker pool, and a task named `write` swallowed `console.log`. Such a symbol now ends with a `$`, which C cannot spell. The `$` is added once every body is checked, so diagnostics name the function as written.

Fixes #610

entries.title: nish/threads against Rust and Go on the same parallel kernels
entries.body:
docs/BENCHMARKS.md compares four parallel kernels, each the same program in
Nish, in Rust on `std::thread::scope` and on Rayon, and in Go on goroutines
and a `sync.WaitGroup`, all printing the same checksum and dividing over the
same number of threads; `node bench/run.mjs --only par` reproduces it. The
comparison runs three times and is read across all three, with the spread of
the ratios beside each reading, because the machine moves between runs by
more than the band inside one shows, and every run past 1.10x is counted
whatever its band says. The work is the same; the checks and the build are
not, and the table says how.

Nish is within 1.10x of the fastest twin on par-compute's minimum and on
par-nbody's minimum and median in every run, and past it on par-compute's
median in one run of three. It loses on par-regions in every run: the map's
chunk loop stores under a bounds guard that keeps it from vectorising (#619).
On par-histogram, a lock taken per value, it is behind Go in every run here,
while another VM of the same kind put it ahead: that kernel is machine- and
load-sensitive.

entries.title: plan S6, the JSON tokenizer on vectors and Eisel-Lemire
entries.body:
WP38 gains S6, which aims SIMD at the gap the json-parity run measured. The
gap is no longer in `std/json`'s older reader, which S1 measured. It is in
`nish/json-tokenizer`, against simdjson, yyjson, serde_json and RapidJSON in
`bench/json-compare`. A new §2.4 records the baseline from the json-compare
record at 06645ecf. It explains why none of those paths uses a vector yet:
`indexOfAny` searches a `string` for at most 16 bytes, and the tokenizer
scans a `u8[]` for the first byte outside a class. It also explains why
canada.json is mostly `strtod`.

S6 is three stages, each with a measured bar:

- **S6a:** byte-class run kernels on `u8[]` for the tokenizer's blank, digit
  and string-body runs and for the writer's escape scan, behind a `std`
  function the compiler recognises.
- **S6b:** Eisel-Lemire in `numberF64`, ported from fast_float, with
  `parseFloat` kept for the ambiguous case.
- **S6c:** the block classifier, re-aimed at the tokenizer, designed and
  decided only after the first two land.

§8 adds two open questions: where the index lives, and which module the
`u8[]` scans belong to.

entries.title: record the AES-GCM kernel run's conventions in CLAUDE.md
entries.body:
Five rules the AES-GCM kernel run (#577) paid for now stand in CLAUDE.md,
each with the incident that taught it:

- A new runtime unit goes into `scripts/build.sh`'s `halves` and
  `src/run-cache.ts`'s `runtimeUnits()` in one commit. In `halves` alone,
  `build.sh --runtime-from` exits 2 on every cached `nish --link` and
  `nish run`; in `runtimeUnits()` alone, the cache entry never gets its key
  and the runtime cache is silently off (#594, #598).
- A declaration added to `src/runtime.ts` moves `docs/IR_COOKBOOK.md`'s
  runtime prelude; `docs/cookbook/regen.sh` regenerates it in the same
  change, or CI's `regen.sh --check` fails (#598).
- A lowering skipped for wasm32 also covers the freestanding
  `--profile wasm` route, which links IR compiled for the host (#598).
- A positive check gated on `/proc/cpuinfo` has a CI step that greps its
  PASS line, or a runner that masks the instructions keeps it green (#598).
- A pull request that conflicts with `main` gets no `pull_request` CI, so a
  push that shows no runs is checked for mergeability first (#594).

entries.title: measure what reading every --cpu level costs, and recommend S2, S3a and S7
entries.body:
WP38's S2 flag ships only once the constant-time checkers read every level
it accepts. This measures that cost before anything is built: the nine
`ct_asm` fixtures and `runtime/runtime-aes.c`, compiled at each candidate
level and read by `tests/ct-asm.js` and `tests/ct-asm-runtime.js`.
`x86-64-v2`, `v3` and `v4`, and ARMv8 without SVE, already pass; the SVE
levels fail (a loop over the vector length, and an unmodelled predicated
store), and `native` cannot be read at all. No x86-64 level holds AES-NI or
PCLMULQDQ, so the flag gives `std/crypto` nothing beyond S5's run-time
branch.

The note now recommends, as open decisions Q7 to Q9: the flag with one
value, `x86-64-v3`, for the module and the runtime alike; a new stage S7
that credits an offset index `i + k` from a test `i + c < n`, which removes
the bounds checks that keep scalar float kernels from vectorising; and a
measurement-only stage S3a before `nish:simd` is built or declined.

Measured: at 6752a82 with the 0.18.0 seed and clang 18.1.3, 50 of 50
fixture readings and 7 of 7 kernel readings pass at x86-64-v2/v3/v4 and
armv8.2-a; at armv9-a, 47 of 50 and 6 of 7

entries.title: parallelMap, parallelFrom and arrows that read the enclosing function's consts
entries.body:
The Rayon one-liners are now spellable with `nish/threads`: a new array from a map, a new array from an index, and a body that reads the function's local constants.

```ts
const ys = parallelMap(xs, (x) => x * k + b)          // k, b: const locals
const sq = parallelFrom(n, (i) => i * i)              // Array.from({ length: n }, ...)
parallelMapInto(xs, dst, (x) => table[x % 8] * k)     // table: a const array, read-only
```

`parallelMap(src, f)` and `parallelFrom(n, f)` allocate their result on the calling thread before the region and then run the existing map: `parallelMap` is `parallelMapInto` into that array, and `parallelFrom` the same region over the indices through a chunk loop of its own. Their `f` is held to the existing data-parallel rules unchanged, and a result that is not a number, a `boolean` or an enum is refused at the call.

An arrow passed to any of the four forms may now read the `const` locals and the parameters of the function it is written in. Each name it reads is appended to the arrow's parameters; every instance between the call and the body carries the value as a parameter of its own, and the region packs it into the context the runtime already passes. A scalar is copied and a reference is read-only: a store through it is a shared write and is refused as one. The rules that follow a local through its reads count a capture as a read of that local where the call runs the body: a scope's destination, an element reference a `push` may have moved, and an array `secret(raw)` took are refused through a capture as they are directly, and `--warn-portability` reports a record copied into an array (NL8003) and a byte offset compared with a count (NL8001) at a captured read as at a direct one, and through the arrow's answer, which the form stores; a captured `i64` is reported where it is declared, never as one of the arrow's parameters (NL8009). A `let`, `this` by that name (`const self = this` is captured), a read from outside a nested arrow, a lock, a guard, a channel, a scope, a `Result`, a value that may be absent and a `Secret` are refused, and so is a capture that could be `parallelMapInto`'s `dst`, unless one of the two is a `const` bound to an array of its own and the other another such `const` or a parameter. No closure is made, and no other arrow captures.

entries.title: let a scoped task read a shared Map or Set, and let only the first panic of a process print
entries.body:
A scoped task, and the body of `parallelMapInto` or `parallelReduce`, may
now look keys up in a `Map` or `Set` other threads share, with `get`,
`has` and `size`, and may call `panic`. A lookup used to be refused as a
shared write: `probe` can panic, and `panic` lowered to a write to stderr
followed by `exit`. `panic`, `r.expect(message)` and a failed range entry
now make one runtime call, `nish_panic`, which counts as a panic rather
than as output. Changing a shared table, walking it with `for...of`, and
output (`console.log`, `console.error`, `write`, `writeError`,
`process.exit`) stay refused. So does the parent walking, or changing,
a `Map` or `Set` before the scope joins, judged by the call rather than by
which tables a task holds.

When several threads panic at once, exactly one message is printed and
the process exits 1. Every panic path in the threads runtime takes an
atomic claim first: the first thread to take it prints its whole message
and exits, and every later one parks until that exit ends the process.
Before, two messages could both print, interleaved, with two threads
racing to the exit. `panic` still exits with `exit(1)`, so atexit
handlers run and stdio is flushed. `panic`, `expect`, and the arithmetic
and out-of-memory panics now retry a `write` that a signal interrupts, so
a host's handler without `SA_RESTART` no longer cuts their message short.

Fixes #611

entries.title: wipe AES key schedules, H and ChaCha state with the volatile wipe
entries.body:
An `AesKey` now keeps GCM's hash key H in `h`, a two-word `u64[]` (high,
low), in place of the scalar fields `hHi` and `hLo`, which no volatile wipe
could reach. The new `aesKeyWipe(key)` zeroes all of `roundKeys`, including
the runtime kernels' powers of H after the schedule, and `h` with
`nish:secret`'s `wipe`. That is one volatile `llvm.memset` per array, over
its whole capacity, and no optimiser removes it. It is how a holder drops a
key. An `AesKey` whose `h` is not two words is refused like any other
hand-built key.

AES and AES-GCM wipe every working copy derived from the key before they
return:
- the bitsliced key schedule's words, last round key and packed batch;
- the single block that H and E(K, J0) pass through;
- GCTR's last batch of keystream and its bitsliced state;
- the tag's E(K, J0) block;
- J0 itself, and for an IV that is not 12 bytes its GHASH state, which
  says something of H;
- on open, the tag it compared.

ChaCha20-Poly1305 wipes the ChaCha20 state, the keystream block, the
Poly1305 one-time key, `r` and the accumulator, and on open the tag it
compared. Both opens wipe on the refusal path too, with one wipe after the
branch rather than one on each path, so that each wipe is counted on its
own.

`hkdfExpandLabelSha256Secret` and `hkdfExpandLabelSha384Secret` are
HKDF-Expand-Label on a PRK held as a `Secret<u8[]>`. They answer a `Secret`
and panic where the plain forms do.

The `-O2` wipe-count check moves to `tests/wipes/`: one file per area, each
a list of groups (program, modules, exact counts per root). A later area
adds its roots to its own file.

Measured: seal+open of 64-byte messages and aesKeyInto, 200,000 a run,
median of 31 interleaved rounds, three runs. Each run's noise band is the
baseline against a byte-identical copy of itself.
- AES-GCM on the hardware kernels: +0.8%, +0.2% (98.1 -> 98.8 ms, bands
  0.1% and 0.8%), inside the noise. A third run read +10.4% against 0.9%
  and did not repeat.
- AES-GCM under NISH_AES=soft: 10.2% to 11.7% faster (739.1 -> 657.6 ms;
  bands of at most 1.8%). The cause is not isolated.
- aesKeyInto: level on the kernels (-0.1% to -2.1%, against bands of
  0.3% to 1.3%); 3.1% to 4.3% faster under soft.
- ChaCha20-Poly1305: -0.3% to -3.2%, inside or just past bands of 0.0% to
  1.9%. On an earlier head and another machine it read +1.4% to +3.9%
  against bands of 0.3% to 2.3%.

entries.title: test dst's length in parallelMapInto's loop condition, so the element loop vectorises
entries.body:
`parallelMapInto`'s element loop now vectorises when its body inlines with no panic path, and so does `parallelMap`'s, which runs through it. `mapRange`, the loop each thread runs over its share of the map, tested `dst`'s length only after the call to `f`. The bounds proof needs that test there, because a call ends every length fact, and the test is what keeps the store unchecked. But it left the store conditional, and LLVM's loop vectoriser does not vectorise a conditional store. The loop condition now tests `dst`'s length as well as `src`'s. Once `f` is inlined, LLVM sees that the test after the call repeats one the condition already made, removes it, and the store becomes unconditional. A body that keeps a panic path, such as an overflow-checked `x + 7` or a table lookup whose index is not proven, still branches to its panic on every element and does not vectorise, here or before. The proof still holds every access, with no new NL9007. `fromRange` (`parallelFrom`) already had this shape and vectorises; `reduceRange` stores nothing. The caller has already checked that the range is inside both arrays, so the new test never ends the loop early.

Fixes #619

entries.title: refuse an exported function that takes a C symbol, and spell private ones apart
entries.body:
A function of the program's own package keeps its name as its symbol. An exported one, or any one under `--no-strict-exports`, named after a symbol the C library defines (`write`, `read`, `free`, `exit`, `sin`, `sbrk`, `abs`, …) or beginning with `_`, `napi_` or `node_api_`, replaced the C one in the linked program: `console.log` printed nothing, `Math.sin` answered with the program's `sin`, or the program crashed. Such a function is now refused with NL3037, on every target. A private function with such a name is no longer folded as the C function: it gets a symbol ending in `$`, so a private `floor(1.5)` or `abs(-3)` returns what the program's own function returns. The reserved names cover the runtime's C calls, libm, the allocator, every name a statically linked wasi-libc member defines or references, and every library function LLVM 18 recognises by name. `tests/run.js` reads them back with `llvm-nm` and `llvm-tli-checker` from the runtime, the N-API shim, the wasi-libc members a wasi link pulls in, LLVM's library-function tables for five targets, and programs that call every `Math` builtin and copy, multiply and print, and fails on any name `src/c-symbols.ts` does not reserve. CI now links both tools.

Fixes #618

entries.title: arrow tasks with captures, tasks without a destination, and a seeded Rng
entries.body:
A scope's task can now be an arrow written at the `spawn`, and it may read
the `const` locals and the parameters of the function it is written in:
`s.spawn(() => binInto(xs, hist))` is the whole spelling of a task. Each
name the arrow reads is copied into the task's payload beside its argument
and read on the task's thread when the scope joins, so every scope rule
holds of it as of the argument: the parent may not write it before the
join by any name, helper or constructor, a destination is never captured,
and a captured `Mutex` is held to R7 and R8. A guard, a channel, a scope, a
`Result`, a value that may be absent and a `Secret` are not captured, and
neither is a `let` or `this`. The arrow is lifted into a function named
after the one it is written in, which is what a debugger shows for the
task's thread.

`s.spawn(entry, arg)` and `s.spawn(() => ...)` run a task that answers
`void` and has nothing to store; the four-argument form still stores an
answer. A task's argument and captures are read again at the join, so a
`push` that may move an element one of them refers to is refused between
the spawn and the end of the block.

A function may write the own slots of an object it made itself without
that counting as a shared write, as it already could an array. A write
below those slots counts as a write into whatever they may hold, so once
the caller's memory is inside the object it is refused as any shared
write is. That is what lets a parallel body or a task step a generator of
its own.

`nish/random` adds `Rng`: `new Rng(seed)`, `nextI32()` and `nextF64()`, a
Weyl sequence through all 2^32 states with MurmurHash3's finaliser on each.
Its wraps are `nish:unsafe`'s, so every answer is the same bits natively
and under Node.

entries.title: P-256's share of a TLS 1.3 handshake, the baseline and the bar
entries.body:
WP34 K5 left P-256's 64-bit or fixed-base-table path waiting on "a
profile of signing". This is that profile, taken before anything is
built, and the bar the table will be judged by.

One TLS 1.3 handshake against `tests/link/net_interop_server` under
callgrind spends 68.9% of the server's instructions in
`std/crypto/p256.ts`, nearly all of it CertificateVerify's signature.
The base-point multiplication `k·G` alone is 58.2%, and 41.7% is its
256 point doublings, which a fixed-base table removes. X25519 is next at
22.8%. So the plan's stop rule, which ends the work here if P-256 is
under 10% of a handshake, does not apply.

`bench/p256.ts` and `bench/p256.mjs` time `p256PublicKey`,
`p256SignSha256` and `p256VerifySha256`. Inputs change on every
iteration, and every answer is folded into a pinned checksum. Verify
must also refuse a tampered copy of each signature before its clock
starts, so a verify that accepts everything fails the bench. `--self`
times a byte-identical copy beside the baseline to give the noise band,
and `--check` holds every later build of the module to the same answers.

The bar, recorded in docs/wp34-hosting-cs.md before the table exists:
- signing's minimum at or under 245.8 µs, that is 3x faster and outside
  the noise band;
- P-256 no longer the largest module in a handshake's server
  instructions, which means under X25519's 3,147,968 Ir;
- verify no slower.

The plan's "under 25% of a handshake" was dropped. The parts of a
signature a table cannot touch, the two inversions and the hashing, are
already 25.6% of a handshake in which `k·G` costs nothing. The
instruction projection, 3,136,541 Ir, about 3.0x, sits level with the
second condition. The doc says the time ratio is known only once it is
measured.

entries.title: measure S3's bar kernels without a nish:simd surface (WP38 S3a)
entries.body:
S3's bar is a `nish:simd` kernel at least 1.5x faster than the same
kernel in scalar Nish. S3a answers it before any type exists. It writes
the two bar kernels in C with the portable `vector_size(16)` vectors
`nish:simd` would lower to, and times them against the fair scalar
comparator in §3.2.1. The kernels are spectral's mat-vec and
`bench/scan.ts`'s depth count.

Each kernel comes in four forms in `bench/simd-s3a/`: C vector, C
scalar, Nish with checked indexing, and Nish with `uncheckedGet`.
`bench/simd-s3a.mjs` builds them and refuses any vector form whose
source or IR reaches an `llvm.x86.` or `llvm.aarch64.` intrinsic. It
times the forms in rotating rounds, fails on a checksum mismatch, and
reports whether each scalar form vectorised. `--self` adds a
byte-identical copy of the Nish checked form to give the noise band.

The record is in `docs/wp38-simd.md` §2.3. At the median, form 1
(C vector) over form 3 (Nish checked) is:
- 1.65x on mat-vec;
- 1.81x and 3.51x on the two depth documents.

All three are outside a noise band within 5%, so both kernels clear
1.5x on x86-64, and S3's design is written next.

About 1.3x of the mat-vec margin is a Nish-vs-C scalar gap that is not
diagnosed here: C vector over C scalar is 1.25x. No AArch64 machine
was at hand.

entries.title: wipe every key a TLS connection holds when it ends
entries.body:
A TLS connection now wipes what it holds at every way it ends, with a
store `opt -O2` keeps.

- A direction's AES key schedules are wiped by `aesKeyWipe`: all of
  `roundKeys`, the runtime kernels' powers of H included, and H. Until now
  they were zeroed by ordinary stores. The key and IV stay `secureZero`'d.
- `TlsRecordServer.fail` seals its fatal alert first, then wipes both
  directions' keys, both traffic secrets it keeps for KeyUpdate and
  everything `TlsServer` holds. Before, a failed connection kept its
  traffic keys until its slot was closed or reused. The client's own error
  alert, a stream cut off without `close_notify`, and `abort` wipe the same.
- `close` wipes the resumption master secret at once. Once the server's
  `close_notify` is sealed, the last record it writes, the write direction
  is wiped; once the client's arrives, after which nothing is read, the
  read direction is.
- `TlsServer.wipeResumption` wipes the resumption master secret's array,
  whether or not `resumptionSecret` points at it yet. `fail` uses it, and
  the record server's wipe of `TlsServer` calls it, so the carrier's slot
  close (`TlsTcpServer.close`) wipes it too. Until now only `fail` and the
  slot's next `restart` did. A caller that wants the secret reads it
  before `close`.
- The x25519 exchange's words (`TlsExchangeWords`), which carry the
  ephemeral key in and the handshake secret out, are wiped whole by one
  `wipe` after the branch on the exchange's alert, so a refused exchange
  leaves them zero too. Before, each secret word was zeroed by an ordinary
  store, and the share's and public key's words not at all.

On a failure and at the slot close everything is wiped at once. After a
clean `close` the wipes come in steps: the write direction and the
resumption secret at once, the read direction at the client's
`close_notify`, and the rest at `wipeKeys`. The carrier's slot close
calls `wipeKeys`, and so does a program that drives `TlsRecordServer`
without `TlsTcpServer`.

This closes TLS-2. It narrows TLS-1 to two things: the one-shot answers
(the key schedule's, and `tlsNextTrafficSecret`, which only tests call)
and the secrets an open connection needs. TLS-4, the carrier's missing
timeout, stays open.

Measured: TlsRecordServer.wipeKeys, which every failed end now runs, on a
connected AES-256-GCM slot, 1,000,000 calls a run, median of 21
interleaved rounds, three runs: 310-317 ns on main, 342-377 ns here, 10%
to 20% (30 to 60 ns) more per connection end. The noise band, this build
against a byte-identical copy of itself in the same rounds, was 5.3% to
9.4%; the rise is outside it in two runs of three. Nothing per record
changed. tests/link/net_tls_wipes reads back 98 checks; 39 of them
fail on ab9099e, before this change. After opt -O2 the handshake's own
wipes count open 16, sign 5, handleFinished 1, start 59 and advance 397,
and deleting any one lowers its root's count.
tests: tls: the wipes survive opt -O2 (both directions' keys
IVs and AES schedules; the traffic
exporter and resumption secrets; the exchange's words)

entries.title: --cpu x86-64-v3 links module and runtime at one CPU level (WP38 S2)
entries.body:
`nish --link` and `nish run` take `--cpu x86-64-v3`. The program, `runtime.c`
and every runtime unit it brings are compiled with
`-march=x86-64-v3 -ffp-contract=off`, and so is the LTO link. Module and
runtime get the level together because the speed profile's LTO inlines
runtime functions into the module.

`-ffp-contract=off` keeps the level's FMA from fusing `a*b+c`, so a float
prints what the baseline binary prints. The IR does not change by a byte,
so no operation changes meaning. A binary built this way dies with
`SIGILL` on a CPU without AVX2, so the flag is for binaries that stay on
known machines. Release binaries stay baseline.

`x86-64-v3` is the only accepted level. Each of the following exits 2
with one line naming it:
- any other value (`native`, `x86-64-v4`, `armv8.2-a`) or a missing value;
- `--profile wasi`, and `scripts/build.sh --profile wasm`;
- a target or host that is not x86-64.

Both cache keys carry the level, so a baseline runtime is never linked
into a v3 program. `--emit-capabilities` records `"cpu": "x86-64-v3"`
when the flag is given. A baseline report is unchanged.

Constant-time verification now reads x86-64 at the baseline and again at
x86-64-v3. That covers every `ct_asm` fixture and the runtime's AES
kernels. CT-16 is narrowed to every level but those two.

entries.title: wipe a connection's packet keys and AES schedules when a level, generation or connection ends
entries.body:
A QUIC connection now wipes every key it holds, with stores no optimiser
removes, at each point a level, a key generation or the connection itself
ends, and QUIC-2 closes.

- **Key slots.** `QuicKeysSlot.wipe` wipes its four AES schedules with
  `aesKeyWipe`, a volatile `llvm.memset` over the whole of `roundKeys` (the
  kernels' powers of H included) and over H, instead of the ordinary stores
  of the deleted `quicPacketClearAes`.
- **Key update.** The generation a key update replaces loses its packet
  key's AES schedule along with its key, IV and secret, in
  `updateWriteKeys` at once and in `prepareNextReadKeys` a probe timeout
  later. The header-protection key and schedule, which every generation
  shares, still go with the level.
- **Connection end.** A connection that closes keeps its keys through the
  closing or draining period, three probe timeouts (RFC 9000 §10.2), and
  `runClocks` wipes them all at the period's end. After `close` or `fail`
  the period starts when the CONNECTION_CLOSE is handed out, not when the
  connection closes, so the close is still sealed however long the caller
  waits before asking for it. A closed connection used to skip `runClocks`
  entirely, so its keys stayed until `release()` or `reset`; `deadline()`
  now names the period's end for a closed connection that has sent its
  close. The CONNECTION_CLOSE is sent once and never again in the closing
  state (RFC 9000 §10.2.1 lets an endpoint answer nothing there), so the
  period is kept for its timing and the keys outlive their last use by it.
  A close owed and never taken keeps the keys until `release()` or `reset`,
  since they must still seal it. Nothing a connection sends changes.
- **What `wipeAll` takes** now includes `TlsServer`'s resumption master
  secret, through `TlsServer.wipeResumption` (#652), which wipes its array
  whether or not `resumptionSecret` points at it yet, and
  discarding the Handshake level wipes `TlsServer`'s handshake traffic
  secrets, which nothing reads after it.
- **Reset tokens and derivations.** The HMAC outputs and scratch hashers of
  each connection ID and stateless reset token, the first ID's token once it
  is in the transport parameters, the Initial secret once both directions'
  are expanded, and the read secret a key update replaces are wiped once used.
- **Each packet.** Sealing and opening wipe the nonce, which is the IV XORed
  with a public packet number and so gives the IV away, and the
  header-protection mask, once each is used.

Each wipe is pinned under `opt -O2` with an exact count over 20 roots, and
each of the 67 wipe lines was deleted in turn: 66 lowered at least one
count, and the 67th, the call to `wipeResumption`, whose wipe the TLS
group counts, fails the read-backs;
a new link test reads back as zero, under all three suites, every key slot
and secret a server connection still holds at each end of life, and at
`release()` and `reset` only also the reset tokens and encoded transport
parameters it lets go of, from a snapshot taken before; it also checks
that the close still goes out ten probe timeouts after `close` or `fail`.
Seven wipes no read-back sees are pinned by the count alone: `wipeAll`'s
loops over the read and write secrets and over the peer's connection-ID
tokens, its wipe of the peer's reset token, its wipe of the other read
generation and `prepareNextReadKeys`', and `updateWriteKeys`' wipe of the
replaced write secret. QUIC-1 now says what is still open: the allocating
key forms, which a connection does not use.
metrics: net_quic_memory (309 connections through one slot, three suites) 193.2 ms against 190.6 ms on main, 1.014x, inside the 1.024x noise band of main against a byte-identical copy of itself (medians of 21 interleaved rounds)

Verify went from 1080.3 to 1065.1 µs, inside its noise band of +0.7% / +4.9%. entries.title: wipe the stateless-reset and Retry token keys and the listener seed when the server is released
entries.body:
A QUIC server kept its two static keys, the stateless reset key and the
Retry token key, and the listener's 32-byte seed for as long as the
process lived, and nothing wiped them when the server stopped (QUIC-5).

`QuicListener.release()` now wipes the listener's seed, its generator's
pool, its tag and HKDF scratch, the Initial secrets and key slots an
INVALID_TOKEN close is sealed with, and the spare answer `handle` keeps,
which holds the last Retry or stateless reset token it sent. After it,
`handle` and `handleWindow` answer no datagram. `Http3Server.stop()` is
the server's one release path: it releases every slot's connection and
the listener, then wipes the configuration's `statelessResetKey` and
`retryTokenKey`, the connection-ID index's salt, the connections' entropy
scratch and the server's own last answer. A new
`QuicListenerAnswer.wipe()` zeroes an answer across its whole room, not
only its current length.

The configuration's two keys are the server's once it is made with them,
and `stop` zeroes them in place: give each server a `QuicServerConfig` of
its own, since any other listener or connection made with the same one
would go on signing tokens under an all-zero key. A program that keeps
its own copy of a key, to start the next server with, wipes that copy
itself.

Every wipe runs only at release, so the Retry tokens and stateless resets
a server sends before it are byte for byte what they were.
metrics: after opt -O2, 3 volatile wipes in QuicListenerAnswer.wipe, 47 in QuicListener.release and 242 in Http3Server.stop; deleting any one of the 21 wipe lines lowers a count (by 1 to 94)

entries.title: TLS and QUIC one-shot key derivations take and answer Secret
entries.body:
TLS 1.3's one-shot key schedule in `nish/net/tls/schedule` (`tlsExtract`,
`tlsExpandLabel`, `tlsDeriveSecret`, `tlsEarlySecret`, `tlsHandshakeSecret`,
`tlsMasterSecret`, `tlsTrafficKey`, `tlsTrafficIv`, `tlsFinishedVerifyData`)
and `nish/net/tls/record`'s `tlsNextTrafficSecret` now take every secret as
a `Secret<u8[]>`, and those that derive a secret answer one. Transcript
hashes, labels and contexts stay plain, and `tlsFinishedVerifyData` answers
its verify data plain, because the peer reads it in the Finished message.
Each function computes inside `expose` and wipes the "derived" salts, the
zero inputs and `finished_key` before it returns.

QUIC's one-shot derivations in `nish/net/quic-packet` (`quicKeys`,
`quicKeysUpdate`, `quicKeyUpdateSecret`) take the traffic secret as a
`Secret<u8[]>`. They wipe each HKDF output once it is copied into the
`QuicKeys`. The new `quicKeysWipe` zeroes a `QuicKeys`' key, IV and
header-protection key and both AES schedules. A generation `quicKeysUpdate`
derives holds its own copy of the header-protection key and its own
schedule of it, so wiping one generation leaves the other usable.

Passing a plain `u8[]` where a secret is expected is now a compile error.
Callers wrap the secret they hold with `secret(...)` and `wipe` what they
are given back. The connection types (`QuicConnection`, `TlsServer`) already
kept their secrets in key slots they wipe, and are unchanged.
metrics: volatile wipes after opt -O2, quicKeys 15, quicKeysUpdate 14, quicKeysWipe 7; tlsEarlySecret 28, tlsHandshakeSecret 57, tlsMasterSecret 58, tlsFinishedVerifyData 57

entries.title: AtomicI32 and AtomicI64 in nish/threads
entries.body:
`nish/threads` gains two lock-free counters, `AtomicI32` and `AtomicI64`,
for tasks that share one number. Each has `load`, `store`, `add`, `sub`,
`min`, `max`, `exchange` and `compareExchange`. Every update returns the
value it replaced, and `compareExchange` returns the value it saw. Each
method lowers to a single sequentially consistent `load atomic`,
`store atomic`, `atomicrmw` or `cmpxchg`, aligned to the width of the
value, and this is valid for wasm32. Under Node they are plain
operations. An `AtomicI64` agrees with Node while its values stay within
±2^53.

An atomic is reached only through its methods (NL2514). The parent may
not touch one inside the block of a scope it was handed to (NL2513).
Calling an atomic method is the one shared write that a `parallel` body
may make. The compiler checks that the access is sound, not that the
updates commute: an answer that does not depend on the schedule needs
updates that commute, and that is the program's obligation.

The scopes one `using` statement opens now share no destination, no
atomic and no lock among their tasks (NL2516). Natively they join one
after the other, the last declared first, while under Node each task
runs where it is spawned. An atomic or a `Mutex` made by `new` in a
`const` of its own is judged by its binding, so disjoint ones stay
accepted. An object literal of any `nish/threads` class is refused
(NL2515).

`examples/histogram-atomic.ts` counts 32 million values into 256 bins
over four tasks. With a local tally and one `add` per bin it is 3.2x
faster than one thread. With one `add` per value it is 9.7x faster than
a `Mutex` per value, but still slower than one thread, since every
increment contends for a shared cache line. Every mode prints the same
checksum.

CI's `test` job now has 25 minutes rather than 15: its first shard took
14m49s on main after the P-256 table (#663).
metrics: histogram-atomic, median of 7 interleaved rounds on 4 cores: one add per bin 24 ms, one thread 77 ms, one add per value 677 ms, a Mutex per value 6,565 ms; noise band 23-37 ms (byte-identical copy, median 24 ms)

entries.title: P-256's fixed-base table against the bar
entries.body:
WP34 K5 now records how the fixed-base comb (#663) measures against the bar its baseline (#641) set. Both builds were measured the baseline's way: a callgrind profile of the interop server's TLS 1.3 handshakes, and `bench/p256.mjs` in interleaved rounds. One build was `main` at `6e11fa6`, which has the comb; the other was `a22a056`, which does not. Each build had a byte-identical copy as its noise column.

A handshake now takes 1.86x fewer server instructions than on `a22a056`, and signing is about 3x faster. Against the bar:

- **Sign is not met.** The gain is not shown outside the noise band. The two samples split: one met its re-based bar (253.2 against 263.4 µs) and one missed it (253.4 against 249.9 µs). Both sit inside this machine's 5.5% band. Reading the lowest minima, a rule chosen after the data, gives 3.04x where the bar asks 3.07x.
- **P-256 is still not under X25519.** P-256 takes 43.9% of a handshake and X25519 43.1%, so P-256 is still the largest module, though down from 70.0%.
- **Verify did not slow.**

The K5 row now says what is done and what is left. Most of what is left is the two inversions, `p256ScalarInvert` and the affine field inversion, which together are 41.5% of a signature. 64-bit limbs and the verify path, which keeps the variable-base window, are left too. Nothing was tuned for the measurement.

entries.title: enum member types such as Kind.Array
entries.body:
An enum's member can now be written as a type. `Kind.Array` in an
annotation is a slot that holds exactly that member, which is what a
`readonly` tag field needs: `readonly kind: Kind.Array = Kind.Array`. A
discriminated union will later read that tag.

Each slot accepts only the member's own constant, or a value already of the
member type. Any other member, and any plain `Kind` value, is refused with
NL2519. This holds for fields, parameters, returns, locals, array elements,
object-literal fields, `Ok`/`Err`/`unwrapOr`, ternaries, `??`, and the
arguments of direct, method, constructor and generic calls.

A member type converts to its enum, and a read of one is the enum wherever a
value is computed with: it compares with `===`, switches, and passes as a
`Kind`. In IR it is the enum's `i32`. `enum_member_type` lowers to the same
bytes as the same program with every member type written `Kind`.

Inference follows `tsc`:
- A fresh constant widens: `let k = Kind.Array` is a `Kind`.
- A value already of the member type keeps it, through `let`, ternaries,
  array literals, `??`, generic arguments and inferred arrow results.
  `map([a], (k) => k)` is a `Kind.Array[]`.
- Two different members in one ternary or array literal are refused, with a
  request to annotate the type.
- `id(Kind.Array)` and `apply(f, Kind.Array)`, where only the constant binds
  `T`, are refused. These are documented limits, stricter than `tsc`.

Codes:
- NL2517: the qualifier before the dot is not an enum.
- NL2518: the enum has no such member.
- NL2519: a member slot was given another value.
- NL2520: `new Array<Kind.Array>(n)` would zero-fill with a different member.
- NL2521: a `parallelMap`, `parallelFrom` or `parallelReduce` body answers
  such a member type, refused at the call.

A field initializer may now be an enum member constant. Typed JSON refuses a
member-typed field. A member type crosses to C and JavaScript exactly where
its enum does, which is nowhere.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: strings and scalar arrays cross threads by copy-at-join
entries.body:
A scoped task, `parallelMap`, `parallelFrom` and `parallelMapInto` can now
answer a `string` or a scalar array, a `Channel<string>` sends and receives
strings, and a `Mutex` guard stores and reads a string.

The value is copied at the join. On the worker, a result built since the
task began is copied into a transfer block. After the join, the block is
copied into the arena of the thread that opened the scope and freed. A
literal, or a string from an outer frame, crosses without a copy. Every
task's temporaries, whatever it answers, and each map element's are
released as soon as the answer is kept, so a long scope or a long map
holds one element's temporaries at a time.

`parallelReduce` stays scalar. A `string[]` element, a nested array, a
class, `Map` and `Set` are still refused, because nothing is copied deeply.
The copy-in is serial, so a map of cheap string-answering elements is
slower than the sequential loop today.

Measured: a 1 MB string task result costs about 1.7 ms per crossing (885 ms
against 536 ms over 200 results at 4 threads); five maps of 1M short strings
take 270 ms at 4 threads against 200 ms sequential (noise band 11 ms); a
million 2 KB element temporaries peak at 64 MB (68 MB on 8 threads); 24,000
tasks answering a string, an i32 or nothing peak at 3 MB on one thread,
3.5 GB without the release; a scalar task with a 1 MB temporary takes
2,239 ms over 1,000 tasks on one thread against 2,238 ms before the release
(noise band 35 ms); runtime-cross.c is 1,170 bytes of .text (1,235
threaded) against a ceiling of 1,280

entries.title: threat model for TLS 1.3 session resumption
entries.body:
* docs(security): threat model for TLS 1.3 session resumption

Records the design of server-side TLS 1.3 session resumption in
`docs/security/tls.md` before any of it is written: the attacker and what
a win is; ticket keys as caller-held `Secret`s (NL2430), sealing for 12 h,
accepted as the previous key for one 2 h ticket lifetime and then wiped;
single-use tickets through a bounded strike register that fails closed;
`psk_dhe_ke` only, so a leaked ticket key exposes no recorded traffic;
0-RTT out of scope; and the fallback-versus-abort table, checked against
RFC 8446's MUSTs, that the later stages are tested against.

Refs: #481

* docs(security): decide the strike register's order, fill cost, clock and key bounds for resumption

Review round 1: tickets are spent once their binder verifies, in one call with no gap
between check and record; the register's fill cost is restated and counted; every
time is monotonicNanos; the module enforces each key's issue window, 14-hour life
and a 2^30 seal cap from a public TlsTicketKeyInfo; the rotation turn is the
caller's; and an opened ticket leaves exposeWith as a fresh array the caller
parses and wipes.

* docs(security): qualify the resumption bounds in awake time and record TLS-5

Review round 2: the key bounds are awake time under CLOCK_MONOTONIC; an early
rotation may end the previous key's tickets, which the design accepts; the
strike register's fill cost is scoped to an attacker without a key, and a
key-holder's is stated; the wipes no test can read are pinned in the IR after
-O2; row 14 wins over the rows that never abort, and row 16 is placed for QUIC.
TLS-5 records the ChaCha20 state that keeps a copy of its key, which #639 closes.

* docs(security): close TLS-5, now that #639 wipes the ChaCha20 state

* docs(security): bound strike entries by the server's lifetime, and count TLS-5

Review round 3: a strike entry lives no longer than one server lifetime after
it is recorded, and a ticket whose sealed lifetime exceeds the server's or whose
chain start follows its issue time fails to open, so a key holder cannot pin
entries past rotation. The T2 result's open-finding sentence is brought up to
date, and the security index counts TLS-5 as a fixed Low.

* docs(security): pin the strike clamp through take, and bound a key holder's fill

Review round 4: the register's own clamp is pinned by calling
TlsTicketStrikes.take directly, since a ticket claiming a longer life no longer
opens; and a leaked key's fill is bounded on both branches, at most about 16
awake hours after the draw, with what retiring a key that still opens as the
previous one takes.

* docs(security): state the strike entry's boundary and what take answers

Review round 5: an entry is held through its expiry inclusive, matching when a
ticket opens, and TlsTicketStrikes.take answers true when it records an id and
false when the id is held or the register is full.

* docs(security): pin the TLS resumption wipes, salt and binder order

Round 7 of review on the resumption threat model. Each of `tlsTicketOpen`
and `tlsTicketSeal` wipes its plaintext once, after its branch, since
`opt -O2` merges per-path wipes. The record now covers the resumed
handshake-secret salt, which is secret, and the PSK, PSK early secret and
binder key on every path, the fail and close wipe included. It also covers
the strike register's probe-chain scan and the time a leaked key's bytes
stay in memory. A ClientHello that hits both a failed binder and a missing
`signature_algorithms` gets `decrypt_error`.

Refs: docs/security/tls.md

* docs(security): pin the resumed salt's wipes and the codec's mode check

The resumed handshake's salt is read and zeroed at the top of tlsExchange,
beside the key's words, and its rebuilt bytes are wiped on every path; the
net_tls_resume pin now covers a low-order share and the row 4 to 8
fallbacks. The wipe-count paragraph names its real roots and says what a
textual count proves. A malformed psk_key_exchange_modes is a decode_error
whether or not pre_shared_key is present.

* docs(security): place the resumed master secret's wipe and pin the exchange salt

A resumed handshake has no sign, so the master secret's derivation and wipe
move into a post-Finished schedule step both paths call, counted by the
wipe-count check. tlsExchange wipes its rebuilt salt array once, at a point
every path reaches, and is a root too. The ticket roots carry their real
counts, with the rotation turn's wipe noted as checker-enforced (NL2442), and
a malformed psk_key_exchange_modes without pre_shared_key is pinned.

* docs(security): spell out the master-secret step and the exchange's salt source

The master-secret step split out of sign is named TlsServer.masterSecretStep
and lists all it does: the application and exporter secrets, the expected
client Finished absorbed into the transcript before the resumption master
secret, the wait-Finished state, and the master's wipe. The caller always
writes the salt's words, the constant's on a full handshake, so tlsExchange
needs no flag and its one wipe is unconditional.

* docs(security): point the master-secret step's fields at the slot's arrays

TlsServer.masterSecretStep points the application, exporter and expected
client Finished fields at the slot's arrays before its arena block opens, as
sign does, so its derivations land where wipeHandshake wipes; it wipes the
master before setting the wait-Finished state. Two stale references to sign
and the roots sentence are reworded.

* docs(security): pin both salt wipes and the master secret's by deletion

The resumption design now says exchangeKeys writes the salt's words and,
on a resumed handshake, wipes the derived salt's bytes before calling
tlsExchange. It pins exchangeKeys at 7, two more than its 5, with each salt
wipe shown counted on its own by deleting it. The master secret's
secureZero in masterSecretStep is shown the same way, and sign and
masterSecretStep together count at least sign's 5.

entries.title: two system calls per keep-alive HTTP/1.1 request, and output buffers borrowed from a pool
entries.body:
`Http1Server` spent four system calls on a keep-alive request where two do
the work, and allocated every slot's output buffer up front. Now:

- `readable` stops at a short read rather than reading until the socket
  answers -11. The loop's readiness is level-triggered, so more input, or
  the peer's close, wakes it again.
- The new `rearm(slot, wants)` answers whether a slot's interest changed and
  a `pollModify` (an `epoll_ctl`) is needed at all. On a keep-alive
  connection it is not, so a request is one `recv` and one `send`.
- `accept` takes a free slot from a stack instead of scanning past every
  busy one.
- The slots of `Http1Server` and `Http1TlsServer` borrow their output buffer
  from one `Http1OutputPool` while they write and give it back once sent, so
  a pool's memory follows the connections the socket is holding back rather
  than its size. The pool makes a buffer only when none is free, so a warmed
  server still allocates nothing per request. A standalone `Http1Connection`
  makes its own buffer on first use and keeps it.

`bench/http1-server.ts` and `bench/http.mjs` are the load test that measured
it: wrk against one `Http1Server` pinned to one core, builds interleaved round
by round, with user and system CPU per request, peak RSS, and `--syscalls`
for strace's count per request. bench/README.md also records the same
scenarios against hyper, nginx, Bun, Go and Node.
metrics: keep-alive /plaintext 153,329 -> 175,303 req/s (+14.3%), /json 153,822 -> 169,507 (+10.2%), 64 connections churning beside 8,000 idle ones 51,003 -> 64,763 (+27.0%), against a byte-identical copy of the base at -2.7%, +3.3% and +0.2% (5 interleaved rounds of 5 s, one 2.1 GHz Xeon core, wrk -t3); system calls per keep-alive request 4.10 -> 2.06; resident size after start-up 4,708 MB -> 251 MB at 65,536 slots and 1,178 MB -> 64 MB at 16,384, peak RSS under load at 9,000 slots 633 MB -> 35 MB, with keep-alive throughput -0.5% and +1.8% against a copy's +2.2% and -3.7% over 7 rounds, and +12.7% at 4,096 connections (copy +2.6%).

entries.title: an h2load harness for HTTP/3 latency, and the cause of the 1 ms stalls
entries.body:
`bench/h3-latency.mjs` measures the HTTP/3 server in `tests/link/net_interop_server`'s `serve` mode against nginx 1.31.7 with h2load 1.70. It runs three scenarios: one connection with one request in flight, 96 connections with one request each, and 96 connections with ten requests each.

- **Noise band.** Every round also times a byte-identical copy of the nish binary, and the spread between the two is printed next to each figure.
- **Pinning.** The server runs on core 0 and h2load on cores 1–3, in interleaved rounds.
- **Latency.** p50 and p99 are taken from h2load's per-request log. Only 2xx rows count, and a run with failed requests fails.
- **Server CPU.** Busy share and CPU per request come from `/proc/<pid>/stat`.
- **Baseline.** `--baseline <rev>` builds and times another revision in the same rounds.
- **Tools.** `bench/h3-latency/build-tools.sh` builds the pinned, checksummed tools under `~/.cache/nish-h3-bench`: OpenSSL 3.6.5, ngtcp2 1.25.0, nghttp3 1.18.0, nghttp2 1.70.0 and nginx 1.31.7.

`docs/h3-latency.md` records what reproduces and why. With a 4 kB body, a single client's p99 was 1.62 ms against nginx's 232 µs, with the server only 29% busy. The cause is the QUIC pacer:

- It works in whole milliseconds.
- A loopback RTT truncates to 0 ms, so it paces as if the RTT were 1 ms.
- Its budget is capped at the 12,000-byte initial window.
- A connection that has spent its budget is filed on the timer wheel for the next tick.

Turning pacing off in a local patch brought that p99 down to 258–316 µs. With a 100 B body the stall does not reproduce on the measuring machine: p99 was 203 µs against nginx's 223 µs. The record also lists the leads it refuted and the ones it did not test. A separate per-byte CPU cost in the QUIC stream path explains the throughput gap under load.

No change to `std/`, `src/`, `runtime/` or `tests/`.

Measured: 4 kB, single connection, p99 1.62 ms (nish) vs 232 µs (nginx), noise band ±0.5 %; pacing off 258–316 µs
Refs: docs/h3-latency.md, bench/README.md#http3-latency
Part of #670

entries.title: HTTP/1.1 responses carry a Date header
entries.body:
Every final response an Http1Server or Http1TlsServer writes, the
server's own 4xx/5xx included, now carries a Date field in IMF-fixdate
form (RFC 9110 §6.6.1), and a 1xx carries none. A program's own `date`
field, in any case, is sent instead, so a response never has two.

`httpDateWrite` (nish/net/http-fields) formats a Unix second without
reading a clock, so it is wasm32-safe and any protocol can share it.
`HttpDate` (nish/net/http1-server) holds the formatted bytes for one
server: it reads `Date.now()` per response and formats again only when
the second changes, in either direction of a clock step, with
`Arena.used()` flat. All of a pool's slots share one, exposed as
`server.date`; `server.date.pin(ms)` fixes the clock for tests that
compare a server's bytes.

Both inside the band, so no change is claimed. System calls a request unchanged (2.09/2.08 keep-alive, 5.11/5.08 close). User CPU a request +0.10-0.15 us (1.21 -> 1.36, 1.44 -> 1.54) against 0.03-0.06 us between main and its copy.

entries.title: discriminated union types
entries.body:
A union of tagged classes and interfaces, `type Shape = Circle | Square`,
can now be declared, stored, passed and returned, and its tag read. A
variant is a non-generic class or interface whose first field is a
`readonly` tag of one enum member type, such as
`readonly kind: Kind.Circle = Kind.Circle`. Every other union is still
refused with NL1053.

A union is one pointer to the variant it holds, typed
`%union.tagged = type { i32 }`. A variant converts to its union by a
`bitcast`. The tag is read by a `getelementptr` to field 0 and a load,
whatever the variant.

A union may be the type of a local, a parameter, a field, a return or
an array element, or of a nullable form of any of these. A variant, or a
narrower union, converts wherever the union is expected. Under `-g` a
union gets a DWARF type. A variant stored into a field or an array
outlives the arena that made it.

Each refusal has its own code and wording:

- NL2522: a generic variant
- NL2523: a variant whose first field is not the tag
- NL2524: tags from two enums
- NL2525: tag fields with different names
- NL2526: two variants with the same tag
- NL2527: a union of one variant
- NL2528: reading a member other than the tag
- NL2529: a write through a union
- NL2530: an inferred tag local
- NL2531: a comparison no variant can satisfy
- NL2532: a `case` no variant can satisfy
- NL2533: a union type argument
- NL2534: a store that only some variants satisfy
- NL2535: a tag that is not `readonly`
- NL4009: a union in a signature or struct field across `--emit-header`,
  `--emit-dts`, `--emit-napi` or `--emit-napi-async`

This version does not narrow by the tag. A second comparison of the tag
after a test, and a comparison of a `const k: Kind = u.kind` local with a
member no variant has, are accepted here although `tsc` refuses them
(TS2367). LANGUAGE.md records the gap; narrowing closes it.

entries.title: measure a 64x64-to-128 multiply on Poly1305; the bar is missed on wasm32
entries.body:
WP41 asked whether a widening multiply, `mulHigh` and `mulLow` on `u64`, earns a place in the language. The bar was committed before anything was timed. The test was Poly1305 rewritten onto the multiply: it had to be faster natively by more than the noise band, and not lose outside the band on wasm32.

The radix-2^64 kernel built on the multiply is 14–21% faster natively on x86-64, well outside the band. On wasm32 it is 19–27% slower, also outside the band. wasm32 has no 64×64→128 instruction, and the `-nostdlib` profile forbids the `__multi3` libcall, so each `mulHigh` becomes a sequence of 16 operations. A radix-2^44 variant was inside the band natively and 94% slower on wasm32.

Under the pre-registered rule, a wasm32 loss is a miss, so the builtin and the kernel are not shipped. `docs/wp41-mul-wide.md` records the figures, the method, the reason for the loss and what would reopen the question. The measured tree is preserved at 8cceabe on the stage's branch.
metrics: native −14.2% min / −19.1% median (noise band +1.1% / −0.4%); wasm32 +18.8% / +22.6% (band −0.8% / −1.7%); 30 interleaved rounds, 2^12 MACs over 64 KiB, checksum 2156522685 in every column

entries.title: HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 responses carry a date field
entries.body:
Every final HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 response head now carries one `date`
field (RFC 9110 §6.6.1), from the same once-a-second `HttpDate` cache
the HTTP/1.1 server uses. Each server holds one cache, exposed as
`server.date`, and refreshes it at its entry points, so the date is at
most one loop turn old. Trailers and 1xx heads carry none. A `date` the
program sets is sent instead of the server's, never beside it.

HTTP/2 sends it as an HPACK literal without indexing on static name
33, so the dynamic table stays empty, and counts it against the output
room. HTTP/3 sends it as a QPACK literal and counts it against the
peer's SETTINGS_MAX_FIELD_SECTION_SIZE; the server's own 431 drops the
date rather than reset a stream whose peer limit has no room for it.
Neither allocates per response.

entries.title: HKDF, TLS schedule and QUIC derivations into a held Secret
entries.body:
`nish/crypto/hkdf`, `nish/net/tls` and `nish/net/quic-packet` gain *Held forms. Each derives straight into a `Secret<u8[]>` the caller already holds, overwriting it in place, so the derived key never exists as a second plain copy beside the Secret that owns it:

- `hkdfExpandLabelSha256Held`, `hkdfExpandLabelSha384Held` and `hkdfExpandLabelHeldInto`
- `tlsDeriveSecretHeld`, `tlsHandshakeSecretHeld`, `tlsMasterSecretHeld`, `tlsFinishedVerifyDataHeld` and `tlsTrafficKeysFromHeld`
- `TlsRecordProtection.installHeld` and `advanceHeld`, which ratchet a held traffic secret in place on KeyUpdate
- `quicKeysHeldInto` and `quicKeyUpdateSecretHeldInto`

Each form builds its output in a plain buffer through `exposeWith`, copies it into the held secret, and wipes the buffer before it returns. Every plain intermediate is wiped on every path: the HKDF output, the extracted PRK, the derived salt, the zero input and the finished key. Hash lengths other than 32 or 48, wrong-length secrets and out-of-range output windows panic before any key material is derived.

The forms are additive. No existing caller or output changes; the TLS and QUIC holders move onto them in the next stages of #668.

entries.title: guard helpers, thread diagnostics that say what to write, and --fix for them
entries.body:
A `MutexGuard<T>` can now be handed to a helper function. The helper reads
and stores through `g.value` the way the block holding the lock does, so the
code under a lock can be split into functions. A helper may not keep the
guard, return it, store it, capture it, hand it to `spawn` or `new`, forward
it where the checker cannot follow, or take a second guard (NL2536). Each of
these would let the guarded data outlive the lock. An arrow's expression
body, `(g) => g.value`, is judged as its `return` would be.

Several writes a scoped task makes to memory it allocated itself used to be
refused, and are now accepted:
- a method call on an object it made;
- `Map.set`, `Set.add` and `Set.delete` on its own collections;
- writes to the array fields of its own objects;
- writes through a second name bound in the same statement;
- writes to an array a helper hands back when the helper returns its argument.

What could still reach the caller's memory stays refused, each shape with a
negative case:
- a holder that keeps a parameter;
- a rebound name;
- a helper that stores its parameter, or returns either of two arrays;
- a write below the top level of a helper's fresh answer that holds an argument.

Ten thread diagnostics, NL2463 to NL2481, now end with the code to write
instead. A `null` stored through a guard is NL2537. A guard copies a string
into memory the `Mutex` owns and frees the copy it replaces, so it has no
`null` to copy, and the message names the `boolean` flag or the empty string
to use instead.

`nish --fix` now rewrites the mechanical thread refusals:
- a `const` bound to `scope()` or `m.lock()` becomes `using` (NL2388, NL2465);
- a `spawn` without a destination gets one (NL2511);
- a captured `let` is read through a `const` snapshot written before the
  statement, `kNow`, `kNow2` (NL2506, NL2500);
- an arrow that uses a `Channel` moves to a top-level `const` (NL2484),
  keeping multi-line template text as written.

Shapes where the rewrite would change behaviour keep the refusal and get no
fix: a `let` written by the arrow, a loop header's `let`, a destination-less
`spawn` in a loop, and an arrow in a method.
metrics: 154 fix cases (23 of them `thread-`), 684 of 684 fix checks before the last two cases; 213 of 213 performance checks with 0 new NL9007 or NL9011 in src/

entries.title: POST /json-echo, a JSON request body through std/json
entries.body:
The HTTP/1.1 load-test server in `bench/http1-server.ts` now reads a request body. `POST /json-echo` takes a 545-byte order (`bench/http-payload.json`), decodes it with `jsonDecode` into a typed `Order`, adds one to its `revision`, and writes it back with `jsonEncode`. `POST /json-echo-doc` does the same exchange through one reused `JsonDocument` (`parse`, `set`, `write`) and answers the same bytes for a valid order. The body is gathered from `H1_BODY` events into a buffer that each slot reuses, so the warm path allocates nothing. A body over 4 KiB is refused with 413 by `Http1Config.maxBody` before it is read. A malformed body, or one with the wrong shape or a `revision` that would overflow, gets 400.

`bench/http.mjs` gains `post-json` and `post-json-doc` scenarios, driven by the new wrk script `bench/http-post-json.lua`. It also accepts `name=path` server arguments, and it checks every server's answer against the expected bytes before it times anything. A 404 turns that server's cells into `n/a`. Any other difference exits 1 and names the first byte that differs. A server that dies or never answers fails the check instead of hanging the run. These hooks are what the cross-runtime comparison servers in `bench/http-twins/` run through.

A byte-identical copy measured against itself gives a noise band of about ±6.3%, so the typed route's 5% lead over JsonDocument is inside the band. The typed route uses about 1 µs less user CPU per request.

entries.title: pace HTTP/3 in microseconds so loopback responses stop waiting for the next millisecond
entries.body:
The QUIC pacer counted whole milliseconds. On a path whose round trip is under a millisecond, three things followed:

- The smoothed RTT truncated to 0 and was floored at 1 ms.
- The pacer earned no credit until the clock ticked.
- Any datagram it held back waited at least a millisecond.

On loopback, a single connection's 4 kB GET had a p99 of 1.55 ms while the server sat 24% busy, waiting rather than working (`docs/h3-latency.md`, the cause recorded by #676).

The pacer now runs on a microsecond clock.

- `Http3Server.clock(micros)` passes the caller's clock to each connection before `serve` and `flushSlot`.
- The pacer keeps its budget, its last refill and its own smoothed RTT on that clock. `pacerRtt` follows RFC 9002 §5.3's UpdateRtt on the same samples as `smoothedRtt`.
- A `micros` value is read only when it falls inside the millisecond `now` names. A stale, missing or foreign one leaves the pacer on `now × 1000`, exactly as before.

A paced flight also starts only once the pacer has earned one millisecond's worth of credit, between one and four datagrams (`pacerQuantum`, `quicListenerFlightTime`). `flushSlot` wakes a slot at that flight time. Without the quantum, a pacer that earns by the microsecond sends one datagram per GSO send and loses throughput under load.

What RFC 9002 requires is unchanged:

- Loss detection and the probe timeout still count milliseconds, with kGranularity's 1 ms floor (§6.1.2, §6.2.1).
- `max_ack_delay` enters the probe timeout only after the handshake is confirmed.
- A burst is still at most the initial window (§7.7).

New checks in `net_quic_recovery`, `net_http3_server` and `net_loopback` (and their f64 twins) pin each of these. The existing millisecond pacer checks keep their expectations. Without the server's clock, the server pacer behaves as it did. Records: `docs/security/http3.md` H3-8, `docs/security/quic.md` QUIC-9.

At 96 connections with one request each and a 100-byte body, throughput is 1.8% lower and CPU per request 2.2% higher than before, outside the noise band. The likely cost is the per-flight pacer work. `docs/h3-latency.md` records it.

Measured: single-connection 4 kB p99 225 µs vs nginx 157 µs (1.43×; before 1.55 ms; noise ±9.2 %); server 99 % busy at c96 4 kB and 98 % at 100 B; c96m10 4 kB 15.9k vs 15.8k req/s (noise ±1.0 %), CPU/request 61.49 vs 62.15 µs (±0.4 %); c96m10 100 B 96.4k vs 94.0k req/s (±0.8 %); c96 100 B 32.9k vs 33.5k req/s (±0.1 %). Measured with `bench/h3-latency.mjs --runs 9 --baseline 249cbe9`; the noise band is nish against a byte-identical copy in the same interleaved rounds
Refs: docs/h3-latency.md#after-the-fix, docs/security/http3.md, docs/security/quic.md
Tests: tests/link/net_quic_recovery, tests/link/net_http3_server, tests/link/net_loopback

entries.title: the cross-runtime HTTP twins under bench/http-twins

entries.title: string parameters on declare function
entries.body:
A `declare function` may now take `string` and `string | null` parameters. That is WP27 S3.1, the first step of letting a Nish program call C APIs that take names, paths and messages without a hand-written shim.

The argument is C's NUL-terminated `const char *`, and C borrows it. The program passes `s->data`, the bytes the string already holds NUL-terminated, with no copy. A foreign function may read them until it returns and may not keep the address. A function that keeps its argument, `putenv` for example, is declared to take a `CPtr` that the program obtains from `strdup`. Nor may C write through the argument: `strtok` and `mkstemp` take a `CPtr` buffer. The compiler states this contract and cannot check it, so it is recorded as RT-14 in the runtime's security record. Escape analysis treats the argument as a read, as it treats the string `console.log` prints, so the arena scope that owns the string is released only after the call returns.

A Nish string may hold a NUL byte, and C would read it as the end of the string. Passing such a string panics with the new `ffi-nul` kind instead of silently truncating. The kind is listed by `--emit-panics` and refused by `--deny-panics`. A string literal with no NUL in it is passed with no check and no panic site. `string | null` passes `NULL` for `null`. `string[]` stays refused, and `--deny ffi` still refuses every foreign call.

entries.title: a thread's arena adopts what a worker copied out, and keeps freed memory
entries.body:
A string or a scalar array that a `parallelMap`, a `parallelFrom` or a task
answers no longer reaches the caller by one copy per element. As a map's chunk
rewinds its arena after each element, `nish_cross_keep` moves the answer to
the end of the chunk's transfer block, a `malloc`'d block of 4 KB doubling to
64 KB. After the join, when the blocks hold 64 KB or more in all, the caller
links them into its own arena's chunk list (`nish_cross_adopt`): one link per
block. A join that kept less copies the elements that lie in a block into the
caller's arena, repoints them and frees the blocks instead, since each adopted
block leaves the caller's current chunk behind and a small map in a loop
would otherwise grow without bound. A single answer of 64 KB or more, from a
task or over a channel, is linked by `nish_cross_in` rather than copied. An
adopted block is the caller's arena memory like any other, freed by the
release that would have freed the copy. This retires the
`nish_cross_out_range` / `nish_cross_in_range` pair and its sorted span table.

Under glibc, `nish_pool_ready` sets `M_MMAP_THRESHOLD` to 32 MB and
`M_TRIM_THRESHOLD` to 64 MB, so the memory a task's or a chunk's arena release
gives back is kept for the next call rather than trimmed and faulted in again.
A worker that freed a large arena and then finds no work for a second hands
the memory back once before it parks, its own arena included. `malloc_trim`
cuts back only the main arena's top, so the worker lowers the trim threshold
to 128 KB, frees a 16 MB block through its own arena so glibc cuts that top
back, and trims. The threshold stays low while the pool is parked, so the
blocks a join adopted from a worker go back too when the caller frees them;
the next region restores 64 MB under the pool lock. The cost is the next
burst's: it faults that memory in again. A pool with no worker (one CPU, or

below glibc's own 64 MB trim, because trimming at every join cost more than
it returned. A region below its grain runs as the loop it would have been and
keeps that loop's costs.

A `parallelMap` or `parallelFrom` inside a task or another region's body stays
refused by the checker, as before; the lifetime fixture hands a map's adopted
answers to a task instead.

entries.title: copy string results out of declare function
entries.body:
A `declare function` may return `string` or `string | null`. C's
`const char *` is copied into the arena at the call, so the string is
the program's own and C keeps its buffer (`strerror`, `getenv`,
`setlocale`). `NULL` is `null` for `string | null` and panics for
`string` (`ffi-null`, refused by `--deny-panics`). Every call's copy is
new and is the calling function's allocation, so a loop keeps the copy
it holds past the pass, and a `using a = arena()` block refuses to
release one held outside it. The copy is lowered in the IR as one
private helper per module, because the C runtime is at its size
ceiling. A result that C allocates for the caller (`strdup`) stays
`CPtr`.
metrics: 94.1 ns per strerror call with the copy against 83.4 ns for C with strlen and no copy (noise band about 2.5%)

entries.title: readCString in nish:unsafe and the literal-null CPtr parameter
entries.body:
`readCString(p: CPtr): string`, the sixth export of `nish:unsafe`, copies
the NUL-terminated bytes behind a C pointer into a string the program owns.
C's buffer can then be released by C's own `free` while the copy lives on,
which is how a `strdup`, `realpath` or `getcwd` result becomes a Nish
string. The pointer must be narrowed with `!== null` before the call, so a
`NULL` never reaches the copy, and the call is named by `--deny unsafe`
like every other `nish:unsafe` export.

A `CPtr | null` parameter of a `declare function` now also takes the
literal `null`, so `realpath(".", null)` asks C to allocate the buffer. A
nullable pointer the program holds is still refused (NL2539): it is
narrowed first, so the argument C receives is either the spelled `null` or
a pointer the program has proved is not null.

The copy is a fresh allocation of the call. A loop pass that makes one
keeps it when it outlives the pass: returned from inside the loop, stored
in a local of the function or pushed into an array the function returns.

entries.title: a frame that calls parallelMap reclaims its result when it does not escape
entries.body:
A function that runs `parallelMap`, `parallelFrom` or `parallelMapInto`
and lets nothing the map made outlive it now releases its frame's arena
when it returns, as its sequential twin does. The map's result array
and the blocks of strings a string map adopts from its workers are
freed with the frame. Before, escape analysis counted the region's
entry as keeping the array it was handed, and lost a string map's
chunk store into its caller's array, so every caller kept every
result: 40 maps of 2^22 peaked at 658 MB.

`using a = arena()` now accepts a map whose body answers numbers or
strings, and a `parallelMapInto` that fills an outer `i32[]`. A map
whose body answers arrays is still refused, and the refusal says what
to write instead: run the map outside the block, or answer numbers or
strings.

Two shapes stay conservative and keep their memory: a `string[]`
result passed whole to a callee, and a frame or block that also
spawns into a `scope()`.

Array literals handed to a map no longer escape and move to the stack.
metrics: 40 x 2^22 maps in returning frames, 9 interleaved rounds against main ef8502b1 and a byte-identical copy of it: on 4 threads the map runs at 1.87x its sequential loop (140.3 against 262.3 ms) where it ran at 0.56x (493.3 against 275.5 ms), and peaks at 33.8 MB instead of 658 MB; on 1 thread it matches the loop (258.8 against 271.6 ms) where it took 2.2x as long. entries.title: a Secret may be a readonly field of a class whose wipe() wipes it
entries.body:
A key that lives as long as a connection or a session can now be kept in an object. NL2430 used to refuse every `Secret` field. It now admits one shape: a `readonly` field typed exactly `Secret<T>` on a non-generic class, which the docs call a holder. The checker proves that the holder's `wipe()` zeroes every such field.

The holder is held to these rules:

- It has `wipe(): void`, and that method calls `wipe(this.f)` directly for every field on every path out of it (NL2540, NL2541).
- A field is set only in the constructor, only from `secret(...)`, and only once (NL2542, NL2543).
- A field is read only as a borrowed call or `new` argument, or as an `===` / `!==` operand (NL2544).
- A holder is made only by `new`, never by an object literal (NL2545).
- A field is wiped nowhere but its own class's `wipe()` (NL2547).

`wipe` now also marks what it reaches as written, so a scope's parent cannot wipe a holder while one of its tasks may still read the key. With `--emit-header`, a holder and a `Secret` are opaque typedefs.

A `Secret` parameter is now borrowed for every caller. A function may neither return one (NL2546) nor wipe one (NL2548). This closes identity laundering, where `id(h.k)` handed out a second owner of a holder's key. It also refuses what 0.18.0 allowed for any `Secret` parameter, so it is a declared break. To fix code it rejects, return a value computed inside `expose`, or a new `secret(...)`, and leave the wipe to the caller.

Wordings, documentation and tests:

- Each of NL2540 to NL2548 has a wording test.
- `docs/LANGUAGE.md` gains the "A `Secret` field" rule.
- The cookbook gains `builtin-secret-field`, and the user guide gains "Keeping a key in an object".
- `docs/security/secret.md` records SECRET-2 to SECRET-5, all found in review and fixed here.
- 72 `reject_secret_field*` cases cover each way in.
- A golden `-O2` check shows that a holder's wipe stays a volatile `llvm.memset`.

Refs: docs/LANGUAGE.md, docs/security/secret.md
Tests: tests/cases/secret_field, tests/cases/secret_field_wipe_o2, tests/cases/reject_secret_field_*

entries.title: TlsServer and TlsRecordServer hold their secrets in Secret fields
entries.body:
Every secret a TLS connection keeps between calls is now a readonly `Secret<u8[]>` field: the X25519 ephemeral key, the handshake, application, exporter and resumption secrets, and the record layer's traffic secrets. The checker, not review, now keeps a copy from leaving them. A field is read only as an argument of `expose`, `exposeWith` or a function that takes a `Secret`. Binding one to a local, logging it or replacing it outside the constructor is refused, and each holder's `wipe()` provably reaches every field.

- **`TlsServer`:**
  - `TlsServer.ephemeral` holds the key. `new TlsServer`, `restart` and `TlsTcpServer`'s accept copy the caller's key in, then zero the caller's array.
  - The other secrets live in two `TlsSecretPool`s, one per hash, read through `secrets()`. A bitmask behind `known`, `readKnown` and `writeKnown` says which ones a connection has derived.
  - `wipeSecret`, `wipeEphemeral` and `wipe()` zero them.
- **`TlsRecordServer`:**
  - Keeps each direction's traffic secret for KeyUpdate in `readTraffic256`/`384` and `writeTraffic256`/`384`, ratcheted in place.
  - Installs keys from a clone that it zeroes before its arena block ends. The in-place `installHeld`/`advanceHeld` forms derive through HKDF forms that cannot run inside an arena block, so they would leave their temporaries behind.
- **`QuicConnection`:**
  - Takes its 1-RTT secrets from `TlsServer` once, guarded by `applicationTaken`, so a retry can never re-derive keys from the zeroed pool.
  - What it sends is byte for byte what it sent before.

TLS-1 is closed. What is left is what every `Secret` leaves: a key's bytes in registers and spills while HMAC, HKDF and AEAD run on it, plus that one transient clone per install and KeyUpdate. The clone is zeroed inside the wrapper, and the -O2 checks pin the wipe through `TlsRecordServer.advance` and `updateReadKeys`. QUIC-2 and QUIC-5 are re-derived, and the wipe counts are recounted by deleting each wipe in turn.
