entries.title: QuicConnection holds its traffic secrets in Secret fields; quicKeys writes into a caller's slot
entries.body:
A `QuicConnection` now keeps its ephemeral key and its 1-RTT read, next-read and write secrets as `readonly` `Secret<u8[]>` fields, one set for each secret width (32 and 48 bytes). They replace plain arrays in a pool indexed by generation. The fields are rewritten in place through `exposeWith`, read only as a call's argument, and ended by the new `QuicConnection.wipe()`, which `wipeAll` calls. The checker refuses to compile a `wipe()` that leaves a field unwiped.

- A key update ratchets the write secret in place, so the replaced secret is overwritten rather than kept beside the next one.
- The connection derives each level's keys through its own HKDF scratch (`keysFrom`, `nextKeys`) and zeroes the plain copy that `expose` hands each derivation.
- The ephemeral key is zeroed once `TlsServer` holds its own copy.
- `applicationTaken` still makes `afterTls` take the application secrets from `TlsServer` exactly once.
- S3's transitional plain copy into the connection's pools is gone. What the connection sends is unchanged.

`quicKeys` and `quicKeysUpdate` now take the `QuicKeysSlot` to derive into and answer its `keys`. The only thing either leaves in the arena is the `HkdfScratch` it makes, which wipes itself. A slot the caller owns is the caller's to wipe, with `QuicKeysSlot.wipe` or `quicKeysWipe`. `quicKeysUpdate` answers `null` and derives nothing when the keys it is handed live in the slot it would write. That closes QUIC-1.

The wipe counts are recounted by deleting each wipe in turn. Of the 66 wipe lines, 56 lower a count, 7 are refused by the checker, and 3 are pinned by read-backs. `net_quic_wipes` now reads the connection's `Secret` fields back as non-zero before each end of life and zero after it. It also checks the next-read secret right after a key update's phase flip, the write-secret ratchet, the ephemeral key once the handshake is established, and the same-slot refusal. The QUIC and TLS security records give the reasons that the reset and config keys and the per-record keys are not yet `Secret` fields.

entries.title: design u8[] buffers and owned handles across declare function
entries.body:
* docs(interop): design u8[] buffers and owned handles across declare function

A design for review, with nothing built yet. It covers two widenings of
WP27's FFI.

The first is buffers. A `declare function` may take a `u8[]` or a
`readonly u8[]`, which crosses as `uint8_t *` or `const uint8_t *`. The
array must be followed by a `u64` byte count, and every call checks that
count against the array's length, panicking with a new `ffi-length` kind
when it is too large. Only the data pointer crosses, so C can neither
resize the array nor keep it.

The second is handles. A class may own one readonly `CPtr` field, set in
its constructor from a foreign call, if its `[Symbol.dispose]` method is
a single foreign call on that field. Such a class is created only as the
initialiser of a `using` declaration, and the compiler emits the close at
every exit of the block. Use after close and double close are refused
statically.

The document gives every sibling path a refusal case, works through the
interactions with escape analysis, the arena, `--deny ffi`, the
generators, wasm32 and the differential oracle, and records the finding
that moving `getenv` into `std/` is not worth a trusted-std mechanism.

Refs: docs/wp27-ffi.md, docs/wp40-ffi-buffers-handles.md

* docs(interop): address review round 1 on the buffers and handles design

A foreign `u8[]` argument now sets the caller's `writesThrough`, so the
caller's attributes, the header's `const` and the wasm copy-back see
C's write. A buffer's `data` and `len` are loaded after every argument
is evaluated, so a later argument that resizes the array cannot leave C
with a stale pointer. One count may serve a run of buffers, which makes
`memcpy` and `memmove` declarable. §1's example reads the field through
a method, as §4a requires.

The open questions about what stays a C contract are laid out with
their costs for the owner rather than decided: a close written by hand
in the class (Q9), the stale-argument rule (Q10), and `syscall` and
fixed-arity variadic declarations (Q11). Every out-of-scope refusal
now names its case and its rolling-freeze status. The design also
wires the emitted close into every exit path, including `orReturn()`
and tail calls, closes the class-template path for generic handles,
and plans wasm32 checks for both routes.

Refs: docs/wp40-ffi-buffers-handles.md
Tests: none (design only; the planned cases are listed in §9)

* docs(interop): address review round 2 on the buffers and handles design

The count is written `toU64(buf.length)` and checked with an unsigned
compare, so a wrapped `u64` fails; the check is elided only for the
buffer's own named length. A foreign call records a `u8[]` argument's
write through `noteSlotWrite`, so field paths and elements reach
`writesReach` and the `scope()` race rule. The handle field is read
only as `this.f` and its uncopyable `const` locals, so Q9's option A
sees every name of the pointer; the dispose shape binds the field
first, since a property path is not narrowed. A new Q12 lays out the
exit inside a later `using` declarator's initialiser. `process.exit`
skips the close as a panic does, and the `async` row cites the
existing refusal.

* docs(interop): write the handle rule as an allow-list

The handle design now states the complete list of positions a handle
object and its `CPtr` field may occupy, and refuses everything else with
one general rule per kind: `reject_ffi_handle_position`,
`reject_ffi_handle_type_position` and `reject_ffi_handle_field_position`.

- The class declares one `readonly` pointer field with no initialiser, a
  required `[Symbol.dispose]`, no type parameters, no `implements` and no
  `export`.
- The field is written once, by a top-level `this.f = g(args);` statement
  in the constructor, and read only as `this.f` passed straight to C or
  bound once to a `const`.
- A handle is bound only by a `using` whose initialiser is exactly `new C()`,
  by a non-exported borrowing parameter, or as `this`. It is used only as
  a receiver or as an argument lent to such a parameter.

A walk of every language form against the list replaces the case-by-case
rows, which are now examples of the rule. The walk covers interface
fields, object literals, assignment used as an expression, ternary and
cast initialisers, `throw`, threads and modules. A new decision, Q13,
records what the list costs.

The buffer check is now elided only when no later argument can resize any
array. That excludes an inline `push` or `pop`, which no callee fact
records. Q12 now covers the same multi-declarator leak for locks and
scopes.

Refs: docs/wp40-ffi-buffers-handles.md#4d-where-an-instance-may-live-the-allow-list

* docs(interop): plan a case per handle refusal and settle the non-null field

A non-nullable `CPtr` field is reachable only from a C function declared
to return `CPtr`, since the one field write takes the foreign call alone.
A second write shape that would narrow `CPtr | null` in the constructor is
now Q14, with its siblings and costs. Every declaration and dispose-body
refusal has a planned case, and each shape gets its own case file.

Also: `new` in the elision rule, the dispose call type-checked, one LIFO
pass for locks and handles, `ffi-length` kept under `--unchecked-indexing`,
the containment consequence of the borrow, and the private-array path tied
to the foreign facts entry.

* docs(interop): make B1.3's test fail without it and name every planned case

B1.3's `ffi_buffer_bounds_survive` now exercises each of the three readers
of `resizesArray` with the foreign call inside the subtree it inspects: a
compound element store whose right-hand side calls `read`, a counted loop
whose body calls it, and a `for…of` whose effect shows as `loopsBounded`
in the checked-facts golden. Section 9 names every case the design
promises, including each handle refusal of section 6, the `panics_ffi_length`
variants and the known-failures, goldens and security-record work each
step carries. Also corrects the wasm-ld claim, names the `static readonly
json` exception on handle classes, admits writes to a handle class's other
fields, and states the close order on `return`.

* docs(interop): correct the bounds-at-a-call and tail-call claims in WP40

The checker's index proof does not carry a length fact across a foreign
call. `callSummary` has no summary for a callee with no body, so the call
drops every array length and path fact (src/bounds.ts:87), and
`resizesArray = false` does not change that. §3c now says so: an index
after the call keeps its check. Q15 puts extending the proof to the owner,
with its costs. B1.3's case is renamed `ffi_buffer_no_resize`.

`return f.readByte()` is never marked `tail`, because `marksTailCall`
refuses a call with a non-scalar argument, so it cannot test H1.2's
widened suppression. `ffi_handle_file` now pins `return twice(n)` inside
the `using` block instead, against the same call marked `tail` outside it.

The anchors move to `main` at 8790ea3, after WP27 S3.1 to S3.3, and
the S3 facts are brought up to date. `reject_ffi_string_array_param`
exists now.

entries.title: a shared byte-buffer pool that zeroes what it takes back
entries.body:
`nish/net/buffer-pool` adds `BufferPool(name, size, ceiling)`: a pool of
fixed-size `u8[]` buffers that a server lends across connections. `take()`
returns the buffer given back most recently, or a new one while fewer than
`ceiling` are lent. `give(buf, used)` zeroes the first `used` bytes before the
buffer can be lent again. `giveSecret(buf, used)` wipes the whole buffer with
the volatile `secureZero`, for buffers that held plaintext under TLS. The pool
grows to its high-water mark and then allocates nothing, so a warmed take/give
loop moves `Arena.used()` by 0 bytes.

It has the same shape as `Http1OutputPool`, and the TLS, HTTP/2 and QUIC
server pools will borrow their per-connection buffers from it instead of
preallocating them per slot.

Misuse is a fatal panic that names the pool: taking past the ceiling, giving
back a buffer of the wrong length, a `used` extent outside `0..size`, a give
with nothing lent, and a size or ceiling below 1. A buffer given back twice
while another buffer is lent is not detected. That limit is documented.

The module is registered in `src/std-modules.ts`, in the three presence
lists of the release workflow, in `std/README.md` and in the standard-library
guide.

entries.title: nish/bytes, endian reads and writes of integers and doubles in a byte array
entries.body:
`nish/bytes` reads a `u16`, `u32`, `u64`, `i32`, `i64` or `f64` from a `u8[]` at an offset, and writes one into it, little- or big-endian (`getU32LE`, `setU16BE`, ...). Each access is an ordinary bounds-checked index, so an offset whose bytes are not all in the array panics `index`, naming the first one missing. In range the answers are those of the private copies `std/` keeps in its hashes, ciphers and codecs, none of which it replaces. A guard in the caller's loop does not yet remove the checks after inlining, and under Node only the `u16` and `u32` functions are expected to answer as natively.

Measured: in a loop guarded by `off + 3 < b.length`, 3 of getU32LE's 4 index checks survive inlining under opt -O3, against 0 when the loop indexes the bytes itself

entries.title: --slots sizes every pool, and the harness that measures memory and throughput
entries.body:
The interop server's `serve --slots <n>` (1 to 4096) now sizes all four
pools. Before, it sized only HTTP/3, while HTTP/2 was fixed at 64 slots and
both HTTP/1.1 pools at 16. The HTTP/1.1 pools are capped at 500 slots. A bad
count exits 2 with a message naming the flag. `--only h1|h1s|h2|h3` builds one
pool at full size and the others at one slot, so the memory of each pool can
be measured on its own.

- `pool-rss.mjs` times a server from exec until all four ports answer, then
  reads VmRSS and VmHWM. A count too large for the machine is reported as a
  timeout or out of memory instead of taking the container down.
- `h2load.mjs` runs h2load against two builds in interleaved rounds:
  HTTPS/1.1 with `--h1`, and HTTP/2. HTTP/3 runs through the interop client
  in process, because the packaged h2load cannot speak it. Running the same
  build twice gives the noise band.

The baseline is in `bench/README.md`. The QUIC pool is 97% of the server's
memory: about 12.5 MB a slot, almost all of it per-stream buffers.

for 16 slots, 809 MB for 64 and 3,227 MB for 256. With 1,024 slots the server

11.6 GB cap. Time to listen was 172 ms at 16 slots, 607 ms at 64 and 4.6 s at
256. Per slot: QUIC 12,460 kB, HTTP/2 278 kB, HTTPS/1.1 160 kB, HTTP/1.1 4 kB.

±20% for HTTP/2.

entries.title: u8[] buffer parameters on declare function, with the run-and-count rule
entries.body:
A `declare function` may take a `u8[]` or a `readonly u8[]`. Buffers come
in runs, and one `u64` parameter closes each run: the byte count C may
touch in every buffer of the run, so `memcpy(dst: u8[], src: readonly
u8[], n: u64)` and `compare(a: readonly u8[], na: u64, b: readonly u8[],
nb: u64)` both declare.

The checker refuses everything outside that shape:
- a run with no count after it (NL2549)
- a count that is not a `u64` (NL2550)
- any other array, such as `string[]` or `readonly i32[]` (NL2551)
- a nullable buffer (NL2552)
- `declare function syscall` (NL2553)
- a class or other non-foreign parameter (NL2555, which replaces NL2322)

A call to a declaration that takes a buffer is refused (NL2554) until
the next stage lowers it, so the declarations check today and no
program can hand C a buffer whose length the compiler has not tied to
its count.

entries.title: resume TLS 1.3 sessions with tickets in nish/net/tls
entries.body:
TlsServer, TlsRecordServer and TlsTcpServer issue a NewSessionTicket after
a full handshake and resume an offered one with psk_dhe_ke, skipping the
certificate and the P-256 signature. Turn it on with enableTickets(); the
TLS_RECORD_TICKET interest asks the caller to lend the ticket keys and the
strike register to resume() during the handshake and to issue() once the
connection is open. Every other offer falls back to a full handshake or
aborts as docs/security/tls.md tabulates. QUIC never resumes.

The PSK, early secret and binder key are Secrets in each TlsSecretPool and
are wiped; the ticket keys and the strike register stay borrowed, never
fields. A replayed ticket is refused by the strike probe before the binder
is computed, and a tampered or expired one falls back to a full handshake.
metrics: server time per handshake, full 416-436 us, its byte-identical copy within 1.2% (the noise band), resumed 256-262 us (0.60-0.62x) over eight of nine runs; 854 bytes on the wire full, 637 resumed

entries.title: the wasi host turns off V8 fast API calls itself
entries.body:
`examples/wasi-host.mjs` now calls `v8.setFlagsFromString("--no-turbo-fast-api-calls")`
before it compiles the module, so a `--profile wasi` program run under Node 22's
WASI no longer dies with SIGSEGV part-way through its output.

Node 22 calls WASI's `fd_write` as a V8 fast API call. uvwasi allocates the
call's buffer through Node's `NgLibMemoryManager`, which reports it to V8 as
external memory; under pressure that starts a full mark-compact inside the
fast call, and the collector's walk of the optimized frame crashes in
`InnerPointerToCodeCache::GetCacheEntry`. `--single-threaded-gc`, which the
p256 agree check passed, only made the crash rarer. Turning fast API calls off
keeps every WASI call on the slow path, where a collection is safe, and doing
it in the host covers every caller (the tests, `scripts/build.sh`'s docs,
`web/wasi.mjs`) rather than each command line. The p256 agree check and the
threads parity loop drop their own flags.

entries.title: pin every route by which sibling scopes share a lock, an atomic or a destination
entries.body:
The scopes one `using` statement opens join natively in reverse order, while
under Node each task runs where it is spawned, so NL2516 refuses a `spawn`
whose task shares a lock or an atomic with a task of another scope of the
same statement, and the destination rule (NL2394) refuses a task that reads
or writes another scope's destination. The rule was pinned for a binding, an
alias, a field and a helper; it is now pinned for every way a task reaches
the shared object.

Twelve new negatives cover the routes the earlier cases left out: an object
whose constructor hands `this` out into a registry, a constructor reached by
`new` (in a named task and in an arrow task), a field of a field, a helper
that takes the lock, an arrow capture, the first and last of three
declarators, and, for destinations, a task that reads the answer another
scope's task returns, through a capture, a constructor or a field reached
through `this`. Every route probed was already refused; no checker change was
needed. `docs/LANGUAGE.md` cites each case beside the NL2516 rule.

Measured: 46 probe programs across the routes, 0 accepted

entries.title: HTTP/2 connections borrow their frame buffers from the server's pool
entries.body:
An `Http2Connection` no longer allocates its input, output and header-block
buffers when it is made. It borrows each from an `Http2Pools` (three
`BufferPool`s from `nish/net/buffer-pool`) the first time it needs it, gives it
back once it is empty, and gives everything back when the connection ends.
Each buffer is zeroed as far as the connection wrote it, so the next
connection to borrow it reads none of the last one's requests, bodies or
headers.

`Http2TlsServer` shares one `Http2Pools` across its slots, each pool's ceiling
the slot count, so a borrow never fails. An idle or partly full server holds
no frame buffers: its memory follows the connections moving bytes, not the
slots it was sized for. A slot mid-handshake holds one output buffer, its
SETTINGS written, until the handshake ends or the slot closes (TLS-4).

A standalone `Http2Connection` makes a private pool of one buffer each. Its
`output` is now empty after the constructor and after `restart`: the opening
SETTINGS are written by the first `wantsWrite`, `next` or response, so a
caller that reads `output` itself calls `wantsWrite` first.
metrics: at 1,024 slots, the HTTP/2 pool's resident memory fell from 295.7 to 195.7 MB (281 → 181 kB per slot) and time to listen from 1,476 to 78 ms (`bench/pool-rss.mjs --only h2`, median of 5). h2load HTTP/2 c=16 m=8 throughput b/a was 0.827, inside the A/A band 0.271–2.739 (5 rounds), so no change is claimed.

entries.title: WP42, a multi-core server from pre-forked processes
entries.body:
A design note for running a Nish server on every core. It chooses one process per core over one thread per core, for three reasons:

- The checker refuses every `nish:net` call in a `scope()` task or a parallel body.
- `std/threads` has no detached thread to run an accept loop.
- A panic or out-of-memory failure ends the whole process, so a process per core keeps a crash to one worker and needs no new checker rule.

The note sketches the pieces the following stages build:

- `tcpListenFlags`, with flag 1 for `SO_REUSEPORT`.
- The WP34 N12 process builtins (`spawn`, `kill`, `waitPid`, `availableParallelism`), with `waitPid`'s answers for no child left and for an interrupted wait.
- A `nish/net/prefork` supervisor. It polls for dead workers on a `pollWait` tick, restarts them with a backoff, and on shutdown forwards `SIGTERM`, then sends `SIGKILL` after a deadline.

It also says what each platform does:

- Linux spreads connections by a hash of the 4-tuple, and resets connections still queued on a dying worker's listener unless `tcp_migrate_req` is set (5.14+).
- Darwin shares the port without spreading connections.
- wasm32 refuses the calls.

It ends with what a worker inherits and the bench method for measuring at 1, 2 and 4 cores. `docs/README.md` and `docs/MASTER_PLAN.md` index it.

entries.title: build thread refusal remedies from the program
entries.body:

entries.title: a --cores mode for bench/http.mjs and N-core twins
entries.body:
`node bench/http.mjs --cores 1,2,4` runs every scenario once per core count, so a server that can use several cores is measured against twins sized to the same N.

For each N:

- The server runs under `taskset -c 0-(N-1)` with `BENCH_CORES=N` in its environment.
- wrk runs on the CPUs that are left. When none are left, it shares the server's cores, and the header and every cell say so.
- The CPU-time and peak-RSS columns sum over the server's whole process tree, including reaped children, so a pre-forked server's workers are counted.

Without `--cores`, the layout and the output are as before, and a `BENCH_CORES` exported in the shell is cleared, so it cannot quietly turn a twin multi-core on one pinned CPU.

Each twin reads `BENCH_CORES`:

- The Go twins set `GOMAXPROCS`.
- nginx sets `worker_processes`, with a master process when N > 1.
- actix sets `workers(N)`.
- hyper runs a multi-thread tokio runtime with N workers, with the accept loop spawned onto it.
- The Bun twins (bun, Elysia, Hono) run N processes with `reusePort`, through a shared `bun-cores.mjs`.
- node-http and uws report `n/a (single-core)` above one core.

The twins README tabulates each twin's setting and what N means for it. It also notes that `check.mjs` covers only the one-core path.

entries.title: tcpListenFlags, SO_REUSEPORT on a TCP listener
entries.body:
`nish:net` gains `tcpListenFlags(host, port, backlog, flags)`, which is `tcpListen` with a flags word.

- **Flag 1** sets `SO_REUSEPORT` before the bind, so several listeners can share one port, in one process or in several.
  - Linux spreads new connections across the listeners' accept queues by a hash of the 4-tuple.
  - Darwin shares the port but hands the connections to one listener.
- **Any other bit**, a negative `flags` included, answers `-22`.
- Like every `nish:net` call, it is refused on wasm32 with NL2404.
- `tcpListen` is unchanged.

The new guide page, Networking, walks through it.

RT-17 records what socket sharing allows: any process of the same uid can join a flagged port's group and take a share of its connections.

entries.title: QUIC streams borrow their buffers on first use and give them back once acknowledged
entries.body:
A QUIC connection no longer allocates a send and a receive buffer for every
stream slot when it is made. Each stream side borrows its data buffer and its
bitmap from a `QuicStreamPools` (two `BufferPool`s from `nish/net/buffer-pool`)
on first use:
- the receive side on its first byte;
- the send side on its first write.

Each side gives its buffers back once it is done:
- the send side once every byte and the FIN are acknowledged, never earlier,
  so a lost packet can always be resent;
- the receive side once the application reads to the end;
- either side on a reset, a STOP_SENDING or a release.

A buffer goes back zeroed as far as it was written, out-of-order data
included. `Http3Server` shares one set of pools across all its connections,
and its header-section and DATA buffers are borrowed the same way.

The pools' ceiling is two buffers per stream slot, so no peer can make the
server allocate past what it was sized for. A reserve primed before each packet
lets a packet open new receive sides without allocating, and a send side that
finds the pool at its ceiling takes a pair from that reserve rather than
failing.

A read after `release()` now answers END and copies nothing, where it used to
report bytes it had not copied. A late ack, loss or PTO after a reset is
ignored.
metrics: at 1,024 slots the HTTP/3 pool's resident memory is 258.5 MB (254 kB per slot, was 12,460 kB) and it is listening in 99 ms. At 256 slots, main before this change took 3.2 GB and 4.6 s to listen, and at 1,024 slots it did not listen. All four protocols together at 1,024 slots: 519.6 MB, listening in 197 ms (`bench/pool-rss.mjs --per-pool --slots 1024`, median of 5). h3load, 11 interleaved rounds of 30k requests: main against this change gave 0.979 (0.943–1.002), against an A/A band of 0.994 (0.976–1.025), so no change in throughput is claimed. Cachegrind counts 5.4% fewer instructions per request.

entries.title: TLS record buffers are borrowed per connection and wiped when given back
entries.body:
A `TlsTcpServer` slot no longer allocates its record buffers when the server is
made. Each slot borrows its four buffers from a set of `TlsRecordPools` (four
`BufferPool`s from `nish/net/buffer-pool`) the first time it needs them:
- the record it writes;
- the plaintext it reads;
- the scratch it seals and opens in;
- the reader.

The slot gives them back when its connection closes. The server shares one set
of pools across its slots, each pool's ceiling the slot count, so a borrow
never fails and a server sized for many slots holds buffers only for the
connections it actually has.

Every give-back goes through `BufferPool.giveSecret`, a volatile `secureZero`
of the whole buffer that the optimiser cannot drop. These buffers held
plaintext and record keys' output, so the next connection to borrow one reads
none of the last one's bytes. A refused seal's partial write counts as written,
so it is wiped too. A free slot is marked failed and seals no alert.

A standalone record layer makes a private pool of one buffer each.

With HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 alongside, all four protocols at 1,024 slots now take 360.6 MB and listen in 152 ms, where main before this series did not listen within 30 s at 10.2 GB. h2load HTTPS/1.1 throughput b/a was 1.009 (0.905–1.342), against an A/A band of 0.980 (0.942–1.028), over 7 interleaved rounds, so no change is claimed.

entries.title: an HTTP router in nish/net/router
entries.body:
`nish/net/router` matches a request's method and path against a table of patterns. Patterns have literal segments, `:param` segments and an optional trailing `*`. The router works on the bytes of the target, so the same table serves HTTP/1.1 (`Http1Parser.head` with its spans) and HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 (`HttpFields.method` and `.path`).

Nish has no function values, so a route is an index: `router.add(method, pattern)` answers 0, 1, 2…, and the program dispatches on what `match` answers with a `switch`. `match` writes each parameter as a `[start, end)` byte range into an `i32[]` the caller owns. It allocates nothing, which `Arena.used()` pins across a warmed burst of lookups.

**Precedence.** At each segment a literal wins over a parameter, and a parameter wins over `*`. A failed literal branch falls back to the parameter, and each node of the table is entered at most once, so a lookup costs at most the target's length plus the table's size, whatever the target.

**Refused when the table is built.** A route is refused with `ROUTER_DUPLICATE` (the same method and shape, whatever the parameters are called) or `ROUTER_AMBIGUOUS` (a `*` that is not last). It is also refused with `ROUTER_TOO_LONG` or `ROUTER_BAD_PATTERN`. A refused route changes nothing, and whether a pattern is refused never depends on the order routes were added in.

**At match time.** A lookup answers `ROUTER_NOT_FOUND` (404) or `ROUTER_METHOD_NOT_ALLOWED` (405). It answers `ROUTER_TOO_MANY_PARAMS` when the caller's storage cannot hold the route's pairs, and then writes nothing.

**Path rules.**
- The path ends at the first `?`, and query parsing is left out until a URL module lands.
- A trailing slash is significant.
- A parameter never matches an empty segment.
- Matching is on raw bytes, so `%2F` never splits a segment. `routerDecode` percent-decodes one matched parameter afterwards, into a buffer the caller owns.

The design note, `docs/wp43-http-app-layer.md`, is the first stage of #485's application layer. It says what goes in `std/net` and what stays an example. It also says why a route table cannot be checked at compile time today, and what the checker would need for that. `docs/security/router.md` records how unmatched and hostile targets are handled (ROUTE-1 to ROUTE-9).

Measured: deep-route lookup over a 112-route table (77 nodes, up to nine segments), 200,000 lookups a round, medians of 15 interleaved rounds, one x86-64 core:
- `nish run`: router 458.8 ns, linear scan 3,495.0 ns (7.6x), against a byte-identical scan copy at 3,316.0 ns, a 51‰ band.
- `--profile speed`: router 154.5 ns, scan 1,028.3 ns (6.7x), band 46‰.

entries.title: the loopback client sends nothing after a CONNECTION_CLOSE
entries.body:
`tests/link/net_loopback` failed now and then under load, on two separate races.

**A late ACK met a freed slot.** The wire client acknowledged the 1-RTT packet that carried the server's CONNECTION_CLOSE, and kept acknowledging after sending its own. By then the server had closed or drained and freed the slot, so its `QuicListener` saw a packet for no connection and answered it with a stateless reset (RFC 9000 §10.3) to the client's old port. On loopback the next client is often given that same ephemeral port, so it read the reset and failed with "the client could not open a datagram the server sent". This hit the quic, http/3 and webtransport carriers. The client now sends nothing once it has sent or read a CONNECTION_CLOSE, as RFC 9000 §10.2 asks of the closing and draining states. New checks in the quic and http/3 carriers pin that the listener sent no stateless reset and limited none. Without the fix they fail on every run (5 of 5).

**A probe timer was already due before the pacer check.** The http/3 check that the carrier wakes a slot when its pacer allows a flight requires that no other timer of the connection's is due as soon. On a slow run, data the server had sent was still unacknowledged, so its PTO was already overdue and that precondition failed. The check now steps the loop until nothing is in flight, so no probe timer is armed when it measures the pacer's wake.

`tests/link/net_loopback_f64`, the same program under `--number-mode f64`, gets the two new lines in its own `expected.out`.

Measured: 12/4000 failures before, 0/4000 after. Each of two interleaved rounds ran the before and after binaries 2,000 times, 64 in parallel pinned to one core, with busy loops on all four cores. Before: 7 and 5 failures (8 pacer, 4 reset: 2 quic, 2 webtransport). After: 0 and 0. The noise band is the 7-versus-5 spread between the two before rounds.
Refs: RFC 9000 §10.2, §10.3

entries.title: store null through a guard into a string | null slot
entries.body:
A guard now stores `null` into a `string | null` slot of a `Mutex`'s data: a nullable field, an element of a `(string | null)[]`, or the value of a `Mutex<string | null>`. Such a store frees the copy the slot held and keeps nothing, and the slot reads back through `?.`. `nish_guard_keep` takes a null string, frees the old copy and returns null. A null stored into a slot that holds an object (`next: Link | null`) is still refused as NL2537, now worded for that case, because a guard stores no object. A `string | null` *value* (a variable, `??`, a conditional) is still refused as NL2468.

A guarded `string | null` read through `?.` used to copy the string before the null test, which would have segfaulted on a null slot; the copy is now made after the test passes, and a `?.length` or `?.charCodeAt` reads in place.

Measured: 30,000,000 locked string stores with an order-sensitive checksum, 9 interleaved rounds, each binary paired with a byte-identical copy. Medians: old 757 / 761 ms, new 792 / 789 ms; noise band 3–4 ms. A repeat run: old 771 / 767 ms, new 805 / 786 ms; band 4–19 ms. So a guard store is about 3–4% slower, about 1 ns per store: the null test in `nish_guard_keep` and the `nonnull` dropped from its declaration.
Refs: docs/LANGUAGE.md (threads, R4)
Tests: tests/link/thread_mutex_null_store, tests/cases/reject_mutex_guard_null_*, tests/wordings/nl2537_mutex_guard_null_store, tests/runtime-test.c (test_guard_keep)

entries.title: claim a divided region's pieces as threads finish
entries.body:
A divided region used to be cut into one contiguous chunk per thread, so a preempted thread held every other thread at the join. `nish_parallel_range` now cuts the range into up to eight pieces per thread, never smaller than the grain. Each thread claims the next piece off a relaxed atomic counter when it finishes the last one, the calling thread runs the first piece, and a pool thread rewinds its arena between pieces.

Over the one-thread loop (2172 ms), on the medians of the same interleaved rounds, par-heavy goes from about 2.6x on main (2172 / 846) to about 2.7x (2172 / 792), about 6% faster at four threads and outside the copy band. It does not reach 3x, and the scheduler is not why: the order-sensitive fold, the fill and the allocation run on one thread, about 286 ms of the 2172 (13%), and by Amdahl that caps four cores near 2.9x. Inside the region, each thread was busy for 87–93% of its ideal time. Having workers touch their own pages first measured within the noise band, so it is not shipped.

Measured: par-alloc, 9 rounds: main 88 (copy 79) → 52 (copy 51); without the arena reset between pieces, 53
Measured: par-scale 277 (copy 266) → 270 (copy 260); par-single 213 (copy 209) → 213 (copy 207): no difference

entries.title: build Http1Server's connections on first accept
entries.body:
`Http1Server` no longer builds an `Http1Connection` for every slot before it listens. A slot's connection is built on the first `accept` into that slot and kept for every later connection there, so the slot count is a cap rather than a cost paid at start-up. A 16,384-slot server now reaches its first answer in 4.7 ms with 2.6 MB resident, where it took 36.2 ms and 65.3 MB.

`size()` still reports the cap, and `H1_POOL_FULL` still comes at exactly `size` busy slots. Accept order stays 0, 1, 2, …. A warmed slot still serves request after request with the arena flat, and peak memory is still bounded by `size` times the per-connection caps.

A free slot comes off the stack of released slots or, failing that, is the next never-used index. A stack seeded with every index would cost the 16,384 words this change removes, and a scan would make each accept O(size).

Every reader answers a slot that was never built as it answers a free one, except `connection(slot)`. It names slot 0's connection, building it if no slot has been built yet, and that connection may be live, as its JSDoc says.

`Http1TlsServer`, `tls-tcp`, `http2*`, `quic*` and `http3*` still build their pools eagerly. They can take the same change now that the pooled-buffer work in #681 has merged.

entries.title: the nish HTTP twin registers its routes on nish/net/router
entries.body:

- the measured routes;
- the 112-route extra table that `bench/router.ts` times, up to nine segments deep with one to three parameters, which only the Nish twin carries;

A refused `add` panics at start-up, so a route can never be dropped silently.

- `HEAD /plaintext` is now a 404;

entries.title: keep the chunk a map element's body grew at one thread
entries.body:
A `parallelMap` at `NISH_NUM_THREADS=1` runs its region on the caller, and
each element is kept with `nish_cross_keep`, which rewinds the arena to the
mark taken before the body. That mark sits at the end of the chunk the
result array filled exactly, so every element's body grew a fresh 64 KB
chunk and the rewind freed it again: a `malloc` and a `free` per element,
and a one-thread map of short strings ran about 30% slower than the loop.

The rewind now keeps the newest chunk when it is a 64 KB one the body grew
past the mark's chunk: it is emptied and left in front of the mark's chunk,
with any chunks between freed, so the next element bumps into it. A mark in
the current chunk rewinds as before, and a mark in no live chunk leaves the
arena as the release would. Number maps never call `nish_cross_keep`; their
benchmark binaries link byte-identical.

`runtime-cross.c` grows from 1,444 / 1,513 to 1,552 / 1,631 bytes of `.text`
(plain / threads), all of it `nish_cross_keep` with the rewind inlined, and
both ceilings move from 1,536 to 1,664.

entries.title: pass u8[] buffers to C, with the count checked against the length
entries.body:
A `u8[]` or `readonly u8[]` argument to a `declare function` is now lowered:
C receives the array's data pointer (`uint8_t *`, or `const uint8_t *` for a
`readonly u8[]`), and the count that follows it in the declaration is compared
with the array's length before C runs. A count larger than the length panics
with `ffi-length` and exits 1, naming the function, the count and the buffer,
rather than letting C read or write past the data block. The compare is
unsigned, because the count is a `u64`, and `--unchecked-indexing` keeps it:
the count is C's to trust, not an index.

The length and the data pointer are loaded after the last argument is
evaluated, so an argument that pushes or pops the same array is seen. The one
count the compiler proves, and does not check, is `toU64(b.length)` of the
buffer itself, where `b` is a `const` local or a parameter and no later
argument can resize it; `--deny-panics` refuses any other count and names
that form.

The pointer is lent for the call, as a `string`'s bytes are. C may write
through a `u8[]`, so an exported function that hands its parameter to such a
function writes it: the header drops `const`, the wasm glue copies the bytes
back, and the `define` loses `readonly`. A spawned task whose body reaches C
with a buffer is refused, as writing memory its caller can see. Every call is
a call site for `--deny ffi`. On wasm32 the pointer is 32 bits and the count
stays an `i64`; docs/LANGUAGE.md records the gap with C's `size_t`. NL2554,
the refusal that stood in until this lowering, is retired.

The checks that pin the lowering live in `tests/ffi-buffer.js`, which
`tests/run.js` runs, and the WP27 string-argument checks move to
`tests/ffi-string.js`, so that `tests/run.js` stays under Biome's size limit.
metrics: 500M calls of a one-byte C fold, medians of 7 interleaved rounds: proved count 394 ms, a byte-identical copy of it 386 ms (noise band about 2%), checked count 391 ms; the check costs nothing outside the band

entries.title: reclaim a frame that spawns into a scope, and accept an arena's array handed to its own scope
entries.body:
Filing a task on a `using s = scope()` no longer counts every pointer
argument as captured. The escape pass reads whether the task's entry,
its result store or the runtime keeps each parameter; one that is not
kept stays local, so a frame that runs a map and also spawns into a
scope gives its arena back when it returns, after the scope has joined.

Inside `using a = arena()`, an array made in the block and handed to a
scope the block itself declares is accepted: that scope joins before the
block releases. A `using` statement disposes its declarators in reverse,
so every declarator ahead of the statement's last `arena()` joins after
that arena releases: such a scope keeps the pass's rule, and an argument
younger than the block is refused (NL2427), including in
`using a = arena(), s = scope(), b = arena()`.

entries.title: design streaming file reads (WP44)
entries.body:
A design note for #710, written before any code. Nish can read a file
only whole today, so a server cannot stream a file larger than the
memory it should use, and no file past 2^31 - 1 bytes can be read.

The note proposes four builtins in `nish:fs`: `fileOpen`, `fileReadAt`
(a positional `pread` into a caller-owned `u8[]` window), `fileSize`
and `fileClose`. They work on a plain `i32` descriptor, as `nish:net`
does, because a server has to keep the file across event-loop wakes,
and WP40's `using`-bound handle class cannot be stored. It also covers:

- how each builtin maps to libc, to WASI through wasi-libc, and to
  Node's `fs.openSync`/`readSync`/`fstatSync`/`closeSync`, with the
  errno set and the pre-checks that make both runtimes agree;
- the `fs.read` capability under WP35 and WP36, and how WP37's
  directory scopes would fit;
- the memory rules: no call allocates, the window is borrowed and
  never kept, and the descriptor is not memory.

Nine open questions are left for the owner, each with a recommendation.
`sendfile` stays deferred to WP39.

entries.title: WP45, name resolution for nish:net — getaddrinfo, a stub resolver, or both
entries.body:
A proposed design note for name resolution in `nish:net`, which today takes
address literals only. It weighs `getaddrinfo` in `runtime-net.c`, a DNS stub
resolver in `std/net/dns`, and both, on three questions: what the capability
report says, whether a program that owns its `pollWait` loop stalls, and what
works on wasm32 and WASI.

It recommends the stub resolver alone. It is the only shape that never blocks
the loop (a blocking call cannot move to a task, since no `nish:net` call may
run in one), the only one whose capability labels are true under WP35's rules
(`net` and `entropy`, `clock` in the caller, and `fs.read` only where the
program reads `resolv.conf` or `hosts` itself, while `getaddrinfo` would
report `net` and read four files, a Unix socket and NSS modules unseen), and
the only one with a part usable on wasm32: the query builder and response
parser, kept in a module with no `nish:net` import. It gives up `nsswitch`.

The note also states the requirements every stage keeps (TTLs, A and AAAA, a
bound on answers, DNS responses as untrusted input with a planned
`docs/security/dns.md` record, N9's pools) and four later stages. Nothing is
implemented.

entries.title: write WP37's note, the OS sandbox
entries.body:
WP35 computes which capabilities a program can reach, and WP36 refuses at
compile time what a policy does not grant. Neither holds a running process
to anything: once `ffi` is granted, C code behind a `declare function` can
do whatever libc can. `docs/wp37-os-sandbox.md` proposes `--sandbox`, which
closes that gap. Nothing is built yet.

How it works:
- The native program confines itself with Landlock and seccomp, before user
  code runs, to the capability mask the compiler computed for `main`.
- The sandbox is applied from a `.preinit_array` entry. `@main` fails closed
  on a libc that skips that entry, such as musl.
- It accepts the `fs.read=<dir>` scopes WP36 refuses today, because the
  kernel can then enforce them.

The note states:
- the flags (`--sandbox` and `--sandbox=best-effort`), where each is
  accepted, and the exact IR of the call;
- the mapping of all eleven capabilities to Landlock rights, seccomp rules,
  or "not confined", with the reason for each;
- the kernel floor (Landlock ABI 1 to 7, seccomp, `KILL_PROCESS`) and the
  fallbacks under strict and best-effort;
- the platforms and the tests;
- a threat model naming what the adversary keeps: code that runs before the
  call, a privileged launch (capabilities are dropped first), io_uring,
  x32, metadata writes, and same-uid IPC.

Thirteen open questions, each with a recommendation, are left for the owner
to decide before implementation. Among them: how an `ffi` program's C code
is granted the capabilities it needs, the exit status of a refused start,
whether best-effort exists, and `fs.write=<dir>`.

The work-package table in MASTER_PLAN.md and its "Next" item, the docs
index, WP35 §7 and WP36 now link the note.

entries.title: refuse an exported function named memory in a wasm build
entries.body:
A wasm module exports its linear memory as `memory`, so a function of the
program's own package that keeps `memory` as its symbol (an exported one, or
any function under `--no-strict-exports`) was a second export of that name, and
Node refused the module with "Duplicate export name 'memory'".

Such a function is now refused with NL3038 in every build whose output is a
wasm module: a wasm `--target`, `--profile wasi`, and an `--emit-dts` compile,
whose loader is for the module `scripts/build.sh --profile wasm` links. IR
compiled for the host with `-o` alone reaches that link without the compiler
knowing, so `build.sh --profile wasm` and `--profile wasi` also refuse, with
exit 2, an input `.ll` that defines a non-internal `@memory`. The wasi module
exports only `memory` and `_start`, so the name does not collide there today;
it is reserved across every wasm build so that a program that builds for wasi
also builds as a freestanding module. A native build has no linear memory and
keeps the name, and a `memory` nobody exported stays internal on wasm too. The
linker's other names (`_start`, `__heap_base`, `__data_end`,
`__indirect_function_table`) begin with `_`, which NL3037 already refuses.

entries.title: build Http3Server's slots on first accept
entries.body:
`Http3Server` used to build every slot's QUIC connection, HTTP/3 connection and address in its constructor. A pool sized for 65,536 clients paid for all of them before the first one came. Now a slot is built on the first Initial accepted into it (`build`, called from `unowned`) and kept. A released slot is taken before a new one, so the first accepts take slots 0, 1, 2, and so on. A pool that never fills never builds its last slots. The slot cap, the `refused` counter and every per-slot bound are unchanged. With lazy slots, the pool's full footprint is reached at run time, one slot per accepted Initial, and it is still bounded by `size` times the per-slot cost.

`streamPools` is now made by the constructor from the configuration rather than from the first connection's stream table. It is made even for a configuration that `quicConnConfigFits` refuses. `build` shares it only with a connection whose stream buffers match its size. Start-up still pays for the fixed per-slot tables, about 232 bytes a slot: the connection-ID index takes 184, the timer wheel 20, and the signature, state, ready, dirty, queued and free tables 28. `connection(slot)` and `quic(slot)` build a slot that is not yet built, and every slot before it, so a program that binds to each slot up front keeps working. A slot built after `stop` is released as soon as it is made, so `stop`'s wipe still covers it.

The interop server and `examples/relay` still bind a `WebTransport` to every slot at start-up, which builds every slot. So their resident memory does not fall yet: 258 MB before and 261 MB after at 1,024 `h3` slots, the median of 3 runs. Binding lazily there is a follow-up in the same plan.

entries.title: record the handshake-time baseline and the bar for P-256's scalar inversion
entries.body:
`bench/tls-handshake.mjs` measures the server CPU of a TLS 1.3 handshake. That handshake uses X25519 and h2 with an ECDSA P-256 certificate, and runs against `net_interop_server`.
- **Each round:** 600 fresh `curl --http2 --tlsv1.3` handshakes, taken after 5 warm-ups. The server is pinned to CPU 0 and curl to CPUs 1–3, and the CPU time is read from `/proc/<pid>/stat`.
- **The noise band:** each target is timed against a byte-identical copy of itself, and the rounds are interleaved and rotate. `--baseline <rev>` adds a target built from another commit.

`docs/wp34-hosting-cs.md` adds "K5: P-256, the inversion — the baseline". It records:
- handshake CPU on `c8a00d6` and on `a22a056`;
- a callgrind profile of one handshake, by module and by P-256 function;
- the `p256` bench against `a22a056`.

It also fixes the bar the scalar inversion will be judged by, before the inversion is built:
1. `p256ScalarInvert` at or under 77,634 Ir, a tenth of its 776,344.
2. P-256 below X25519 in self Ir.
3. Signing at least 3x faster than `a22a056`, outside a fixed 4.2% band, in both samples. Verify no more than 4.3% slower.
4. Server CPU per handshake below `c8a00d6`'s, outside a fixed 1.67% band (two ticks), in both samples.

Each band is the largest absolute copy gap this baseline measured. The formulas govern, and the figures beside them are worked examples.

entries.title: TCP_NODELAY on accepted sockets, as tcpListenFlags flag 2
entries.body:
`tcpListenFlags(host, port, backlog, flags)` takes a new flag, `2`. Every connection `tcpAccept` takes from such a listener has `TCP_NODELAY` set, so Nagle's algorithm no longer holds a small answer back for a round trip — what a pipelined HTTP/1.1 server such as WP39's TechEmpower entry wants. Flags add, so `3` is `SO_REUSEPORT` plus `TCP_NODELAY`. Flags `0` and `1` behave exactly as before, and any other bit, a negative word included, is still `-22`.

The option is set on the listener and, because only Linux copies it to an accepted socket, set again by `tcpAccept` on every connection it hands out. The listener is the record of the flag: `tcpAccept` reads it back with `getsockopt` rather than keeping a table beside the descriptors, so it holds however the program came by the descriptor and a reused descriptor number leaves nothing stale. A set that fails closes the new socket and returns the error, so no connection is handed out without the option. The cost is one `getsockopt` per accept on every listener; `runtime-net.c`'s `-Oz` text stays under its 2,560-byte budget.

A runtime unit test pins the accept-side set on Linux, where inheritance would otherwise hide it: the option is put on the listener only after the handshake has completed, so the connection reads 1 only if `tcpAccept` set it. The test was checked by disabling that code and watching it fail.

entries.title: build TlsTcpServer's and Http1TlsServer's slots on first accept
entries.body:
`TlsTcpServer` and `Http1TlsServer` used to build every slot at start-up: each slot's `TlsRecordServer`, its server random and, for `Http1TlsServer`, its `Http1Connection`. A pool sized for its peak paid for that peak before its first connection. Now a slot is built on the first accept into it and kept, as `Http1Server` already does. The descriptors grow by push up to a high-water mark, and closed slots go on a free stack. `accept` takes the top of the free stack, else the next never-used slot, else answers `TLS_TCP_POOL_FULL`. Accept order (0, 1, 2, …), O(1) slot finding, `size()` and the pool-full answer are unchanged.

Building a slot allocates its record server over a `TlsServer` that holds a placeholder zero key and the slot's own random, and marks the slot failed, so a stray call on a free slot answers as before. Neither placeholder ever reaches a handshake: every accept copies fresh randomness into the slot and restarts it with the server's key, as a reused slot always was. Handshake security is therefore unchanged. Tickets enabled before a slot exists are applied when it is built.

A slot never built holds no descriptor. It answers done to every call, and -22 to reads and writes. Its `connection()` is `vacant`, one shared, failed connection that no slot holds. `vacant` has no ALPN and is not open, so `alpn` and `refused` read `""` and `false` on both TLS servers, `Http2TlsServer`'s included. They never read another client's slot 0. A slot out of range still names slot 0's connection. `Http1TlsServer`'s `readable`, `next` and `flush` read a slot only once its HTTP/1.1 connection is built (`live`), as `Http2TlsServer` does.
metrics: a 16,384-slot TlsTcpServer takes 41,640 bytes before its first connection, Http1TlsServer 58,296 (ceilings 41,728 and 58,368); interop-server RSS at 1,024 slots: h1s 31.2 -> 4.6 MB, h2 78.2 -> 27.8 MB, all pools 358.7 -> 281.7 MB; listening at 1,024 h1s slots 21 -> 6 ms; noise band (each build against a byte-identical copy, interleaved): within 0.1 MB and 2 ms

entries.title: add the crypto twin harness with the hash kernels
entries.body:
`bench/crypto/run.mjs` times `nish/crypto` against OpenSSL 3, Go, Rust (RustCrypto) and Node's `crypto`. It reads each family from a `bench/crypto/<family>/family.json`, and this first family is the hashes: SHA-256 and SHA-512 at 64 B, 1 KiB and 1 MiB, HMAC-SHA256 and HKDF-SHA256.

Every twin draws the same inputs from one generator, written once per language in `bench/crypto/lib/`. Each changes its input on every iteration and folds every output byte into an FNV-1a checksum, so the benchmark doubles as a differential test. `--validate` holds every twin to the checksums pinned in the family's `expected.txt`.

Every assembly twin has a portable column beside it: `OPENSSL_ia32cap` masks, Go's `purego` tag and RustCrypto's soft backends. The runner proves each mask took effect, by different bytes and by a measured slowdown on a CPU the mask reaches. Columns are timed in balanced interleaved rounds, beside a byte-identical copy of the Nish binary that gives the noise band.

The runner accounts for every column. Each one ran, or says why not: the family has no such twin, or this machine has no toolchain for it, or one too old, or no registry access. The `crypto-bench` check in `tests/run.js` takes that account as given. On GitHub's x86-64 runners it also requires every twin to run and the OpenSSL and Go proofs to be measured.

`node bench/run.mjs --only crypto` delegates to the new runner. Its full runs carry the crypto section of `docs/BENCHMARKS.md` over unchanged.

entries.title: a TechEmpower-shaped json and plaintext entry, measured against the HTTP twins
entries.body:
WP39 E5: `bench/techempower/` is a one-core Nish server, one `pollWait` loop on `Http1Server`, that answers the TechEmpower Framework Benchmarks' `json` and `plaintext` tests the way the TFB verifier checks them.

- `GET /json` returns `{"message":"Hello, World!"}`. A `JsonWriter` writes it into a reused buffer on every request, because TFB forbids caching the serialization.
- `GET /plaintext` returns `Hello, World!`. Sixteen pipelined requests are answered in order.
- Every response carries `Server`, an IMF-fixdate `Date` from `HttpDate`, and `Content-Length`. Any other path gets a 404, and a malformed request gets a 400.
- Accepted sockets set `TCP_NODELAY` through `tcpListenFlags` flag 2 (#770).
- When the process runs out of descriptors, the listener leaves the poll set and is retried on a bounded wait, so the server neither spins nor hangs.

The entry has no `using a = arena()` pass scope. NL2424 refuses one around a serve that stores into `Http1Server`'s slots. Instead, the verifier case checks that `Arena.used()` moves by nothing on every call across 200 warmed requests.

`tests/link/tfb_entry` runs the verifier's header and body rules over loopback in `npm test`. It overwrites the JSON buffer between requests, so a cached body fails the case. It also covers pipelining, the 404 and 400 answers, a pool of zero slots, and the paused listener. `bench/techempower/run.sh` times the entry against a byte-identical copy of it (the noise band) and every HTTP twin in `bench/http-twins/`, under wrk, in interleaved rounds. A failed measurement is recorded as n/a, never as 0. The upstream `nish.dockerfile` and `benchmark-config.json` are written but not submitted: submitting is the owner's call (WP39 D1). Multi-core waits for #719's prefork supervisor.
metrics: one entry core, client-shared on 4 cores (server on CPU 0, wrk on CPUs 1-3), 3 interleaved rounds of 10 s. `/plaintext` (16 pipelined): medians 290,467 to 324,456 req/s from 256 to 16384 connections; below `uws` at every level, and below `go-fasthttp` from 256 to 4096. `/json`: ahead of every twin at every level by more than the band; the narrowest lead is 11.4% over `uws` at 16 connections (62,677 against 55,513, band 1.4%). The noise band, entry against its copy, is 0.4-1.4% on `/plaintext` and 0.1-6.0% on `/json`. `TCP_NODELAY` against the same build with it off: faster outside the band at four levels (`/plaintext` 256 +2.0%, 4096 +0.9%; `/json` 128 +7.5%, 256 +8.2%), within it at the other six, and slower at none, so it is on by default.

entries.title: define the struct an imported generic's inferred result names
entries.body:
A local whose type is inferred from a call to an imported generic, such as
`const key = secret(bytes)` from `nish:secret` or `const b = box(7)` with
`box` from another module, now compiles to IR that assembles and runs. Before
this, the instantiated struct (`Secret$arr.u8`, `Secret$$Leaf`, `Box$i32`) was
minted in the declaring module and never registered in the calling one. Only an
annotation reached `instantiateStruct`, so the unannotated local named an
undefined `%struct` and `llvm-as` refused the module (#613).

`instantiate` now registers, in the module that asks, every struct its
instantiated signature's result and parameters name. That is the same
`registerForeignLayouts` path an annotation takes, and it registers the
constructor and methods with the layout. What a module is owed no longer
depends on the order in which an instance first reached it. A struct first
received as a type argument, layout only, gains its `declare`s when a later
request needs them, and so does every struct in its closure: fields, arrays,
nullables, `Result`s, and nested instances. A module never declares a symbol it
defines itself, and a library copy such as `std/secret` keeps skipping the
symbols it defines.

NL2445, the error for reading a local after `secret(...)` moved it, now names
what the local held: the array, or its class or interface, instead of always
saying "the plain array".

entries.title: refuse an object literal typed as a class with methods
entries.body:
An object literal can no longer stand for a class that has methods. Natively such a literal took the class's layout, so its methods dispatched. Under Node it was a plain object with no prototype, so a method call on it threw `TypeError`, and the two disagreed (#656). The checker now refuses it with NL2556, and the message names the remedy:

```
`Counter` has methods, so it is made only by `new`: an object literal would be a plain object under Node, with none of the methods the class is used through. Write `new Counter(...)`
```

The check sits at the top of `checkObjectLiteral`, the one place an object literal is typed against its context, so every route that hands a class type to a literal reaches it: declarations, `return` and arrow bodies, call, method, `new` and compile-time function arguments, array elements, `push`, `indexOf` and index assignment, `Map.set`, fields of an enclosing literal, assignments and compound assignments, ternary arms, parentheses, every branch of `??`, `===` operands, `Math.min`/`Math.max`, unary operands, nullable targets, type aliases, imported classes and generic classes. A generic method counts as a method; a constructor does not.

Literals stay legal for a class with fields alone and for an interface, since Node agrees with native for both. The `nish/threads` classes keep NL2515, and a class holding a `Secret` keeps NL2545.

Fixes #656

entries.title: invert P-256's nonce by constant-time safegcd instead of Fermat
entries.body:
`p256Sign` and `p256SignSha256Into` now invert the ECDSA nonce modulo the group order with a fixed-iteration Bernstein–Yang safegcd. Before this they computed k^(n−2) by Fermat, which was 24% of a signature's instructions and the largest cost left in the TLS server's CertificateVerify once the comb (#663) had sped up k·G.

**The port.** It follows libsecp256k1 v0.6.0's constant-time `modinv32` (MIT; `std/crypto/LICENSE-libsecp256k1`):
- 9 signed-30 limbs and 20 batches of 30 divsteps, against the proven bound of 590 for 256-bit inputs;
- a branch-free transition matrix per batch, applied to f and g and to d and e mod n;
- then a normalisation.

The divsteps invert aR, and one Montgomery multiply by R³ mod n returns a⁻¹R to fiat's scalar domain. Every select is a mask and every product is i32×i32→i64, which wasm32 has natively. No branch or address depends on the nonce, every loop count is a constant, and there is no divide. Fermat's `p256ScalarInvert` stays: it is the reference the new function is held to, and verify's public `s⁻¹`.

**Verified by disassembly.** `ct_asm_p256` reads copies of one 30-divstep batch and both matrix updates on x86-64, aarch64 and x86-64 at `x86-64-v3`. A `tests/run.js` check holds the divstep copy to the module's loop body text. A seeded `leakyDivstep`, the `if` form, is refused as a branch on all three.

**Agreement and wipes.** The new inverse matches Fermat bit for bit on 10,794 scalars, natively and as the `--profile wasi` build under Node. The scalars are 0, 1, n−1, powers of two, limb boundaries and a 10,000-scalar seeded corpus. The inverse's intermediates d, e, f, g and t are wiped. d, e and f are counted by the wipe groups. g and t, which `opt -O2` turns into volatile stores, have a check of their own that fails if either wipe is deleted.

`.github/workflows/release.yml` names the new licence file in its three presence gates.
metrics: 776,501 → 33,661 Ir per inversion (23.1x fewer), callgrind, net of seam overhead

entries.title: keep field-initialiser stores in an empty explicit constructor
entries.body:
A constructor's prologue stores the class's field initialisers, a
discriminated-union variant's tag among them, into `this` before the
body runs. The attribute analysis walked only the written body, so a
constructor whose body stored no field itself was marked as never
writing memory and its `this` as `readonly`. At `-O2` LLVM then deleted
the prologue stores, and the object came back holding zeros: natively,
`class Dn { n: i32 = 7; constructor() {} }` printed `0` where Node
prints `7`.

The analysis now counts those prologue stores as writes to `this`, the
same facts a body `this.n = 7` gives. Like that store, they initialise
the fresh object, so they are not a shared write and the constructor
keeps every other attribute it had. A constructor with no initialiser,
and a method that only reads `this`, keep `readonly`.

entries.title: nish/net/url, percent-decoding and query-string parsing
entries.body:
* feat(std): nish/net/url, percent-decoding and query-string parsing

`nish/net/url` reads a request target the way a handler needs to: it splits a
path into segments, percent-decodes them and reads a query string as key/value
pairs. The byte API allocates nothing. It works in place on a window of the
caller's bytes: `urlQueryStart`, `percentDecode`, `percentDecodeErrorAt`,
`percentDecodePathSegment`, the reusable iterators `UrlPathSegments` and
`UrlQuery`, and `urlQueryFind`. `urlDecode` and `urlQueryGet` are the string
forms, for code that wants an answer rather than offsets.

Decoding is strict unless asked otherwise. With no flags, a `%` not followed
by two hex digits and `%00` are refused with a negative code, and `+` stays
`+`. Each repair is a flag of its own: `URL_DECODE_LENIENT` copies a
malformed escape as it stands, `URL_DECODE_FORM` reads `+` as a space and
`URL_DECODE_ALLOW_NUL` lets `%00` through. All three together read a query
as `URLSearchParams` does. A path is split on the raw `/` before it is
decoded, so `%2F` never starts a segment. A query yields at most
`UrlQueryLimits.maxPairs` pairs, 100 by default. Past the cap, `next()`
answers `URL_QUERY_ERR_PAIRS` and stays spent, so a target full of `&` costs
one linear scan. Nothing a peer sends panics. Only a window outside its array
does, which is the caller's bug.

The byte API does not check that the bytes it decodes are UTF-8, and the
string forms do. A repeated key is answered by its first value. A refused
decode leaves the bytes it wrote before the refusal. These three are recorded
as accepted in docs/security/url.md, with the divergences from Node.

Measured: 10,000 changing targets split, decoded and searched with Arena.used() unmoved; 3,000 seeded inputs agree with decodeURIComponent, URLSearchParams and the strict rule, natively and under Node, byte for byte
Refs: docs/guide/using-nish/standard-library.md#nishneturl, docs/security/url.md
Tests: tests/link/std_url, tests/link/std_url_escape, tests/link/std_url_pairs, tests/link/std_url_space, tests/link/std_url_window

* ci(release): ship std/net/url.ts in the release presence gates

The three presence gates in release.yml name every std module so that
none can ship missing; nish/net/url is added to each.

* test(std): windowed escapes and a non-ASCII url fuzz corpus

`std_url` now cuts `ab%41` after the `%` and after the `%4`, so the
bytes past the window would complete the escape. `percentDecode`,
`percentDecodePathSegment` and a query value each refuse the cut
escape at 2, and copy it as `%` or `%4` when lenient. A key cut before
its escape's last digit matches nothing. Changing the window guard in
`percentDecode` to read past the window now fails `std_url` both
natively and under Node.

The seeded fuzz corpus mixes UTF-8 sequences into its alphabet, valid
and invalid, escaped in either case or written as raw bytes. The
invalid ones are overlong, a surrogate, past U+10FFFF, a lone
continuation, truncated, and `0xFF`. `decodeURIComponent` must throw
exactly where the strict bytes are not UTF-8, and must give the same
bytes everywhere else, multi-byte included. `std_url` also pins one
multi-byte decode as hex.

`urlQueryFind`'s `name` is documented as ASCII, a divergence from Node
now recorded in the guide and in the security record. The guide says
`URL_DECODE_ERR_SPACE` comes from a buffer shorter than the decoded
result. The release check counts sixty-eight required paths.

Refs: docs/security/url.md
Tests: tests/link/std_url

* test(std): pin urlDecode's UTF-8 check and the nish/net/url guards

The string forms' RFC 3629 check now runs through the fixed cases and
the seeded fuzz, which compares `urlDecode` with `decodeURIComponent`
and `urlQueryGet` with `URLSearchParams.get`. Each boundary of the check
is pinned: the F4 upper bound, the E0 and F0 lower bounds, truncation,
and the continuation loop.

Four panic programs pin the window and `at` guards of `percentDecode`,
`urlQueryStart` and `UrlPathSegments.reset`, under Node and natively.
The query finder gains prefix-key cases. The guide and the module
header guard a target with no `?`. The docs say `URLSearchParams`
matches for valid UTF-8, and name `percentDecodeErrorAt`.

Refs: docs/security/url.md
Tests: tests/link/std_url

* test(std): pin url windows, hex edges and every UTF-8 lead; guard the guide's decode

The guide's `route` example and the `nish/net/url` header now test every
negative answer before reading `out`, and the guide's run includes a
malformed `?name=%zz` and a malformed segment, so the example shows the
refusal rather than a panic in `String.fromBytes`.

`tests/link/std_url` gains path-segment windows at a non-zero offset where
the bytes around the window would change the answer, one of them not
starting with `/`; the bytes either side of each hex range (`:`, `@`,
`` ` ``, `G`), strict and lenient; each unrestricted UTF-8 lead well formed
and with a byte past its continuation range; and panics for a negative
`len` and a negative `at`. The fuzz alphabet and sequences carry the same
edges, and `docs/security/url.md` cites each line.

Tests: tests/link/std_url

* docs(std): state exactly what the url panics and Node runs pin

The record now names which program pins each panic and how it is run, counts the four refusal programs apart from the six panic programs, and states the input half of the Node divergence: a code unit above 0xFF makes urlDecode and urlQueryGet answer null under Node, where the native build decodes the string's UTF-8 bytes.

entries.title: warn NL8003 on a record copy reached through an alias or a helper
entries.body:
NL8003 warns when a record copied into an array is written on one side and read on the other, since TypeScript shares the object and a native build holds two copies. Until now it saw only the copy's own names, and only writes in the function being checked. So `const q = p` read after a write through `ps[0]` went quiet, as did a helper that wrote an element (`setFirst(ps)`), wrote the record (`bump(p)`) or did the copy itself (`add(ps, p)`). Native and Node printed different answers in each case.

The row now follows a `const` alias of a record back to the binding it names. It also reads the body of each function a call or `new` reaches in the same module, to learn what that function does with each record or array of records it is handed: write a field, copy the record into an array, or store into the array. It follows the callee's own calls up to eight deep, reads a recursion once, and treats a method or constructor as a call. A call that writes, or copies into an array it stores into, counts as a write or a copy at the call. A callee the row cannot read (imported, generic, a function value, or a builtin other than the read-only array methods) may do anything with what it is handed.

Fixes #620
Part of #763

entries.title: re-take the Rust and Go parallel table and add an atomic par-histogram
entries.body:
The "Data parallelism against Rust and Go" table in `docs/BENCHMARKS.md` is re-measured on current `main`, three runs of eleven interleaved rounds after a warm-up, each binary beside a byte-identical copy that sets the band.

A fifth twinned kernel, `par-histogram-atomic`, bins the same four streams as `par-histogram` into an `AtomicI32` per bin with one sequentially consistent `add` per value, where `par-histogram` takes a `Mutex` per value. Its Rust twins use `AtomicI32::fetch_add` with `SeqCst` (on `std::thread::scope` and on `rayon::scope`) and its Go twin `atomic.Int32.Add`; all print `56760 3200000`, the lock version's checksum.

Nish loses this one: 1.59x to 1.95x behind Rust on the minimum, past 1.10x in all three runs, and level with Go. Taking the lock out moves Rust from 308 ms to 61 and Go from 194 to 93, and Nish only from 116 to 101. `bench/README.md` says what differs in the program (Nish's overflow and bounds checks per value, and bins reached as objects through the task rather than inline counters) and that which of them costs it is not yet measured.

par-nbody fell from level with Rayon (0.96x to 1.06x at a1a5bf8a) to 1.11x to 1.17x behind it. Part of that is #731, which cuts a divided region into up to eight pieces per thread: the same par-nbody IR linked against the runtime from just before #731 and from b1bf78f is slower outside the copy band in every run. #743 does not touch it, since a number map never calls `nish_cross_keep` and its binary links byte-identical to #731's. The rest of the move is the machine between sessions. Which part of #731 costs it is not measured; the partitioner is not changed here.

entries.title: follow aliases of an element reference in NL2290
entries.body:
NL2290 refuses a reference to an array element that is read after a push
may have moved the array's storage. It tracked only a local initialised
straight from an element read (`const p = ps[0]`), so `const q = p` gave
the same element a second name the check never followed. Reading `q`
after the push compiled, and native code read freed storage.

A local now takes on the element references of whatever it is
initialised or assigned from:

- a `const q = p` alias, and so a chain of them
- either side of `c ? p : p2` and of `m ?? p`
- `q = p` inside an `if`, loop or `switch` body: a block drops only the
  references bound to locals it declared itself, so an alias assigned
  there outlives the block as its local does

An assignment that is a statement of its own block replaces what its
local was bound to in that block (`q = ps[0]; q = { x: 3 }` holds no
reference); one in an enclosing block stays, since the inner block may
not have run. A call's result does not carry the references passed to
it: a helper given an element may return a copy (`clone(ps[0])`), and
refusing it would be a false positive.

A read of any alias after the push is refused, wherever the read sits,
nested blocks included. An alias that is dead before the push still
compiles.

Fixes #646
Part of #763

entries.title: read the P-256 inversion bar on main
entries.body:
`docs/wp34-hosting-cs.md` adds "K5: P-256, the inversion — the result". It measures `main` at `2a5912d`, which has the constant-time safegcd nonce inversion from #780. The method is the one the baseline section (#772) fixed, and so is the bar, read here exactly as written with nothing tuned:
- **Profile:** one TLS 1.3 handshake under callgrind.
- **`bench/tls-handshake.mjs`:** two samples against `c8a00d6` and `a22a056`, each with a byte-identical copy.
- **`bench/p256.mjs`:** two samples against the same builds.

All four conditions are met:
1. **The scalar inversion.** `p256ScalarInverse` is 33,620 Ir in a handshake, against a bar of 77,634 and Fermat's 776,344, 23.1x fewer.
2. **P-256 below X25519.** P-256 is 2,465,352 Ir against X25519's 3,147,968, and it is no longer the largest module in the handshake: X25519 is now, at 43.7–44.6%, against P-256's 34.2–34.9%.
3. **Sign at least 3x faster than `a22a056`, outside the fixed 4.2% band, in both samples.** Its minimum is 226.6 and 219.4 µs, against bars of 267.9 and 271.5: 3.70x and 3.87x faster. Verify is not slower than `c8a00d6`.
4. **Server CPU per handshake below `c8a00d6`'s, outside the fixed two-tick band (1.67%), in both samples.** It is 2,317 and 2,433 µs, against bars of 2,343.9 and 2,459.0: 2.8% and 2.7% under, four ticks against a band of two.

The record discloses one caveat. In the first sample, `main`'s own byte-identical copy ran 2.9% under `main`, more than its 2.8% margin over `c8a00d6`. That sample's handshake gain is therefore inside its own copy's noise, although the band fixed in advance governs the verdict. §5a's K5 row now records what landed. It also records what is left: the field inversion `p256FieldInvert`, now 22.4% of the signature; 64-bit limbs; and the verify path.

entries.title: narrow a discriminated union by testing its tag
entries.body:
The checker now narrows a discriminated union by testing its tag, as
TypeScript does. Inside `if (s.kind === Kind.Circle) { ... }`, `s` is a
`Circle`, and its fields and methods read through it. In the `else`, and
after an `if` whose body always leaves, `s` holds the variants that remain.
Codegen reads a variant's field through the narrowed variable with a bitcast
of the union's pointer.

Narrowing follows `===` and `!==` either way round, the `if` and the `else`,
a ternary, `&&` and `||`, each `case` of a `switch (s.kind)` (with `default`
holding the variants no `case` named), the code after an early `return`,
`break`, `continue` or `panic(...)`, and a test through an assignment such as
`(t = next()).kind === Kind.Square`.

Plain enums narrow the same way: any enum-typed variable, a parameter
`k: Kind` as much as a tag local, narrows in every form above and in
`switch (k)`. Before this change Nish accepted a second `k === Kind.A` after
`if (k === Kind.A) return`, which `tsc` refuses as TS2367. Comparisons the
earlier tests have ruled out, a tag no variant has, and a dead `case` are now
refused, as TypeScript refuses them (TS2367, TS2678).

The checker also tracks:

- property paths and single-element indexes (`h.s.kind`, `xs[0]`, `xs[i]`
  with an unassigned `i`, a module constant index), dropped on a store to the
  path, a prefix or its root;
- the join of every exit of an `if`, ternary, `switch` and `||`/`&&`;
- loops, through a side-effect-free dataflow pre-pass (`src/loop-flow.ts`)
  that computes each loop head's state before the one real check of the body.
  Anything the pass cannot read is widened to its declared type, and an
  always-on internal assertion proves the state it imposed covers every state
  the checker then reaches, so a narrowed read can never miscompile. The few
  shapes the pass reads more loosely than `tsc` are listed in LANGUAGE.md and
  pinned in `enum_loop_join_gap`.

Stricter than TypeScript, each documented and pinned by a reject case: no
field read through a narrowed property path (NL2558), no `never` type for a
variable whose tests excluded every variant (NL2557), and a tag typed with the
whole enum is refused (NL2559).

`src/` uses no union or narrowing in its own source, so the rolling freeze
holds. `tests/perf-baseline.json` admits one NL9011 for `src/loop-flow.ts`.

Verification: the full `npm test` passed on a168140 (23,072 passed, 0
failed; skips are the container's missing WASI sysroot and aarch64 `crt1.o`,
which CI has). The final head 01dcb01, with main at f950e4a merged and the
checked goldens regenerated, is 26/26 green in CI, which runs the whole
suite, `wasi` and the performance ratchet. About 5,600 programs were checked
against `tsc --strict --noImplicitReturns` over seven review rounds, with
node running `tsc`'s output as the oracle: no variant read is accepted that
`tsc` rejects, and no output differs.

entries.title: switch on a union's tag, with exhaustiveness
entries.body:
A `switch` on a discriminated union's tag now narrows each clause to the
variants its labels name, and `default` to the ones they leave out. A switch
whose labels name every variant, with no `default`, counts as complete. When
every clause leaves, the switch ends the path, so a non-void function may end
with it, as `tsc --noImplicitReturns` allows:

```ts
const area = (s: Shape): f64 => {
  switch (s.kind) {
    case Kind.Circle: return 3.14159 * s.r * s.r;
    case Kind.Square: return s.side * s.side;
  }
};
```

Leave a case out and both Nish and `tsc` refuse the function for a missing
return. The LLVM `switch` of a complete union switch sends its default to a
block holding only `unreachable`. That is sound because a variant's tag is
`readonly` and can be written only with its own member, so no other value
can reach the switch.

Whether a switch is complete depends on what its subject is, not on what a
path currently holds. Only these are complete:

- a read of a union's own tag field (`s.kind`, `h.s.kind`, `xs[i].kind`,
  `get().kind`) whose labels name every tag of the whole union
- a tagged local narrowed to the variants its labels name

A plain enum switch, a tag copied into an enum local or field, and a path
narrowed by an earlier test stay open and still need a trailing `return` or
a `default`. Plain enum and integer switches lower byte-identically; no
existing `.ll` golden moved. A `Secret` wiped in every clause of a complete
switch is accepted, and a clause that misses the wipe is refused.

BREAKING CHANGE: code after a `switch` that covers every variant of a union's
tag is now unreachable and is refused with NL2251. A program that kept a
trailing `return` after such a `switch` deletes that line.

Verification on 5745090: CI 21/21 green. Locally the union (255), switch
(107), enum (315), self (198), differential (22), performance (223) and wasi
(67, no skips) sections, plus check, lint and lint:dead. The full `npm test`
on 1ec6fe4 passed 23,154, with only a timing-ratio bench failing, which
passes alone. Review probes ran about 250 programs against `tsc` with node as
the output oracle, and re-linked every accepted one with its `sw.unreachable`
patched to trap. None fired.
