entries.title: keep the checked goldens one file per module, with body-relative lines
entries.body:
`tests/self/goldens/checked.txt` and `checked-self.txt` were two files that
nearly every pull request touching `src/`, `std/` or `tests/cases/` rewrote,
so two open pull requests conflicted there however unrelated they were. Four
things made that so, and each is gone:

- **A running count in each header** (`# 1087 programs, 158805 dump lines.`)
  changed with every added case, so any two such pull requests conflicted on
  it.
- **Absolute line numbers.** A `local` or `callee` line named its position in
  the file, so one line added near the top of `src/checker.ts` rewrote every
  later position in the module. Positions are now counted from the first one
  in their body (`local +4:14`): a line moves only when its own function does,
  and the column and every position relative to the body are still pinned.
- **Two large files.** The dump is now one file per module, at the module's own
  path (`checked/src/checker.ts.txt`, `checked/tests/cases/add_plain.ts.txt`),
  so git merges two changes to two different modules by itself.
- **The corpus outside `src/` stored whole dumps per program**, so a change to
  one `std/` module was written out again under every case that imported it.
  Every program is now deduplicated by module the way `src/` already was; the
  generator still runs all of them, reads every byte, and fails if two
  programs dump one module differently.

A program's own file opens with its `entry` line (the modules it loaded, in
load order) or its `reject` line (the wording it was refused with).
`--update` removes the file of a module that left the corpus, and the check
fails on one rather than comparing nothing. Without `--verbose`, a failing run
shows the differing lines of its first five files only.

An open pull request picks this up by merging `main`, removing the two old
files where git reports modify/delete, and running
`node tests/self/goldens.js --update`.
metrics: a line added at the top of src/checker.ts moved 790 golden lines before and moves 0 now; 1,237 golden files, 13.3 MB, against 13.5 MB in the two files before

entries.title: enforce QUIC's AEAD limits and detect optimistic ACKs
entries.body:
A QUIC server connection now keeps the AEAD limits of RFC 9001 §6.6 and detects optimistic ACKs, as RFC 9000 §21.4 suggests. This closes QUIC-6 and QUIC-7 in `docs/security/quic.md`.

- **Confidentiality limit.** The server counts the packets sealed under the current 1-RTT write key. Under AES-GCM it starts a key update itself from three quarters of the 2^23-packet limit. A connection that reaches the limit with no update possible closes with AEAD_LIMIT_REACHED, and nothing more is sealed under that key. ChaCha20-Poly1305 has no confidentiality limit.
- **Integrity limit.** Packets that fail to authenticate are counted across every key for the life of the connection. The first failure past 2^52 (AES-GCM) or 2^36 (ChaCha20-Poly1305) closes the connection with AEAD_LIMIT_REACHED.
- **Skipped packet numbers.** Once the 1-RTT keys are in, the server skips one Application Data packet number in every 128 to 1024, drawn from the connection's ID seed. It remembers the last eight, and an ACK whose ranges include one is closed as PROTOCOL_VIOLATION.

The test clients now acknowledge only the 1-RTT packets they received. `QuicConnection`'s new fields are ordered widest first, so its size stays 584 bytes.

Part of #474
Part of #759

entries.title: run runtime-net.c's Darwin branch on a macOS runner
entries.body:
`runtime/runtime-net.c` keeps a Darwin branch: kqueue in place of epoll, `SO_NOSIGPIPE` in place of `MSG_NOSIGNAL`, and errno translated to Linux's numbers. CI's Darwin `bootstrap` rows compiled that branch, but no job ran it. A new job, `runtime-net (macos-latest)`, on an AArch64 mac, now runs the runtime unit tests (plain and threaded) and every `net_` check. Each fix below is pinned by a check that failed on that runner.

- **kqueue answers like epoll.** The Darwin poll loop now folds kqueue's per-filter records into epoll's answers: a repeated add answers -17, a descriptor watching nothing can be modified or removed, and one ready both ways comes back as one pair.
- **TLS flights are read whole.** Darwin's loopback hands over each TCP write on its own, so the client now reads until the flight ends in its Finished.
- **`H1Loop.connect` waits for the accept**, since Darwin can report the SYN-ACK before the listener is readable.
- **Arena growth is measured with `Arena.mark()`**, the absolute bump address, rather than the offset into the current chunk, a bug Linux shared without having hit a chunk boundary yet.
- **The checks drop Linux-only facts.** They account for `ru_maxrss` in bytes, for `ps` where there is no `/proc`, and for GSO/GRO being absent. Section GC links with `-dead_strip` on Darwin. Two runtime-object links write one output path, because ld64's `LC_UUID` depends on it. The relay's offload check names state both arms. `net_tls_tcp`'s GET is now made by Node's `https`, since macOS's curl cannot pin a TLS 1.3 suite.

The two runtime unit test checks now run under their own `runtime_test` filter.

Fixes #358
Part of #751

entries.title: add npm run sync-main and run CI in the merge queue
entries.body:
Bringing `main` into an open pull request used to take five steps by hand: fetch, merge, `git rm` each modify/delete conflict in the self-goldens, `node tests/self/goldens.js --update`, and `node tests/differential/goldens.js --update`. `npm run sync-main` (`scripts/sync-main.mjs`) does all of them.

It removes each conflicted file under `tests/self/goldens/` so that regeneration writes it fresh, runs both generators and stages what they wrote. It never commits: the staged diff is read before `git commit --no-edit`. Any other conflict stops the script with the merge left open, and `-- --continue` resumes once it is resolved and added. The frozen differential store counts as such a conflict, because a deleted `rewrites.txt` would unfreeze every program.

CI, `pr-title.yml` and `pr-body.yml` now also run on `merge_group`, so with the merge queue switched on in `main`'s ruleset each pull request is tested on top of the ones queued ahead of it. Two pull requests green against `main` alone could otherwise be red together, because the goldens and the `.ll` they share move without a textual conflict (#549 after #547). The title and body checks skip their step in the queue and report success. The lockfile check knows the Release PR there by its commit subject. `interop.yml` is path-filtered and stays off the queue.

entries.title: non-blocking spawn, kill, waitPid, availableParallelism and totalMemory
entries.body:
* feat(runtime): non-blocking spawn, kill, waitPid, availableParallelism and totalMemory

`nish:process` gains what a supervisor needs to run a pool of worker
processes. `spawn(argv)` starts a child and answers its pid, or a negative
errno, without waiting for it. `kill(pid, sig)` signals it, with `sig`
limited to 0, 2, 9 and 15 (anything else is -22). `waitPid(pid, flags)`
reaps it and answers `[pid, status]`. There, `status` is the exit code, or
128 plus the signal. A pid of -1 waits for any child, and flag 1 is
WNOHANG. `[0, 0]` means a child remains but none has exited, and a failure
answers `[-errno, 0]`.

Two host facts size the pool:

- `availableParallelism()` is at least 1 and needs no `--threads`.
- `totalMemory()` is the machine's physical memory in bytes, or -1.

`spawn`, `kill` and `waitPid` carry the `process.spawn` capability. The two
host facts carry none, because like `process.platform` they describe the
machine rather than reach anything. On wasm32 each builtin is refused with
NL2404. `nish_cpu_online` moves from runtime-parallel.c to runtime-os.c, so
an unthreaded program links it without the pool.

Measured: runtime-os.c .text 2,383 / 2,560 bytes; runtime-parallel.c threaded .text 2,325 / 2,560 bytes
Refs: docs/LANGUAGE.md#children-and-the-machine-spawn-kill-waitpid-availableparallelism-totalmemory
Tests: tests/cases/os_spawn, tests/cases/os_kill, tests/cases/os_wait, tests/cases/os_cpu, tests/cases/os_memory, tests/cases/caps_process_wait, tests/cases/caps_host, tests/cases/reject_os_*, tests/runtime-test.c test_process

* fix(codegen): keep the arena for a function returning waitPid, and reserve kill

`waitPid` answers a fresh `[pid, status]` array from the arena, so it joins
`isAllocatingBuiltin`: a function returning it no longer gets an automatic
arena scope that would release the pair before the caller reads it.
`kill`, which runtime-os.c now calls, is reserved in `isCLibrarySymbol`.

Tests: tests/cases/mem_wait_pid_scope

* test(runtime): regenerate caps_process_wait for the waitPid arena scope

The pair `stop` reads one element of is now released locally, and its
allocation is listed as a possible out-of-memory panic.

* docs(runtime): tidy the arena-scope comment and a blank line

* refactor(runtime): fold the wasi branch of spawnSync's wait and rewrap a comment

* revert(runtime): keep spawnSync's two wasi branches, which are 10 bytes smaller

The fold in fe31d7da grew runtime-os.c's .text* at -Oz from 2,383 to 2,393 bytes, which the figure in tests/runtime-budgets.js does not record.

* fix(runtime): count CPUs with sysctl hw.activecpu on Darwin

`nish_cpu_online` read `sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN)`, which Darwin's
headers hide at the `_POSIX_C_SOURCE` level runtime-os.c selects, so the
unit did not compile on macOS. Darwin now asks `sysctlbyname("hw.activecpu")`,
through the declaration `totalMemory` already uses; Linux and WASI are
unchanged, byte for byte after preprocessing.

* fix(runtime): drop willreturn from nish_kill and pin process builtins in tasks

`kill` of the program's own pid with 9 or 15 never returns, so
`nish_kill` is declared `nounwind` without `willreturn`. `spawn`,
`kill` and `waitPid` are now pinned as refused in a scope's task, in a
parallel body and under an import alias, and the two host facts as
allowed there. The IR cookbook gains a section for the five builtins,
and the docs say to test `pid > 0` before passing a pid on and to
supervise with WNOHANG on a `pollWait` tick, since a blocking wait
restarts through SIGTERM after `signalFd()`.

Refs: docs/LANGUAGE.md#children-and-the-machine-spawn-kill-waitpid-availableparallelism-totalmemory
Tests: tests/cases/reject_os_kill_task, tests/link/thread_host_facts_task

entries.title: prove OpenSSL's portable hash column on SHA-256 first, falling back to SHA-512
entries.body:
The `crypto-bench` check's portable proof timed OpenSSL against its
`OPENSSL_ia32cap`-masked run at SHA-512 over 1 MiB and required the masked
run to take 1.2x the time. SHA-512 has no SHA-NI path, so on GitHub's
runners the mask only moves OpenSSL from its AVX2 assembly to its scalar
one, which measured 1.17x to 1.19x, just under the gate. Pull requests that
never touched the hash family failed shard 1 on it.

`portableProof` now takes an ordered list of cases as well as a single one.
A twin is proved by the first case that reaches its ratio. Each case is
timed in 5 interleaved rounds and retried over 11, and a short case prints
`short … trying <next>` before moving on. Only the last case's shortfall
counts as `NOT PORTABLE`. The hash family proves on SHA-256 first, where a
SHA-NI CPU loses its SHA instructions under the mask, and falls back to
SHA-512 on a CPU without them. `portableProofFlags` gains `ssse3` and
`sha_ni`, the extensions OpenSSL's SHA-256 paths use.
metrics: openssl-portable at sha256@1048576 took 4.16x, 4.24x and 5.33x the time of openssl across three local validate runs, and go-purego 6.84x to 8.29x. openssl-portable at sha512@1048576 took 1.29x to 1.33x locally and 1.17x to 1.19x in CI runs 39538515030 and 39541277135.

entries.title: accept any crypto family's main.ts in the --only crypto forwarding check
entries.body:
The check that `bench/run.mjs --only crypto` hands its `--compiler` to

entries.title: time one full TLS 1.3 and one QUIC handshake against the twins
entries.body:
Adds the `handshake` family to the crypto twin harness (`bench/crypto/`): two kernels that each run client and server in one process and then echo one record. `tls13` is one full TLS 1.3 handshake (TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 over X25519, ECDSA-P256 leaf); `quic` is one QUIC v1 handshake to 1-RTT followed by a stream echo.

Nish uses std's `TlsRecordServer` and `QuicConnection` against the client from `tests/link`, which checks CertificateVerify against the parsed leaf. The twins are OpenSSL 3.0 (`tls13` only; it has no QUIC server), Go `crypto/tls` and quic-go, rustls and quinn-proto, and Node `node:tls` (`tls13` only). Only Go has a portable column (`-tags purego`); OpenSSL 3.0's P-256 and X25519 assembly ignores `OPENSSL_ia32cap`, so the family sets no `portableProof`. The README discloses Nish's fixed randoms and keys, the per-column setup differences and Node's session tickets.
metrics: tls13 449 op/s (Nish) vs 1,062 go-purego (2.364x slower) and 3,763 rust (8.375x slower); quic 401 vs 580 go-purego (1.446x slower) and 2,551 rust (6.356x slower); noise band 1.1%–5.3% against a byte-identical copy

entries.title: time X25519, P-256, Ed25519 and X.509 against the twins
entries.body:
Adds two families to the crypto twin harness (`bench/crypto/`), timing `std/crypto`'s public-key code against OpenSSL, Go, Rust and Node.

`curves` has six kernels: X25519 against the base point and a variable point, ECDSA P-256 sign and verify, and Ed25519 sign and verify. Every scalar goes in as a `Secret<u8[]>` and is wiped. `p256-sign` folds each digest and whether its signature verifies, since Go's and OpenSSL's ECDSA is randomised; the verify runs outside the clock. Both verify kernels cycle 16 signed messages, one tampered and required to answer false. std/crypto has no Ed25519, so those kernels run the twins only (#788 tracks it).

`x509` mints the certificate `x509MintSelfSigned` writes and parses a fixed 338-byte certificate, verifying its self-signature. Node has no mint, because `X509Certificate` cannot write one.

The portable columns are an OpenSSL `OPENSSL_ia32cap` mask (AVX, AVX2, BMI2 and ADX off), Go `-tags purego` and, for `curves`, Rust's serial and soft backends. `curves` proves the mask at `x25519@32`. `x509` sets no `portableProof`, because the mask moves OpenSSL by less than the noise there.
metrics: X25519 5,820 op/s (3.27x slower than openssl-portable's 19,008), P-256 sign 3,538 (9.58x slower), P-256 verify 698 (17.2x slower), X.509 mint 2,145 (1.69x slower), X.509 parse 687 (6.16x slower), on a Xeon 2.80 GHz with avx2, bmi2 and adx; noise bands 0.7%–8.3% against a byte-identical copy
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: time AES-128/256-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 against the twins
entries.body:
Adds the `aead` family to the crypto twin harness (`bench/crypto/`). It seals and opens AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 at 64 B, 1,350 B, 16 KiB and 1 MiB, against OpenSSL EVP, Go (`crypto/aes` GCM, `x/crypto/chacha20poly1305`), Rust (`aes-gcm`, `chacha20poly1305`) and Node `createCipheriv`.

Iteration `i` XORs `i` into the message and the nonce, so no nonce repeats. Each open kernel opens one entry of a ring of 16 messages sealed before the clock starts, so every timed open checks a real tag; a failed open exits 1. The portable columns are an `OPENSSL_ia32cap` mask that clears AES-NI, PCLMULQDQ and the SIMD bits, Go `-tags purego`, and Rust's soft backends. The proof is `aes128gcm-seal@16384`, gated on the `aes` and `pclmulqdq` flags. Node keys a cipher per message, because `node:crypto` keeps no expanded key across nonces; the README says so.
metrics: AES-128-GCM seal at 16 KiB 624 MB/s (1.107x slower than Go's 690), AES-GCM within 1.09x–1.20x of the fastest assembly twin from 1,350 B up and 1.3x–1.8x behind at 64 B; ChaCha20-Poly1305 2.4x–3.0x slower than OpenSSL, masked or not (16 KiB seal 187 vs 525 MB/s portable); Xeon 2.80 GHz, noise band 0.1%–12.6% against a byte-identical copy
